lineage: An early entry in Radcliffe's long solo catalogue that eventually feeds into the twangier Ohio Vision.
Grew out of Steiner and Sagan's college-band beginnings at Notre Dame; set the twangy-indie template the band expanded on GN and Printer's Devil.
Sounds part of the same Run for Cover/Topshelf-adjacent 2010s indie underground as Ratboys.
Bridges the band's early alt-country leanings with the bigger, distorted guitar sound they'd bring on Printer's Devil.
Sounds like an early sketch of the bedroom-recorded songwriting Lenderman developed on his Dear Life releases.
Grew out of Asheville's DIY bedroom-recording scene before Lenderman joined Wednesday full-time; a direct line to the funnier, sadder songwriting of Boat Songs and Manning Fireworks.
Marks the move from their earlier folk-adjacent sound toward the anthemic guitar rock of The Window and Singin' to an Empty Chair.
Sounds indebted to Parsons' Cosmic American Music and Neil Young; precedes the caustic barroom twang of The Holey Bible.
A Dear Life Records release recorded as Lenderman's own songwriting was starting to draw notice alongside his role in Wednesday.
Fits between Ghost of Your Guitar Solo and Boat Songs as Lenderman's songwriting sharpened toward the deadpan style that broke through in 2022.
A victory-lap record marking Ratboys' first decade before their Chris Walla-produced pivot.
A former LVL UP member's move toward twangier songwriting, released on Philadelphia's Lame-O Records alongside Slaughter Beach, Dog; its country tint sounds akin to the wider indie-twang turn.
Bandleader Tyler Jordan met Jake Ames at Kerrville Folk Festival song swaps (where they also crossed paths with Buck Meek and Adrianne Lenker); Keeled Scales labelmates of Katy Kirby.
Part of the Burlington, Vermont scene around Freeman and Lily Seabird; it set up his later label releases.
Builds directly on Neil Young & Crazy Horse's guitar tone and the deadpan-funny-sad lineage of Drag City songwriters; opened the door to Manning Fireworks and his growing profile in Wednesday.
Sounds rooted in the alt-country storytelling lineage of Townes Van Zandt and Jason Molina.
Part of the same Burlington scene as Greg Freeman; its songwriting sounds indebted to Judee Sill, Alex Chilton and Elliott Smith.
Part of the same Dear Life Records-era run of scrappy, caustic Philly country as The Holey Bible.
A Dear Life Records release that sounds of a piece with the indie-twang of Greg Freeman and Lily Seabird.
Captures the touring band that would carry over into the Manning Fireworks era, showing how the songs mutate on stage.
Sounds of a piece with Wednesday and MJ Lenderman in the current wave of twangy Midwest/Southern indie rock.
Farrar's production ties Squirrel Flower directly into the Asheville Drop of Sun network that also produced Wednesday and MJ Lenderman.
A UK band that sounds steeped in the American alt-country/Crazy Horse tradition, close in spirit to Wednesday and Greg Freeman.
Sounds indebted to the Neil Young/Crazy Horse and Molina/Magnolia Electric Co. lineage that defines indie twang.
Sounds like a Midwest continuation of the Crazy Horse guitar-jam trunk line that also runs through Wednesday and MJ Lenderman.

album: May You Live Forever in Cowboy Heaven
lineage: Sounds indebted to Neil Young and Silver Jews, sitting within the same trunk lines as the rest of the Core.
Continues the band's blue-collar Austin storytelling from Bummer Year into a bigger, more electric sound.

album: Watch Me Drive Them Dogs Wild
lineage: Sounds close to the Asheville indie-twang of Florry and Wednesday.
Sounds indebted to Neil Young's guitar sound and the funny-sad Drag City songwriting tradition; released the same year he played a key role on Waxahatchee's Tigers Blood.
Sounds close to the Asheville guitar tone of MJ Lenderman's circle, applied to Prine-style conversational storytelling.
Follows 90 in November, whose country sound sits near Waxahatchee and Wednesday, before opening out toward Broken Social Scene/HAIM-style pop-rock.

album: How to Get Away with Nothing
lineage: Sounds part of the small-label DIY twang network alongside Ohio- and Midwest-based indie-country peers like Spencer Radcliffe.
Sounds indebted to Lucinda Williams, Jason Molina and Silver Jews; part of the UK's small but active indie-twang scene.

album: I Saw A Galloping Horse Cover No Ground
lineage: Sounds indebted to Lomax-style folk documentation and cosmic Americana, close to the Northeast's alt-country underground.
Continues the Dear Life Records run of The Holey Bible; sounds close to the Asheville indie-twang of MJ Lenderman and Wednesday.
Builds on the cult success of I Looked Out and Freeman's place in the Burlington scene alongside Lily Seabird.
Sounds indebted to outlaw country and Wilco's Being There; close in spirit to young Southern indie-twang songwriters like Thomas Dollbaum and i26connector.
Connects Lenderman's Asheville circle directly to Waxahatchee's through shared members.
Sounds of a piece with the current wave of Midwest indie-twang alongside Ratboys and i26connector.
Brings Dollbaum's alt-country storytelling into the Dear Life Records fold alongside Florry.
Continues the band's alt-country arc from Reservoir and All the Right Weaknesses.
Sounds close to the Northeast slowcore/twang orbit of Horse Jumper of Love and Friendship.

Sounds close to the Asheville scene around MJ Lenderman and Wednesday, blending twangy Southern rock with an emo-adjacent intensity.
Sounds part of the Vermont/Northeast indie-folk-to-twang orbit of Greg Freeman and Lily Seabird.
Sounds close to the Asheville-adjacent indie-twang of Wednesday and MJ Lenderman.
Continues the arc from AOID's quiet twang through The Window's alt-rock/country/emo blend.
Sounds indebted to Townes Van Zandt and Jason Molina while stepping out of their shadow.
Part of the current New Orleans indie-twang scene alongside Thomas Dollbaum, touring with Kurt Vile.
Sounds like Wild Pink's turn toward the Core indie-twang sound; ruled into C1 as a specific stylistic pivot rather than the band's whole catalogue.

Early-period State Champion, before Davis's Roadhouse Band turn; sounds indebted to the Drag City/Palace lineage that runs to Silver Jews and Purple Mountains.
Follows Dad Country (2013); as Jonny Corndawg-turned-Fritz's later work, it sits at the more experimental, funny-sad end of the outlaw-adjacent Nashville scene.
The starting point for Poole's country-by-way-of-DIY-indie sound that would develop through The Freelancer's Blues and The Rainbow Wheel of Death.
Direct predecessor to Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band through Davis himself; sounds rooted in the Drag City deadpan lineage.
Sounds rooted in scrappier punk and emo rather than the storytelling style of the countrygaze bands.
Follows his debut Wideass Highway; sounds like Haggard/Nelson/Kristofferson-style storytelling country moved into an ironic, digital-age idiom.
David Berman's return after Silver Jews, rooted entirely in the Drag City deadpan lineage that runs from Starlite Walker through this final album.
Debut predecessor to Schlemiel; sounds indebted to Elliott Smith and fingerstyle players like Leo Kottke and William Tyler.

Directly anointed by John Prine, who signed Burt to his own Oh Boy Records, tying Burt's storytelling explicitly to the Prine/Tom T. Hall deadpan tradition that feeds the modern barroom-storyteller scene.

Extends the Philadelphia Friendship/Orindal circle's plainspoken, half-spoken songwriting, itself indebted to the Drag City deadpan school of Silver Jews and Smog that runs through the whole 2020s barroom-storyteller scene.
Released on John Prine's Oh Boy Records, keeping Burt's storytelling tied to his mentor Prine and the plainspoken folk tradition he represents.
Live companion to Made In America, recorded shortly after that LP's release.
Follows Goodall's time in Ona; sounds indebted to the Randy Newman/Warren Zevon line of wry piano storytelling.
Meadows co-runs Dear Life Records and plays in Fust, linking this solo record directly to that North Carolina/Brooklyn alt-country network.
Missoula, Montana songwriter whose work sits at the folk/country-adjacent end of the deadpan-storyteller lineage.
Predates Losin'; sounds close to the Asheville scene around MJ Lenderman and Wednesday.
Poole's country songwriting sounds descended from Haggard/Nelson/Kristofferson filtered through Brooklyn's DIY scene; the drum-machine-plus-pedal-steel sound recalls Silver Jews.
Follows his 2021 LP Calico Jim, cut at the same Little Rock studio; part of a loose north-Georgia Appalachian storytelling trilogy completed by Thus Spoke the Fool.
Follows Davis's work fronting State Champion; sounds indebted to Souled American, David Berman and Neil Young.
Predates and directly seeds the full-band Fust sound heard on Genevieve and Big Ugly; a look at the songwriter's home-recording origins before the Dear Life Records band era.
Sounds like a revival of the Guthrie/Prine topical-folk lineage for the social-media era, reaching listeners through viral video rather than the club circuit.
Follows Calico Jim and North Georgia Rounder in his run of north-Georgia story records.
Sounds close to the Nashville dive-bar scene of Lambchop and Silver Jews, and to Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band.
Follows Miller's debut Haw Creek; sounds of a piece with the Asheville scene around MJ Lenderman and Wednesday.
A borderline Core inclusion: less bar-band than her C2 peers, but shares the funny-sad lyrical mode with Prine/Berman-style songwriters.
Follows Sweet Creep (2016) after a near-decade recording gap; continues his idiosyncratic, joke-laced country songwriting.
Follows Halper's 2020 debut Alrightnik; a Nashville songwriter working the same wry, wordy vein as his singer-songwriter peers.

Precedes Fenceline as the band's first release.

lineage: Sounds close to the Northeast indie-twang of Greg Freeman and Lily Seabird; extends jokey, confessional indie-folk songwriting into anthemic rock territory.

Sounds indebted to the deadpan-songwriter lineage of Berman and Darnielle, within the small Brooklyn Ruination Record Co. circle.
Follows Made In America and a Levon Helm Studios live set; continues his piano-based storytelling, which sounds indebted to Zevon and Newman.
Fourth Daughn Gibson LP, following Carnation (2015); continues his deadpan-narrator persona in a stripped-down mode.
Sounds of a piece with the funny-sad, plainspoken songwriting in the barroom-storyteller lane.
Sounds close to Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band and MJ Lenderman and the Wind.
A non-US example of the Prine/Berman deadpan-storyteller mode, showing the style's reach beyond its American scenes.
Establishes Meek's separate honky-tonk-adjacent solo identity outside Big Thief, rooted in his Texas upbringing.

Draws on Nashville's neo-traditional and outlaw country vocabulary but bends it toward emo's confessional mode, a hybrid Kelly himself named 'dirt emo' and one that seems to echo across later indie-adjacent country songwriting.
A one-off widening of Kacy & Clayton's traditional-leaning catalog through collaboration with Marlon Williams, closer to breezy country rock than their usual austere folk.
Sounds close to Tyler Childers and Ian Noe in the Kentucky storyteller wing of the new country scene.

Grows out of Crutchfield's earlier lo-fi indie-rock work into full country songwriting, leading directly to the Plains project with Jess Williamson and sitting at the front of a wider wave of indie musicians leaning into twang.
Deepens Meek's alt-country songwriting voice ahead of his move to 4AD for Haunted Mountain.
Fust's founding document, before the fuller alt-country sound the band pursued once signed to Dear Life Records.
Sounds steeped in the 1980s-'90s college-rock and No Depression alt-country lineage that C3 grew from.

album: I Walked with You a Ways
lineage: A direct collaborative offshoot of Waxahatchee's country pivot, pairing Crutchfield with Jess Williamson's own move from folk toward country songwriting.
Extends Old Time Feeling's western-Kentucky storytelling into darker territory; sounds close to Ian Noe and the post-Childers Kentucky scene.
Sounds like the Appalachian bluegrass tradition seen through a young Canadian songwriter's lens.
Part of the wider Bandcamp-driven alt-country underground, sharing the banjo-and-drawl approach of countless small self-released country EPs of the early 2020s.
Meek's first release for 4AD, the label Big Thief also records for, bringing his alt-country solo work to a wider audience.
Expands Evil Joy's lo-fi songwriting into a fuller band sound after signing to Dear Life Records, setting up Big Ugly.
Sounds of a piece with 2020s indie-Americana peers who bring 2010s indie-folk intimacy into recognizably country arrangements.

A cowpunk-to-honky-tonk arc in miniature: Daniel's background in California punk bands leads into a self-consciously traditionalist sound that recalls Bakersfield, released through the independent, Nashville-based Lightning Rod Records.

album: JP Harris Is a Trash Fire
lineage: Follows Harris's years fronting JP Harris and the Tough Choices, landing him on Bloodshot's insurgent-country roster.
Sounds akin to the wider Black country and cosmic-country revival within the neighboring C3 scene.

An Anti- release that sounds close to the Waxahatchee/Snocaps country-rock circle.
Continues Meek's alt-country solo catalog after his earlier records.

Sounds like a Midwestern-to-Nashville songwriter story typical of the current alt-country scene.

Sounds close to the Chicago cosmic-country scene around Tobacco City.
Part of the same Chicago DIY-country network as Case Oats and Tobacco City, blending Midwestern roots music with classic honky-tonk and outlaw touches.

album: How Do You Let Love Into the Heart That Isn't Split Wide Open
lineage: Part of the pre-Lenderman early catalog that shows the band's sound before its shoegaze/noise elements arrived.
The starting point of Hartzman's project, years before the shoegaze/country fusion of Twin Plagues and Rat Saw God.
Bridges yep definitely and the fuller-band sound of I Was Trying to Describe You to Someone.

lineage: First album to show the full band's mix of noise rock and alt-country, setting up Twin Plagues.

Sounds like a transitional sketch between the band's first two albums.
Sounds indebted to Velvet Underground-descended noise textures grafted onto Southern storytelling in the Skynyrd-to-Drive-By-Truckers line.
A snapshot of the band mid-transition from lo-fi project to full-throated noise-country outfit.
Sounds close to the countrygaze Bandcamp scene around Wednesday; precedes There You Ain't.

Third album for a band who came up recording to tape; sounds of a piece with Wednesday and Shallowater in the 2020s countrygaze scene.

album: God's Gonna Give You A Million Dollars
lineage: Second Shallowater LP, expanding the noise/twang balance of There Is A Well into longer, more patient song structures; sounds of a piece with Dutch Interior and Wednesday.
Continues the countrygaze sound of the band's own Twin Plagues and Rat Saw God, now bigger and more anthemic.

album: Say a Prayer to the Gods of Getting Going
lineage: Continues Squirrel Flower's move toward the countrygaze-adjacent, guitar-wall sound of Wednesday's circle.

Zac Little's Columbus, OH string-band project, drawing on Appalachian instrumentation (balalaika, dulcimer, mandolin) filtered through indie folk-rock.

Zac Little's Columbus, OH string-band project, drawing on Appalachian instrumentation (balalaika, dulcimer, mandolin) filtered through indie folk-rock.

Oak Park, Illinois-raised fiddler turned Nashville songwriter; sounds rooted in the politically engaged old-time and bluegrass-folk tradition.

Tamara Lindeman's long-running Toronto folk project, moving from 2000s singer-songwriter records toward the more expansive, band-driven indie folk of its 2020s run.

Montreal songwriter whose spare, direct folk songwriting fits the same lineage as Gillian Welch by way of Joni Mitchell.

Tamara Lindeman's long-running Toronto folk project, moving from 2000s singer-songwriter records toward the more expansive, band-driven indie folk of its 2020s run.

Continues Bonny Light Horseman's folk-revival project between Mitchell, Johnson (Fruit Bats) and Kaufman (Muzz, The National circle).
Part of the Earth Libraries roster's patient, string-laced strand of Midwest indie folk.

lineage: Tamara Lindeman's long-running Toronto folk project, moving from 2000s singer-songwriter records toward the more expansive, band-driven indie folk of its 2020s run.

Sounds close to the Burlington, Vermont indie-country crew (Greg Freeman, Lily Seabird, Dari Bay), with more Laurel Canyon polish.
The culmination of Cornfield's steady solo run after Highs in the Minuses.

A Gary, Indiana bedroom-folk project that grew out of the same Bandcamp DIY networks as Chicago's indie-folk scene, laying groundwork for the fuller-band goblynmarkytt.
A Montreal singer-songwriter lineage that runs parallel to Ada Lea and other Canadian indie-folk artists of the same scene.

lineage: Part of the Chicago folk scene alongside Free Range, Jessica Risker and Hannah Frances; Jackson is also a former National Youth Poet Laureate.

lineage: Sounds like a companion to Bright Future, outside the Big Thief album cycle.

Sits in the same self-released Bandcamp run as Winner and Race, the DIY foundation that eventually caught Orchid Tapes' and then Domino's attention.

Sounds indebted to Pavement's shambling guitar pop and Flying Nun-style DIY jangle; its own influence on the 2010s slacker-rock and bedroom-pop wave that followed is well established.
Sounds like the clearest 2010s inheritor of Pavement's slacker guitar-pop songwriting.
Grows out of the same Philadelphia DIY scene as Waxahatchee and Radiator Hospital, with a guitar-pop sound that seems indebted to Pavement and GBV.

Grows out of the DIY punk and cassette/Bandcamp network Crutchfield came up in, and sounds indebted to the deadpan funny-sad songwriting line; it seeds her entire catalog, including her later, more country-leaning work covered elsewhere in this atlas.

album: The Double EP: A Sea of Split Peas
lineage: Grows out of Melbourne's DIY scene and Barnett's own Milk! Records label, the base for the deadpan Australian songwriting wave around her.
Grew out of Melbourne's Chapter Music scene alongside Boomgates and Twerps; its sound feels like a template for later Melbourne jangle bands such as Chook Race.
Vile was a founding member of The War on Drugs in Philadelphia; his sound here seems descended from Pavement's loose-limbed guitar rock and Neil Young's amp-drone side.
Part of the same Philadelphia DIY network as Swearin' and Waxahatchee, with a lo-fi guitar-pop sound that recalls Guided by Voices.
Sounds indebted to Guided by Voices/Pavement's loud-quiet guitar-pop songwriting.
Continues Swearin's Philadelphia DIY guitar-pop songwriting, which sounds indebted to Pavement and GBV.
Rooted in Chicago's teenage DIY scene, with a sound that recalls garage rock and Pavement-style slacker guitar-pop.
Extends American Weekend's DIY lo-fi songwriting with Swearin'-band muscle; a key transitional record between bedroom-pop slacker rock and Crutchfield's later, more countryish songwriting.
The culmination of his self-released Bandcamp period, and the record that plugged him into the Orchid Tapes/bedroom-pop scene before Domino signed him.
Refines the '2' blueprint into DeMarco's signature sound; a touchstone for the 2010s jangle/slacker revival.
Sounds indebted to the deadpan funny-sad songwriting line (Silver Jews/Drag City) crossed with VU-style jangle guitar; the start of one of the decade's most consistent guitar-rock runs.
Sounds indebted to Flying Nun/Feelies jangle crossed with garage-rock energy, rooted in Chicago's DIY venue scene.
Continues Radiator Hospital's lo-fi pop-punk songwriting within the Philadelphia DIY scene, with a sound that recalls Guided by Voices.
Sounds indebted to GBV/Pavement guitar-pop songwriting by way of the East Coast DIY scene.
Sounds indebted to Flying Nun/Byrds-style jangle-pop, transplanted to the Korean indie scene.
Continuation of Twin Peaks' garage-jangle songwriting, moving toward wider recognition.
Sounds indebted to Sonic Youth's interlocking-guitar vocabulary, part of the Atlanta post-punk/jangle underground.
First release for Domino after his Bandcamp/Orchid Tapes run, expanding his cult audience while keeping the same bedroom-pop DNA.
Bridges Toledo's run of self-released Bandcamp albums with the full-band Matador era that produced Teens of Denial and beyond.
Sounds descended from Flying Nun jangle, within Melbourne's jangle-pop scene.

album: Sometimes I Sit and Think, and Sometimes I Just Sit
lineage: Sounds heir to Pavement's talky slacker rock, alongside Australian jangle peers like Dick Diver.
Sounds akin to the Pavement-to-Silver Jews thread of deadpan funny-sad songwriting, in a more folk-inflected register.
The scrappy basement pop-punk starting point of Remember Sports' own arc, which grows toward the more collaborative, fuller songwriting of Slow Buzz and Like a Stone.
Continuation of Speedy Ortiz's Pavement/GBV-indebted noise-pop songwriting.
Continues Twerps' jangle-pop, which sounds indebted to Flying Nun and the Go-Betweens.

Bridges Cerulean Salt's basement sound with a more expansive, era-blurring indie rock palette; part of the same Merge-era run that established Crutchfield as an indie rock and later Americana songwriter.
Toledo self-released many albums on Bandcamp before signing to Matador; the result sounds fused with Pavement's slacker irony.
Part of Toronto's Buzz Records jangle-pop roster alongside acts like Weaves; a direct forerunner to Mercy Works and Knows No Kindness.
Part of the Melbourne DIY jangle-pop scene that also produced Dick Diver and Terry, distributed internationally by the American slacker-rock label Trouble in Mind.
Part of Philadelphia's Lame-O Records power-pop circle; the sound is indebted to Big Star and Superchunk.
Sounds squarely indebted to the Guided by Voices four-track power-pop tradition, filtered through the 2010s Portland DIY scene.
Continues the band's jangle songwriting, which sounds indebted to Silver Jews and the Velvet Underground.
Grows out of the Go-Betweens/Triffids strand of Australian jangle-pop filtered through a more driving, Feelies-like guitar interplay.
Grows out of Melbourne's DIY jangle/post-punk scene and sounds related to the same Australian guitar-pop wave as Rolling Blackouts Coastal Fever and Twerps.
A quieter turn from the Weezer/Teenage Fanclub-sounding power pop of Dissed and Dismissed toward the acoustic Big Star and Byrds side of the same lineage.
Builds on Wild Onion's Chicago garage-jangle sound while sounding newly indebted to '70s classic rock.
Follows directly from Tesseract's jangling post-punk template, refined after the band's move to Bayonet Records.
Broadens the bedroom-pop template of Beach Music with country and folk textures that anticipate his later, more song-oriented Domino albums.
Follows directly from Lips & Skull on Buzz Records, continuing Toronto's jangle-pop lineage into a fuller studio sound.
A direct collaboration linking the American slacker-guitar lineage (Vile) with the Australian deadpan-songwriter tradition (Barnett), each feeding the other's fanbase.
Shows the slacker-rock lineage bending toward hushed singer-songwriter territory.
Continues the GBV-indebted power-pop songwriting of Beloved, tightening the hooks in a way that anticipates Natural Beauty's more melodic turn.
Continuation of NE-HI's jangle/garage-rock songwriting within Chicago's DIY scene.
Descends from Pavement/GBV-style shambling guitar-pop crossed with West Coast noise-punk.
Sounds of a piece with the Swearin'/Waxahatchee axis of DIY guitar-pop, sharing its fuzzy, confessional directness.
Bridges Talk Tight's homemade jangle-pop and the fuller, driving sound of Hope Downs, with an interlocking-guitar approach that sounds indebted to the Feelies.
Part of the Melbourne DIY scene around Total Control/UV Race members, extending Terry HQ's terse punk-pop into slightly more orchestrated territory.
The full-band endpoint of Waxahatchee's slacker/DIY period before she moved toward the more countryish Saint Cloud and Tigers Blood.
Grows out of Chicago's DIY guitar-pop scene, sounding kin to acts like Dehd; connects bedroom-pop songwriting to the bigger power-pop sound of the later Blame Game EP.
Continues the band's hushed country-folk sound on the Woodsist label, sounding close to the broader 2010s Kurt Vile/Real Estate axis.
A direct remake of Toledo's own Bandcamp-era masterpiece, connecting his DIY lo-fi songwriting roots to his mature full-band sound.

album: Tell Me How You Really Feel
lineage: Follows directly from Sometimes I Sit and Think..., sharpening the same slacker-guitar and deadpan-lyric approach into more overtly political territory.
Sounds akin to the Philadelphia jangle-pop of Hurry and 2nd Grade.
Extends the loose, hypnotic guitar-drone side of his songwriting from Smoke Ring for My Halo, sounding indebted to Crazy Horse's long-form jams.
Third album in Nap Eyes' jangle/talk-song lineage, moving toward a bigger label and wider audience.
Continues the Philadelphia DIY-to-power-pop path, sounding of a piece with the later power-pop revival of Lawn and Sharp Pins.
Sounds indebted to Antipodean jangle-pop (The Clean, The Go-Betweens); part of the 2010s Australian guitar-pop wave alongside The Goon Sax and Twerps.
Continues Say Sue Me's jangle-pop songwriting, which sounds indebted to Flying Nun and the Byrds.
Sounds indebted to 90s and 2000s guitar songwriters like Liz Phair and Rilo Kiley and to the Bandcamp-era DIY scene; it became a touchstone for the wave of young guitar-pop songwriters that followed.
Grows out of the Bandcamp/DIY bedroom-pop network and 90s alt-rock guitar songwriting; a borderline case whose pop instincts push toward Context-lane crossover on later records.
Continues Speedy Ortiz's noisy, angular guitar-pop lineage from Major Arcana and Foil Deer, tightening the pop hooks without losing the dissonant guitar tangle.
A return, after a mid-2010s hiatus, to Swearin's own Philadelphia DIY guitar-pop lineage, a scene it shares with Waxahatchee, the project of Allison Crutchfield's twin sister Katie.
A continuation of the Melbourne post-punk/pop songwriting of Total Control and UV Race's overlapping membership, staying close to Terry HQ's terse jangle-punk template.
Splits the difference between Dissed and Dismissed's full-band crunch and Confront the Truth's acoustic intimacy, still sounding rooted in the Byrds/Big Star power-pop seam.
Builds on the genre-collage approach of Rocket while tightening the emotional focus, setting up the more expansive God Save the Animals.
DeMarco's move to self-release on his own label echoes the DIY spirit this lane traces.
Grows out of the Pavement/GBV lineage of loud-quiet indie rock filtered through Raleigh's DIY basement scene; feeds directly into the tighter, more melodic songwriting of Running From the Chase.
Later-period Twin Peaks, still rooted in the band's Chicago garage-jangle scene origins.
Sounds directly descended from Guided by Voices' song-fragment power pop, and comes out of the same Philadelphia scene as Hurry and Golden Apples.
A deliberate break from the Crazy Horse and jangle-rock guitar sound of Teens of Denial, showing the DIY-to-major-indie pipeline can still take creative risks.
Part of the You've Changed Records roster connecting Maritime Canada's indie scene to the wider lo-fi/jangle underground; feeds into Hex's continued collaboration with Jay Crocker.
Grows out of Toronto's DIY guitar-pop scene and the Pavement/Guided by Voices lineage; set up the band's jump to Sub Pop for Cooler Returns and Chopper.
Sits between Lawn's earlier, more post-punk-tinged material and the tighter power pop of Bigger Sprout and God Made The Highway.
A more melodically direct turn from Troper's earlier GBV-style scrappiness, sounding closer to the Kinks and Teenage Fanclub end of the power-pop lineage.
Continues the band's jangle/talk-song lineage into a fourth album.
Sounds like second-generation Flying Nun-indebted jangle-pop, continuing the band's refinement of the sound.
Grows out of Slow Pulp's Chicago/Madison shoegaze-pop beginnings, a lighter, poppier cousin to Wednesday's countrygaze template.
Continues the Chicago guitar-pop lineage of Prom Queen, sharpening the hooks as the band's audience grew.
The most developed entry in Casper Skulls' Buzz Records run, later followed by Kit-Cat on Next Door Records.
Barnett's songwriting, which sounds indebted to Pavement, softened toward indie-pop.
Comes out of the Toronto DIY scene and sounds indebted to the Flying Nun/Go-Betweens jangle-pop lineage; set up Harm's Way's fuller studio sound.
Founding member Louis Forster is the son of the Go-Betweens' Robert Forster; the band's jangle sounds descended from the Go-Betweens and Flying Nun.
Sounds descended from the lo-fi college-radio-to-Bandcamp lineage of Duster and Alex G.
Sounds indebted to Big Star and Superchunk, filtered through the Philadelphia DIY scene.
Sounds directly indebted to Pavement and Guided by Voices.
Sounds indebted to Big Star/Flying Nun jangle-pop songwriting by way of the Midwest DIY circuit.
Continuation of Pardoner's Pavement/GBV-descended noisy slacker-pop songwriting.
The most ambitious entry in Remember Sports' arc from scrappy basement pop-punk (All of Something) toward richly arranged power pop.
Second chapter of Snail Mail's slacker-to-art-pop evolution.
Continues Peter Gill's GBV-indebted power-pop songwriting, part of Philadelphia's power-pop revival alongside Hurry.
Grew out of Bandcamp-era home recording; its fragmentary lo-fi songcraft sounds indebted to Guided by Voices and Elliott Smith.
Sounds akin to the New Zealand jangle-pop tradition around Flying Nun, crossed with American power pop.
Sounds of a piece with the UK DIY garage-pop underground that runs parallel to the American slacker/jangle revival; the band later signed to Sub Pop.
Sounds indebted to Big Star and Fountains of Wayne melodicism, blown out with fuzz-pedal DIY energy.

album: If You Knew Would You Believe It?
lineage: Part of Hunt's ongoing self-released Bandcamp catalog that runs from lo-fi power pop through to the more studio-polished American Pyramid.
Sounds indebted to Pavement and Sonic Youth's guitar interplay, filtered through Chicago's all-ages DIY scene.
Sounds of a piece with the Chicago-area DIY power-pop underground around Lifeguard and Sharp Pins, sharing their Nuggets-inspired hooks.
Continues the band's jangle, which sounds descended from Pavement and GBV.
A return to the DIY, self-produced instincts of his earliest lo-fi tapes, now filtered through two decades of studio experience.
Sounds indebted to the Big Star power-pop line crossed with post-punk tension, part of the mid-2020s power-pop revival.
Direct descendant of the Big Star/Teenage Fanclub power-pop lineage, part of the 2020s power-pop revival alongside Sharp Pins and Lawn.
Shows the band stretching its Flying Nun-indebted jangle sound toward denser, more textured arrangements.
Continues the Busan band's pristine throwback indie-pop, which sounds close to Alvvays, turning inward after Where We Were Together.
A Texas band's move from dream pop toward a more country-and-alt-rock-inflected sound, resembling the wider indie-twang turn without being a straight country record.
Part of the DIY/Bandcamp jangle-pop network this lane traces from Flying Nun and college radio.
Slacker-folk that sounds indebted to the Silver Jews and Palace, filtered through Detroit's indie scene.
Continues the band's garage sound, which sounds indebted to Nuggets, at maximalist length.
Moves Broderick's earlier lo-fi Diners records toward the wider power-pop revival, sounding indebted to Petty, Big Star and Fountains of Wayne.
Big Star melodicism via Philadelphia's power-pop revival.
Sits between If You Knew Would You Believe It? and Timeless World Forever in Hunt's self-released discography.
Sits between shoegaze fuzz and the jangle-pop tradition, sounding indebted to Guided by Voices' song-fragment economy.
King Tuff's catalog runs from 2000s garage-punk through Sub Pop glam-rock; Smalltown Stardust pulls him into the same jangly, twang-adjacent revival as his 2010s peers.
A Marquette, Michigan strain of pop-punk-inflected power pop, indebted to Fountains of Wayne's hook density and 1990s Midwest punk energy.
Extends the bedroom-pop haze of his Captured Tracks records into instrumental territory, closer to Jim O'Rourke's ambient side than to Pavement.
Sounds indebted to the Big Star power-pop lineage by way of lo-fi, self-recorded bedroom pop.
Extends Moveys' shoegaze-pop into more overtly Americana-tinged territory, sounding close to the countrygaze lineage of Wednesday and Great Grandpa.
The most expansive entry in Speedy Ortiz's noisy indie-rock lineage from Major Arcana onward, still rooted in the same angular guitar tangle.
A Columbus, Ohio power-pop project in the Teenage Fanclub/Superchunk lineage, part of the same 2020s power-pop revival as Sharp Pins and Hurry.
A late-period expansion of the same Melbourne art-punk lineage, sharing members with Total Control and UV Race, that produced Terry HQ.
Continues Truth Club's basement-scene, Pavement/GBV-descended jangle-and-noise songwriting into a more polished, emotionally direct register.
Direct descendant of classic jangle-pop (The Feelies, early R.E.M., Flying Nun bands).
Descends from breezy 70s pop-rock songwriting filtered through 2010s New Orleans indie pop.
The latest entry in 2nd Grade's GBV/Big Star-indebted-sounding power-pop project, part of Philadelphia's mid-2020s jangle-pop scene.

album: On the Intricate Inner Workings of the System
lineage: Sounds indebted to Nuggets garage and the talky deadpan of Jonathan Richman and the Modern Lovers.
Builds on Modern Fiction's jangle foundation with a bigger, more collaborative studio sound.
Released on Tiny Engines, a label historically associated with emo and twangy emo crossovers, connecting it to the C9 emo-crossover lane as well as straight power pop.
Sounds of a piece with the current Midwest DIY noise-rock underground where it overlaps with the slacker/jangle scene at its loudest edge.
Continues Hovvdy's lo-fi slacker-pop arc toward fuller production.
Continues the Crocker/McKiel partnership begun on Bobby Joe Hope, part of the same You've Changed Records lineage.
A solo offshoot of Twin Peaks' garage-jangle songwriting, filtered through cleaner electronic production.
Extends Major Murphy's own hybrid of 1990s indie rock and 1970s soft-rock songwriting established on Access, sounding indebted to Big Star's more orchestrated moments.
Latest chapter in Nap Eyes' jangle songwriting, which sounds indebted to Silver Jews and the Velvet Underground.
A solo power-pop outlet that sounds indebted to Wilco's Summerteeth-era studio pop.

album: Box for Buddy, Box for Star
lineage: Sounds indebted to Big Star power-pop songwriting, filtered through home-recorded, synth-augmented indie pop.
Sounds indebted to the Big Star power-pop line crossed with 90s alt-rock guitar tones.
Continues Alex G's arc from Bandcamp lo-fi into a wider, still jangle-rooted indie-pop palette.
Sounds of a piece with Chicago acts like Smushie and Shoulderbird, connecting classic-rock revivalism to the current power-pop/jangle underground.
Sounds indebted to Melbourne's interlocking-guitar jangle rock in the Rolling Blackouts C.F. mold, now on Third Man Records' power-pop and garage-rock roster.
Continues the band's garage-punk-to-power-pop evolution begun on Green Dream in F#, now filtered through a major indie label's reach.
A return to the anthemic guitar-rock lineage of Teens of Denial after the band's synth-pop experiment, keeping Toledo's literary songwriting intact.
Sounds indebted to Neil Young & Crazy Horse fuzz, with Wilco's Americana-pop as a touchstone.
Continues the jangle-pop lineage established on Buzz Records, now on Next Door Records with a warmer, more assured sound.
Part of New Orleans' current jangle/slacker cluster alongside Lawn.
A long-running New York DIY act that sounds indebted to Drag City-style funny-sad songwriting, filtered through the lo-fi Bandcamp underground.
Sounds indebted to Big Star and Elephant 6 melodicism, sitting within Philadelphia's current power-pop scene.
Sounds indebted to Pavement's loose song-suite structure and Built to Spill's guitar interplay.
Sounds indebted to Guided by Voices and Beat Happening's DIY-jangle lineage.
Part of Hunt's ongoing solo catalog that runs directly into American Pyramid's bigger studio sound.
Continues Horsegirl's post-punk and jangle sound, akin to Pavement, toward cleaner pop songwriting.
Continues Lawn's power-pop/post-punk hybrid songwriting into a bigger, punchier register.
A return to the vocal jangle-pop songwriting of Salad Days and This Old Dog after an instrumental record, still rooted in his Captured Tracks-era slacker sound.
Sounds indebted to the DIY jangle/college-radio line (Big Star, Flying Nun), filtered through 2020s Midwest indie rock.
Extends Sharp Pins' Nuggets/Big Star-sounding jangle-pop into a longer, more song-crammed format, released through K Records and Perennial.
Follows Turtle Rock in the 1960s-garage-into-Big-Star jangle-pop lineage; its release through K Records/Perennial places it in a long-running indie-pop label network.
A deliberate reconnection to Amos's earlier lo-fi Bandcamp songwriting, following Box for Buddy, Box for Star.
Continues The Tubs' jangle-pop, which sounds indebted to '80s British and Antipodean guitar pop.
Continues Zook's homemade jangle/synth-pop hybrid songwriting, which sounds indebted to Pavement's slacker guitar-pop.
Gill's membership in Friendship ties 2nd Grade to the same Philadelphia scene as Friendship and Hurry; the songwriting sounds indebted to Big Star and Guided by Voices.
Signed to the New York label Ever/Never, which ties the band into the current DIY jangle/twang underground.

album: Well Once There Was A King
lineage: Sounds indebted to the lo-fi, kitchen-sink home-taping tradition of GBV and Sebadoh, filtered through a 2020s Bandcamp DIY sensibility.
Released via Fire Talk's Angel Tapes imprint, which ties the band into the current DIY guitar-pop underground.
Hunt's self-released catalog moving from bedroom recording toward a bigger studio sound while keeping the same playful, hook-heavy songwriting.
Formed within North Carolina's twang-and-shoegaze scene before relocating to Brooklyn; its sound sits between C4 countrygaze and straighter, heavier guitar rock.
Part of the same small Brooklyn songwriter-collaborator scene as Adeline Hotel, Office Culture and The Bird Calls.
Sounds indebted to Nuggets-era garage rock and '90s indie jangle.
Sounds akin to the current Chicago Bandcamp slacker/lo-fi network around acts like Sharp Pins.
Sounds like a former jam/psych-rock guitarist moving toward a more concise, jangle-adjacent indie-pop songwriting style.
Latest chapter of Remember Sports' Philadelphia DIY power-pop lineage.
A continuation of Yard's shoegaze-meets-Americana synthesis, pushing further into polished, radio-ready alt-rock.
Continues Snail Mail's own lineage from Lush through Valentine, staying within confessional, guitar-led jangle-pop songwriting.
A direct 2020s continuation of the Flying Nun/C86 jangle lineage that runs through this whole lane.
Builds directly on Dead Meat and Cotton Crown's jangle-pop songwriting, deepening the band's British folk-jangle hybrid.
Continues Wishy's fusion of shoegaze guitar-wall production with 1990s power-pop songwriting established on Triple Seven.
Sounds indebted to Duster and Codeine-style slowcore fed through a melodic, riff-driven Boston indie-rock lens; precedes the band's run of Run for Cover albums.
A direct predecessor to Teethe, tying Dead Sullivan to the same Texas slowcore lineage that runs through this lane.
Early Philadelphia-era record; the twisted, ambient-pedal-steel take on Americana heard on Friendship's later Merge records seems to start here.
An early Lomelda record and precursor to M for Empathy and Hannah; its hushed songs sound akin to the 2010s Bandcamp folk scene.
Follows All Yours and lays groundwork for the country-tinged twang that deepens on Plum and The Jacket.
A late-career reinvention of Low's own slowcore template, pushed into noise and glitch textures that resemble what younger hushed and noise-leaning bands were exploring in the 2010s.
A 2019 reunion by a 1990s V12 band that lands squarely in the modern slowcore revival it helped inspire; filed primary in C8 with V12 as secondary.
A bridge between Friendship's rougher early records and the fuller Merge albums to come; its unhurried, country-inflected hush sounds akin to Lomelda.
First album for Run for Cover, the label that would house the band through its most acclaimed run; still sounds indebted to Duster/Codeine slowcore.
The quietest turn in Lomelda's catalog between Thx and Hannah, sounding akin to the hushed Texas and Bandcamp folk of the 2010s.
Consolidates the hushed songwriting of Thx and M for Empathy into a fuller sound.
An early, quieter entry in a catalog that grows steadily louder and sounds more countrygaze-indebted with each release.
Sounds rooted in Texas DIY slowcore; a rawer predecessor to the more polished Magic of the Sale.
Follows Expect the Best and precedes The Jacket in Widowspeak's later-career turn toward a twangier, more overtly country-inflected version of their dream-pop sound.
The record that established Bnny's hushed, grief-soaked sound, setting up the fuller-band, more shoegaze-inflected One Million Love Songs.
Friendship's move to Merge after earlier small-label records carried their slow-burn, country-tinged indie rock to a wider audience.
Early, fully self-recorded hemlock LP that establishes the hushed, song-a-day approach Chauffe later builds on; sounds close to Lomelda's plainspoken Texas hush.
Continues the band's Run for Cover run; sounds akin to Duster and Bedhead and sits among 2020s slowcore revival bands.
A small-market Midwest counterpart to the slowcore-adjacent bands (Horse Jumper of Love, Teethe) this lane tracks.
The most explicitly twangy Widowspeak record, extending the country turn begun on Plum.
A side outlet for villagerrr's songwriter, sharing that band's hushed, homespun sound.
Part of Powell's long-running, prolific solo bedroom-folk catalog; sounds like a lo-fi Canadian counterpart to the American hushed-twang scene this lane tracks.
First widely heard record from Hataałii; establishes the slow, serene surf-country sound he expands on Waiting for a Sign and I'll Be Around.
A steady continuation of the band's Run for Cover-era sound between Natural Part and Disaster Trick.
Extends Meernaa's hushed songwriting, which sounds suspended between Duster-style haze and modern indie folk.
Sounds akin to the Durham/Triangle DIY folk-rock circle around Fust; its hushed, country-tinged songwriting leads into Companion.
Sounds akin to Philadelphia's hushed, homemade strand of indie folk.
Sounds akin to the hushed-folk collaborator network around Babehoven and Lomelda.
Continues the grief-driven songwriting of Everything with a fuller, noisier Chicago band sound.
Part of the current hushed-twang wave that pairs slowcore dynamics with bluegrass instrumentation, in the vein of Duster-descended acts.
Second Dangerbird Records LP, continuing the hushed, ornate Americana Hataałii built on Singing Into Darkness.
hemlock's most fully-realized full-band record to date, built from years of solo song-a-day recordings; a direct peer to Lomelda and Little Mazarn's Texas/Midwest hushed-folk circle.
Bridges hemlock's earlier solo phone-fi work and the full-band 444; sounds rooted in the same Texas hushed-folk orbit as Lomelda.
The band's most recent full-length, continuing its Run for Cover run as one of the most visible modern slowcore-adjacent groups.
Toronto songwriter Kenny Boothby's project shares Orindal Records with Friendship and sounds akin to that label's quiet, folk-leaning roster.
A Canadian counterpart to the hushed American folk-rock this lane tracks, working at its own unhurried pace outside any particular scene.
Sounds akin to the Burlington, Vermont DIY scene around Greg Freeman that feeds this lane's softer end.
Sounds akin to the Boston indie-rock underground of Horse Jumper of Love, mixing slowcore heaviness with a lighter, country-tinged jangle.
Sits at the emo-adjacent, slowcore-leaning edge of this lane, closer to Horse Jumper of Love and Joyer than to overt twang.
Continues Friendship's slow, twang-inflected songwriting with more polish and range, staying rooted in the same understated, funny-sad register.
Sounds akin to the Florist/Told Slant hushed-folk orbit that also feeds the C8 lane.
Third full-length, moving from Dangerbird to the Panther Mountain imprint while keeping the same hushed, baritone-led sound.
A touring-diary document in Hour's catalog before Ghost Bridge, part of the same Dear Life Records world as Cormier-O'Leary's band Friendship.

album: On the Other End of the Line...
lineage: Its pull toward folk and twang, after a more purely shoegaze-pop prior record, sounds akin to Horse Jumper of Love and places it at this lane's edge.
Austin's Little Mazarn sounds rooted in the same hushed, Texas folk network as Lomelda and hemlock, following Texas River Song.
Shares Fire Talk Records with Bnny and Fran, part of that label's hushed, home-recorded strand of indie rock.
McKnight (formerly of Speedy Ortiz and Grass Is Green) built Maneka as a showcase for genre-crossing songwriting; the slowcore passages sound akin to Horse Jumper of Love and Joyer.
Released through the WNOADIARWB collective; its hushed, pedal-steel-laced sound is akin to Friendship and Lomelda's country-tinged quiet.
A small, self-recorded entry in the same breezy, low-key bedroom-folk vein as klark sound and kitship.
Teethe's sophomore LP, refining the slow, hushed sound of their self-titled debut with richer, more country-tinged arrangements.

album: I See Them, I See Me
lineage: Babehoven's move toward a fuller, more countrified sound, still close to the hushed-folk network of this lane.
A quieter, ambient-leaning entry that sounds akin to the modern hushed-folk scene this lane tracks.
Cormier-O'Leary also plays in Friendship, and Hour shares Dear Life Records with that Philadelphia deadpan/slowcore circle.
Sounds indebted to '90s pop-country and Cosmic American touchstones while keeping the duo's own understated, plainspoken songwriting.
Follows Shep Treasure's earlier EPs; its hushed, murky sound is akin to Joyer's East Coast DIY folk-rock.
A follow-up to Radial Gate, deepening Sluice's hushed, conversational folk-rock.
Second vega LP, continuing Molly Meehan's plainspoken, gently twangy Burlington indie-folk songwriting.
Follows Widowspeak's quieter Captured Tracks albums (Expect the Best, Plum, The Jacket), continuing what sounds like a late-career drift from dream pop toward the C8 sound.
Originally released on Hot Green Records; its emo-adjacent songwriting sounds like an antecedent to later Core bands such as Cusp.
Grew out of New Jersey DIY house shows; the seed that Cardinal refined into an alt-country/emo hybrid that later Core bands sound indebted to.
First Hop Along album on Saddle Creek; sounds like an antecedent to the emotionally direct, character-driven indie rock of younger Core bands such as Cusp and Wednesday.

Followed the self-released Meridian and the Everything So Far anthology; its blend of Crazy Horse-lite guitar and confessional emo phrasing is echoed by Slaughter Beach, Dog, Cusp and other Core bands.
Jake Ewald's post-Modern Baseball project, moving from pop-punk toward the alt-country and heartland-rock songwriting of Slaughter Beach, Dog's later records.
The starting point of what became Strange Ranger's emo-twang crossover songwriting; it sounds akin to the Tiny Engines-adjacent DIY scene of bands like Free Cake for Every Creature.
Follows Welcome; continues the band's move from Modern Baseball-adjacent emo toward a full alt-country and heartland-rock sound.
Continues the twangy emo-crossover songwriting begun as Sioux Falls, moving toward the fuller sound of Remembering the Rockets.
Third full-length from the Philadelphia band; its emo-to-indie-rock arc sounds akin to fellow Philadelphia acts like Slaughter Beach, Dog.
Bridges Cardinal and the Rough Trade era; released independently in 2018 after the band's hiatus.
Third LP; deepens the alt-country storytelling of Welcome and Birdie with more ambitious production.
The culmination of Strange Ranger's twangy emo-crossover songwriting before the band moved toward electronic textures on later records.
First album on Rough Trade, following the band's independent years; represents the emo-twang crossover moving toward a more polished, festival-ready sound.
Follows the more emo-scaled Brokenlegged; sounds like a step toward the twangier indie rock of the Core.
Follows Safe and Also No Fear in the band's run on Lame-O Records.
Set the template for the band's fusion of American Football-style emo with country and folk instrumentation that the whaler expanded on.
Sounds descended from 2000s emo and pop-punk filtered through 2020s indie-rock production, close in spirit to the emo-twang crossover of bands like Strange Ranger.
Second Rough Trade album; continues the band's move from DIY confessional songwriting toward larger, more communal themes.
Sounds close to the Chicago emo-twang axis of Friko and to Warehouse, Mothers and Ovlov.
Second LP, following the breakout i became birds; sounds like proof the emo-twang crossover extends beyond the Wednesday/MJ Lenderman axis, alongside Cusp and Twine.
Fifth full-length; the fullest, most settled version yet of the alt-country songwriting Ewald began developing after Modern Baseball.
A return to guitar-based twangy indie rock after a synth-pop detour, closing the band's arc from Rot Forever through Remembering the Rockets.

album: Where We've Been, Where We Go From Here
lineage: Emerged from Chicago's DIY scene; folds Midwest emo's emotional extremity into anthemic indie rock that sounds as close to Broken Social Scene and Neutral Milk Hotel as to twangier Core peers.
Third full-length; the clearest example yet of Sinai Vessel's drift from emo toward Americana-inflected indie rock.
Sounds indebted to Unwound and Fugazi's post-hardcore dynamics, carried into the twangier, string-laced emo of the 2020s Core scene.

album: What I Want Doesn't Want Me Back
lineage: Follows You Can Do It All; the move to Exploding In Sound places them near other Chicago and Northeast emo-twang crossover acts.
Follows New Old Horse; continues the Fugazi-to-countrygaze pull the earlier LP set out.
Follows Where We've Been, Where We Go From Here; the band's continued expansion of Chicago DIY emo-rock into more orchestral, art-rock territory.
Folk-punk-leaning emo that sounds indebted to Titus Andronicus's rowdier moments and the Pinegrove-era emo-twang crossover; its acoustic instruments tie it to the DIY folk revival around the Core.
Released on Good English Records; sounds akin to the emo-into-twang wave of Cusp and Twine, but with a more explicitly folk, pedal-steel palette.
Launches Will Johnson's Centro-matic and, with it, the Denton, Texas wing of the Molina/Magnolia orbit.
A same-year companion to the Songs: Ohia debut LP, part of the flood of early Secretly Canadian releases that established Molina's stark solo sound before the full band arrived.

Molina's first single came out on Will Oldham's Palace Records, and this album sounds kin to the same lo-fi, DIY folk underground; it established the voice-and-guitar minimalism that later Songs: Ohia and Magnolia Electric Co. records built from or reacted against.
Bridges the stripped-down debut and the fuller-band Axxess & Ace, part of Molina's rapid early run of Secretly Canadian-adjacent releases out of the Bloomington/Chicago underground.
Continues Centro-matic's fast, fuzz-heavy development toward the fuller alt-country/Crazy Horse sound of 'Distance and Clime' and 'Love You Just the Same'.
Continues the Secretly Canadian run that runs from Songs: Ohia's debut through The Lioness, tightening the songwriting that would fully bloom on Didn't It Rain and Magnolia Electric Co.

album: All the Falsest Hearts Can Try
lineage: One of several rapid-fire early Centro-matic releases building the fuzz-guitar, alt-country sound the band would refine through the 2000s.
Sounds indebted to Low- and Codeine-style slowcore more than any other Songs: Ohia record, sitting between the folk-noir of The Lioness and the gospel-country turn of Didn't It Rain.
A between-albums tour-only release from the same 2000 stretch that produced The Lioness and Ghost Tropic, showing the stripped-down solo mode Molina kept returning to between full-band records.
Made with Alasdair Roberts and members of Arab Strap in Scotland, linking the Songs: Ohia catalog directly to the UK folk underground that also produced Roberts's own records.
Splits off from Centro-matic as Will Johnson's hushed, slow-tempo alter ego, establishing a quieter parallel track to the Crazy Horse fuzz of his main band.
Marks Centro-matic settling into its core lineup (Johnson, Pence, Danbom, Hedman), the same band that would carry through 'Love You Just the Same' and 'Fort Recovery'.

album: Mi Sei Apparso Come Un Fantasma
lineage: A snapshot of the touring Songs: Ohia band, showing how the sound opened up once Molina had a full electric group behind him, pointing toward Didn't It Rain and The Magnolia Electric Co.
Directly links Jason Molina to Will Oldham's Drag City deadpan-folk lineage (V2) through a shared acoustic side-project with Alasdair Roberts.

The field guide's other suggested starting point alongside Magnolia Electric Co.; its gospel-tinged small-band sound is the direct bridge from the earlier solo Songs: Ohia records to the full-band Crazy Horse-scale group that followed.
Opens Will Johnson's solo catalog, a stripped-down extension of the same Denton songwriting that fed Centro-matic and South San Gabriel.
Represents the fully formed Denton version of Centro-matic's Crazy Horse-indebted country rock, sounding like a sibling to Magnolia Electric Co.'s work of the same period.
Sounds deeply indebted to Neil Young and Crazy Horse's ragged guitar rock, and gave its name to Magnolia Electric Co., the band Molina led for the rest of the decade.

album: Who Will Walk in the Darkness with You?
lineage: A Columbus, Ohio band working the same haunted, Midwestern gothic-folk atmosphere as Jason Molina's Songs: Ohia, sharing scene and tone rather than direct collaboration.
A solo counterpart released the year after The Magnolia Electric Co., returning to the hushed, voice-and-instrument minimalism of the earliest Songs: Ohia records.
Continues Will Johnson's stripped-down solo work alongside his ongoing Centro-matic and South San Gabriel output.
Documents Jason Molina's pivot from the hushed Songs: Ohia sound toward Crazy Horse-scale guitar rock, a move that set the template for Magnolia Electric Co.'s studio albums.
Extends Songs: Ohia's haunted folk into full-band country rock, cementing the Magnolia Electric Co. sound that Will Johnson's Centro-matic and South San Gabriel records run parallel to.

album: The Carlton Chronicles: Not Until the Operation's Through
lineage: Pushes Will Johnson's South San Gabriel project toward a sound indebted to Low and Codeine, a quieter sibling to both Centro-matic and Magnolia Electric Co.
A high point of Centro-matic's Denton guitar rock, running parallel to Magnolia Electric Co.'s mid-2000s records.

album: Let Me Go, Let Me Go, Let Me Go
lineage: Continues the solo, stripped-down thread running from Pyramid Electric Co. through Molina's later work, released as a quiet counterweight to the same year's full-band Fading Trails.

A transitional Magnolia Electric Co. record whose sessions were later collected whole on the 'Sojourner' box set, showing Molina's late-2000s method of recording in pieces across different studios and bands.
Sounds indebted to the Neil Young/Crazy Horse guitar lineage that also runs through Magnolia Electric Co., pushing it toward heavier, stoner-rock-adjacent territory from Baltimore.
Continues The Black Swans' hushed, Midwestern gothic-folk sound, part of the same regional atmosphere (Ohio, small-town gloom) that produced Songs: Ohia.

Collects the same 2005-2007 Magnolia Electric Co. sessions that produced 'Fading Trails' in their entirety, including material otherwise unavailable, and stands as the fullest document of the band's road-band, Crazy Horse-indebted period.
Unites Will Johnson's two parallel bands, Centro-matic (loud) and South San Gabriel (quiet), on one release, showing both halves of the Denton sound side by side.
Continues Arbouretum's heavy-guitar folk rock, which sounds indebted to Neil Young's Crazy Horse records and sits near Molina's electric work.
Joins Jason Molina and Centro-matic's Will Johnson directly, making explicit the kinship between Songs: Ohia/Magnolia Electric Co. and the Denton scene.
Closes out Magnolia Electric Co.'s studio catalog as a memorial record for bassist Evan Farrell, before Molina's final years of illness.
The fullest expression of the Baltimore band's heavy-guitar folk rock, which sounds indebted to Crazy Horse and sits near the Molina/Magnolia-adjacent V1 lane.
Late-period Centro-matic, released as the band's Denton run wound toward its final album.
One of Molina's final releases before his 2013 death, extending the hushed solo-acoustic mode of Pyramid Electric Co. and Let Me Go, Let Me Go, Let Me Go into a briefer, more fragile form.
A 2010s continuation of Will Johnson's solo songwriting, running parallel to the final years of Centro-matic and his collaboration with Jason Molina.
Closes Arbouretum's core lane-era run of Crazy Horse-scale Baltimore guitar rock, a sound the band would continue past 2013 largely unchanged.

album: Take Pride in Your Long Odds
lineage: Closes out Centro-matic's run as a band, the year after Jason Molina's death; in effect the end of the classic Molina/Magnolia-era Denton circle.
A post-Centro-matic Will Johnson solo record continuing the hushed, plainspoken songwriting he established in the Molina/Magnolia era.
A 2020 continuation of Arbouretum's long-running Crazy Horse-scale sound, unchanged enough from their 2007-2013 records to belong with the rest of their V1 catalog.
A posthumous release of 2000s-era Molina recordings, closing out the catalog begun with Songs: Ohia's 1997 debut and continued through his solo and Magnolia Electric Co. work.
Continues Johnson's solo work after Centro-matic and his 2009 collaboration with Jason Molina (V1), in a quieter, more skeletal register.
Johnson recorded a joint album with Jason Molina (Molina and Johnson, 2009), a direct link to V1; this solo record carries that haunted, Crazy Horse-shaded Americana into a quieter register.
The most recent entry in Will Johnson's solo catalog, extending the Centro-matic/South San Gabriel/Molina and Johnson lineage.
Sounds like a direct ancestor of the Drag City deadpan style; Hurley was later embraced by the 2000s freak-folk circle, releasing on Gnomonsong.
Continues directly from Armchair Boogie in the same Raccoon Records run; its loose, deadpan delivery sounds like a template for Will Oldham and the Drag City roster.

artist: Michael Hurley, the Unholy Modal Rounders & Jeffrey Frederick & the Clamtones
lineage: A collaboration between Michael Hurley and the Holy Modal Rounders circle; its mix of humor and plainspoken sadness sounds like an ancestor of the line running from Prine through Drag City.
An early Drag City release that shared a label with Silver Jews and Smog; its damaged, uncommercial sound seems to have set the tone for the label's willingness to release difficult records.
The earliest Smog release, predating Callahan's move to Drag City proper; its bedroom-tape austerity set the low bar of fidelity that Julius Caesar and Wild Love would build outward from.
One of Silver Jews' earliest Drag City releases, predating Starlite Walker and documenting the band's shambling origins alongside Pavement's Bob Nastanovich.
Callahan's first Drag City release, part of the same early-1990s Chicago catalog as Silver Jews' first records, establishing the label relationship that carried through the rest of his career.

album: There Is No-One What Will Take Care of You
lineage: The starting point of Will Oldham's decades-long catalog under the Palace and Bonnie 'Prince' Billy names, released on Drag City alongside the label's early Silver Jews and Smog records.

Follows Twin Infinitives as a slightly more song-oriented record, part of the same early Drag City catalog as the label's first Silver Jews and Smog releases, though pursuing a rock-damaged noise aesthetic rather than plainspoken songwriting.
The last Silver Jews EP before Starlite Walker, part of the same early Drag City run that also produced Dime Map of the Reef.

Part of Callahan's early Drag City catalog alongside Silver Jews and Palace, establishing the deadpan-over-lo-fi template that later Smog and Bill Callahan records built on; later artists like MJ Lenderman sound indebted to it.
The most stripped-down entry in the early Palace catalog, deepening the lo-fi confessional style of There Is No-One What Will Take Care of You before the fuller-band Viva Last Blues.

Chicago roots-rock contemporary with the early Drag City catalog; Tim Rutili carried the band directly into Califone, and its loose, Americana-inflected sound resembles the roots-inflected 2000s indie lane (V4).

Grows out of the Pavement/Drag City slacker-rock axis (Malkmus and Nastanovich as sidemen) and sounds indebted to Prine- and Dylan-style talking-blues songwriting; it set the template Berman would refine through American Water, alongside Drag City peers like Bill Callahan and Will Oldham.

album: The Cowardly Traveller Pays His Toll
lineage: Developed independently of Drag City in Omaha, Nebraska, but sounds close to Silver Jews, like a bridge between Prine-style plainspoken folk and the Berman school of deadpan songwriting.
Sits between Julius Caesar and Wild Love in the early Smog catalog, part of the same Drag City run that established Callahan's deadpan template.

The most 'rock band' sounding of the early Palace records, produced by Steve Albini and pointing toward the full-band sound Oldham would use once he retired the Palace name for his own name and later Bonnie 'Prince' Billy.
Links Red Red Meat's roots-damaged rock to the Califone that followed, and its murmured vocal style sounds close to the Drag City circle even though the band stayed on Sub Pop.

Shows the classic-rock songwriting under the noise of the early Drag City records becoming explicit after a move to Virgin, before the band returned to Drag City for Accelerator and Veterans of Disorder.
Bridges the stark four-track Smog records and the more arranged, country-adjacent sound of Red Apple Falls and Knock Knock, part of the same Chicago Drag City circle as Silver Jews and Palace.

The last album released under a Palace name before Oldham recorded as Will Oldham and then Bonnie 'Prince' Billy; its drum-machine austerity sounds like a precursor to Smog's own sparer, rhythm-box moments on Rain on Lens.

Follows directly from Starlite Walker but trades Pavement's band chemistry for a barer, more personal sound, pointing toward American Water; its plainspoken sadness sounds like a model for later Drag City songwriters.
Released alongside The Doctor Came at Dawn, part of the same mid-1990s stretch of Smog's catalog and Drag City's growing UK partnership with Domino.
The quietest, most minimal entry in the Smog catalog, sounding kin to Palace's early lo-fi records and to the hushed, glacial style of later modern slowcore acts.
Released on Drag City alongside the Palace records, and sounds rooted in the Scottish and British folk-rock tradition of the V30 lane.
Part of the mid-1990s Chicago Drag City roster alongside Smog and Jim O'Rourke, and sounds close to the label's other stripped-down, plainspoken songwriters.
The clearest bridge in the Smog catalog between Callahan's stark early records and the full-band, country-inflected sound of Knock Knock and his later Bill Callahan solo albums.
The bridge record between the Palace name and the Bonnie 'Prince' Billy identity Oldham adopted for I See a Darkness, part of the same Drag City Louisville catalog running through both eras.
Direct offshoot of Will Oldham's Palace world through Ned Oldham and the Palace Records label; sits at the experimental, lo-fi fringe of the Drag City deadpan school.
Her second Drag City album, sitting in the label's 1990s Chicago roster alongside Smog and Jim O'Rourke and sharing their plainspoken, unpolished approach.
Part of the same late-1990s Chicago Drag City circle as Jim O'Rourke and Edith Frost, extending the label's deadpan aesthetic into piano-led chamber pop.

Marks Royal Trux's return to Drag City and a swing back toward the noisier end of their sound, part of the same label ecosystem as the deadpan songwriters even as their own music stayed far from that style.
Reunites Berman with Pavement's Stephen Malkmus; its wry, novelistic writing sounds like the model for MJ Lenderman and other 2010s-2020s indie-country songwriters.
Represents the peak of Joyner's 1990s Omaha lo-fi run, cited by Conor Oberst and other Nebraska songwriters as a foundational influence parallel to, but independent of, the Drag City deadpan school.

album: Songs From Robert Louis Stevenson's "A Child's Garden of Verses"
lineage: Fronted by Will Oldham's brother Ned Oldham and released on Oldham's own Palace Records, making The Anomoanon a direct, documented extension of the Louisville Palace/Bonnie 'Prince' Billy family circle.
The album that cemented the Bonnie 'Prince' Billy persona and, through the Johnny Cash cover, carried the Drag City deadpan-country sound into the mainstream Americana conversation.

Released on Drag City during the same Chicago scene as Smog and Edith Frost, connecting O'Rourke's chamber-pop songwriting to the deadpan Drag City catalog even though his arrangements lean more ornate than the label's typical sparse rock.
Grows directly out of Pajo's work in Slint and Aerial M; its patient, glacial pacing also sounds akin to the slowcore lane (V12).
A late entry in Royal Trux's Drag City run, from a decade in which the band and the label's deadpan songwriters shared a label without sharing a sound.
A fuller-band peak of Callahan's Drag City run as Smog, followed by the more song-oriented Dongs of Sevotion and Supper and eventually by his solo Bill Callahan albums.
Sits between Knock Knock's full-band pop and the sparer Rain on Lens and Supper, part of the same Drag City circle of deadpan Chicago-and-after songwriters as Silver Jews and Palace.
Follows I See a Darkness with a warmer, harmony-led sound that looks ahead to Oldham's duet album The Letting Go with Dawn McCarthy.
A direct continuation of Red Red Meat through Tim Rutili and bandmates, extending the Chicago roots lineage into a more sample-based, collage-oriented sound.
Continues O'Rourke's Drag City run after Eureka, from the same Chicago scene as the label's deadpan songwriters.
Hagerty's solo debut, years before he produced Bill Callahan's 2007 Woke on a Whaleheart, part of the wider Drag City-adjacent circle.
Continues Pajo's move away from the noisier Slint and Aerial M projects toward a hushed acoustic style that sounds close to Will Oldham's quietest Drag City records.

Marks the Silver Jews' move from a Pavement-adjacent side project to a Nashville-based band in its own right, a shift that feeds directly into Tanglewood Numbers and the countrified wing of the Drag City roster.
A deliberate contraction after the full-band Knock Knock era, closer in spirit to Callahan's earliest four-track Smog records, before he opened back up again on A River Ain't Too Much to Love.

A link between the 1960s Greenwich Village folk scene, where he first recorded for Folkways, and the Drag City circle that admired him; his loose, funny-sad style is often heard in Will Oldham and Silver Jews.
Roberts' move from the band name Appendix Out to solo billing on Drag City, continuing the label's cross-Atlantic folk strand.
The most minimal of the early Bonnie 'Prince' Billy albums; its hushed, close-miked sound resembles the quietest Smog records in the same Drag City deadpan school.
Extends the Red Red Meat/Califone Chicago lineage into denser, more Southern-gothic territory, sounding like a regional cousin of Smog and Palace.

Restores the full-band, country-adjacent sound of Red Apple Falls and Knock Knock after the leaner Rain on Lens, directly preceding A River Ain't Too Much to Love and the eventual move to releasing under his own name.

Directly reworks material from There Is No-One What Will Take Care of You, Days in the Wake and Viva Last Blues, making explicit the country lineage that was always latent in the early Palace records.
The noisiest entry in the Califone catalog, carrying the Red Red Meat lineage into territory that sounds closer to the experimental noise wing of Drag City represented by Royal Trux.
The first major pairing of Oldham with Matt Sweeney, part of the Drag City Bonnie/Smog circle, later revisited on Superwolves in 2021.

Continues the full-band Nashville sound begun on Bright Flight while pulling in more rock energy, leading into Lookout Mountain, Lookout Sea; it sounds like a forerunner of the barroom-storyteller songwriters of C2.

album: A River Ain't Too Much to Love
lineage: Closes the Smog era before Callahan began recording as Bill Callahan with Woke on a Whaleheart, and its stripped-down, spiritual tone anticipates the hushed folk records of his solo career.

Extends the duet format of Ease Down the Road into a fuller, more internationally produced setting, showing how far the Drag City deadpan songwriting style could stretch without losing its core plainspoken character.

The most polished entry in Califone's catalog, showing how far the Chicago deadpan-roots lineage begun in Red Red Meat could stretch toward conventional song structure while keeping its core vocal character.

The first Bill Callahan solo album, produced by Royal Trux's Neil Hagerty and marking the formal end of the Smog persona; it opens the run of solo records that runs through Apocalypse and Dream River.
A relaxed counterpart to the darker I See a Darkness and Master and Everyone, sounding closer to the classic-country side of the Drag City deadpan lane.
Closes out the Nashville-band phase of Silver Jews begun on Bright Flight; Berman retired the band after its release and did not record again until Purple Mountains a decade later.

album: Sometimes I Wish We Were an Eagle
lineage: Continues the loosening begun on Woke on a Whaleheart toward a sparer, more country-folk sound that carries through to Apocalypse and Dream River.
The most ornately arranged Bonnie 'Prince' Billy record of the 2000s, showing how far the core deadpan-country songwriting could be dressed up without changing its essential plainspoken character.
Released on Andy Cabic and Devendra Banhart's Gnomonsong, part of the 2000s freak-folk rediscovery of Hurley; his rambling, deadpan folk sounds like an ancestor of the Drag City deadpan-folk lineage.
A documented link between Hurley's decades-old deadpan-folk style and the 2000s indie-folk revival, through a full collaboration with Ida released on Banhart and Cabic's Gnomonsong label.

artist: Bonnie 'Prince' Billy and the Cairo Gang
album: The Wonder Show of the World
lineage: Part of a string of duo and small-group Bonnie 'Prince' Billy collaborations (with Matt Sweeney, Dawn McCarthy and here Emmett Kelly) that kept the Drag City deadpan style alive through constantly shifting instrumental settings.
Niblett's move to Drag City for this album connects her raw, minimal singer-songwriter style to the label's broader deadpan-adjacent roster, extending the sound to a harder-edged British voice.
Sits between the folk austerity of Sometimes I Wish We Were an Eagle and the more expansive, groove-based Dream River, loosening his arrangements toward full-band jams.

Marks Angel Olsen's early work as a backing singer for Oldham before her own career in the rootsy indie-folk lane (V5/C5), a direct documented link between the Drag City deadpan school and the next generation of indie folk.
The clearest fulfillment of the loose, groove-driven direction begun on Apocalypse, later paired with the dub companion piece Have Fun with God and continuing into Shepherd in a Sheepskin Vest.
Continues Niblett's run on Drag City, extending the raw, minimal singer-songwriter approach that links her to the label's other stripped-down artists.
A dub reworking of Dream River's grooves, extending that record's loose, rhythm-forward direction into a mostly instrumental register.
Follows a long gap after Dream River and Have Fun with God, extending Callahan's plainspoken, domestic songwriting into a new, calmer register that continues on Gold Record.
A late-period Drag City record from Oldham, whose catalog shares a label and a deadpan-country sensibility with Silver Jews and Smog.
A leaner companion to Shepherd in a Sheepskin Vest, continuing Callahan's late-career turn toward plainspoken, almost prose-like songwriting that carries into YTI⅃AƎЯ.
Directly continues the 2005 Superwolf collaboration, extending one of the most documented recurring partnerships within the Drag City deadpan school.

Pushes the plainspoken Callahan songbook toward looser, more atmospheric territory than Shepherd in a Sheepskin Vest or Gold Record, while staying within the same Drag City deadpan lineage he has worked in since Smog.
A recent continuation of the Bonnie 'Prince' Billy catalog begun on I See a Darkness, keeping the plainspoken, homemade intimacy of the early Palace material.
Sounds like a 2020s continuation of the classic-country instincts Oldham explored on Sings Greatest Palace Music, carrying the Palace songbook's roots into a polished Nashville setting.

Came out of the mid-1990s Denton, Texas scene that also produced Centro-matic, and later spun off Brent Best's the Drams; it sounds closely parallel to the Uncle Tupelo-descended insurgent-country movement DBT emerged from in Georgia.
Continues directly from Crow Pot Pie, deepening the band's reputation within the Denton scene before New West Records picked up the group's next two albums for wider distribution.

Grew out of Hood and Cooley's earlier Alabama band Adam's House Cat, and sits in the cowpunk and insurgent-country underground that followed Uncle Tupelo; it is the root of the Drive-By Truckers catalog that later took in Jason Isbell.
A direct continuation of Gangstabilly and the Adam's House Cat lineage, and a warm-up for the fuller concept-album ambitions of Southern Rock Opera two years later.
A bridge between the DIY early studio albums and the breakthrough of Southern Rock Opera, documenting how the band's reputation was built onstage before wider notice arrived.

album: Everything You Thought Was Right Was Wrong Today
lineage: The high point of the band's New West run; later storytelling-rock bands like American Aquarium and Two Cow Garage sound indebted to its loud-choruses, plain-verses formula.

Explicitly built on Lynyrd Skynyrd's story and the Southern-rock tradition, filtered through Uncle Tupelo-style alt-country songwriting; later Southern story-rock from Lucero to Wednesday sounds indebted to it.
Sounds like a product of the same Southern punk-to-country pipeline as Slobberbone and Two Cow Garage, with a Drive-By Truckers-like storytelling instinct delivered in a rawer, more punk-rock style.

Draws on Bare's upbringing as the son of country singer Bobby Bare Sr., but his rock-leaning storytelling sounds closer to Drive-By Truckers and his Bloodshot Records labelmates than to Nashville's country mainstream.
Released on Memphis label Madjack Records, the same imprint behind Lucero's early albums, placing Branan within the same Mid-South storytelling-rock network from the start.
A direct continuation of the band's self-titled debut, recorded for the Memphis independent label Madjack as Lucero's touring base widened beyond Tennessee.
The last studio album of Slobberbone's original run, after which frontman Brent Best formed the Drams with fellow Denton musicians before the band eventually reunited.

album: Please Turn the Gas Back On
lineage: The first record of the band's run on Shelterhouse Records, establishing the two-songwriter format Schnabel and Sweeney would keep on later albums.

Builds on Southern Rock Opera's harmonized three-guitar sound and points directly toward Isbell's own solo career; later story-song bands such as Lucero and American Aquarium sound indebted to its model.
Sounds like part of the same Texas alt-country underground as the Old 97's and Slobberbone, pushed toward a harder-rocking, harmonized-guitar sound indebted to Drive-By Truckers.
Continues the road-worn, live-in-the-room approach of Lucero and Tennessee, released as the band's national touring profile began to grow beyond the Mid-South.

album: From the End of Your Leash
lineage: A direct follow-up to Young Criminals' Starvation League on the same Bloodshot Records roster, keeping Bare's storytelling rock distinct from his father's outlaw-country lineage.
Extends Decoration Day's three-songwriter structure into more overtly political, working-class territory, a mode that Lee Bains III & the Glory Fires and American Aquarium sound indebted to.
A solo outlet for songs too personal or too sparse for Drive-By Truckers, drawing on Hood's upbringing as the son of Muscle Shoals session bassist David Hood.
Released on John Prine's Oh Boy label, placing Snider squarely in Prine's funny-sad storytelling line; his talky Southern delivery also sounds close to Patterson Hood's.
Follows the band's debut out of the Columbus, Ohio punk-and-country scene, and sounds close kin to Southern storytelling bands like Lucero.
A step up from the road-worn sound of That Much Further West; later alt-country and Southern-rock bands with punk roots sound indebted to this version of Lucero.
Part of the Alabama Southern-rock underground around Drive-By Truckers, whose sound it resembles; Lee Bains III played in the Dexateens before forming the Glory Fires.
Formed by Brent Best from the ashes of Slobberbone, keeping his songwriting within the same Denton, Texas storytelling-rock scene.
The last studio album to feature Jason Isbell before his 2007 departure, closing out the three-songwriter lineup that began with Decoration Day.
Expands on the full-band direction of Nobody's Darlings, moving the group's sound closer to the harmonized-guitar Southern rock of Drive-By Truckers, which it sounds increasingly indebted to.
A more political follow-up to East Nashville Skyline, continuing Snider's plainspoken, funny-sad storytelling tradition into more direct commentary on mid-2000s American politics.
Faucett's independent early work, predating his Last Chance Records releases.

album: The Better Angels of Our Nature
lineage: An early Glossary record predating Feral Fire; its Southern storytelling rock sounds akin to Lucero and Drive-By Truckers.
