Written and largely recorded while Isbell was still a member of Drive-By Truckers, with several bandmates appearing as guests, making it the direct bridge between his DBT songwriting and his solo catalog.
Continues the band's punk-inflected storytelling-rock sound from The Wall Against Our Back, sounding increasingly like a Midwestern cousin of Lucero.
The first post-Isbell album, with the band carrying on by expanding Shonna Tucker's role as a third songwriting voice alongside Hood and Cooley.
An early entry in American Aquarium's run on Last Chance Records, preceding the band's breakthrough with Burn. Flicker. Die.
Released on Suburban Home Records alongside Two Cow Garage; its punk-to-country arc sounds akin to that label's Midwest storytelling rock.
Continues the Tuscaloosa garage-Southern-rock sound of Hardwire Healing, released on the same Birmingham-based Skybucket Records that supported several Alabama bands in the DBT orbit.
A Suburban Home Records release from Florida; its small-town storytelling rock sounds akin to the Drive-By Truckers-descended scene further north.
The formal launch of the 400 Unit as Isbell's backing band, continuing the Southern rock approach of his Drive-By Truckers years before his sound moved toward V7-adjacent territory with Southeastern.
A major expansion of the full-band Southern rock sound introduced on Rebels, Rogues & Sworn Brothers, adding horns in a nod to the band's adopted hometown of Memphis.
Hood cut it with members of Drive-By Truckers backing him, making it a close cousin of the band's own records.
Continues the Schnabel/Sweeney two-songwriter format of III, released jointly by Shelterhouse and Suburban Home Records.
An early American Aquarium record that leads toward the songwriting of Burn. Flicker. Die. two years later.

album: A Storm, A Tree, My Mother's Head
lineage: A more elaborately produced follow-up to Bare Jr.'s Bloodshot Records albums, released on his own Nashville-based independent operation.
First of a loose pair with Go-Go Boots, drawn from the same sessions, and a sign of the band tightening its lineup around Hood, Cooley and Tucker before Tucker's departure.
Part of the same Liberty & Lament / Last Chance Records-adjacent Southern storytelling-rock network as Lucero and Water Liars, sharing labels, tours and producers across the scene.
A transitional record that moves the band from a shouted punk outfit toward the more personal storytelling of its later work.
A companion piece to The Big To-Do that leans into the Muscle Shoals country-soul side of the band's Alabama roots rather than the harder rock side.
Extends the full-band Southern rock direction of Feral Fire with a bigger, more anthemic sound.
Produced by Jason Isbell, a direct link to the Drive-By Truckers storytelling line; the band's Raleigh roots and roadhouse sound also sound indebted to Lucero.

Released on Chicago's Bloodshot Records, the flagship insurgent-country label that also carried Bobby Bare Jr. and Lydia Loveless, placing Branan within the wider alt-country network beyond his Memphis roots.

artist: Lee Bains III & the Glory Fires
album: There Is a Bomb in Gilead
lineage: Bains came out of the Alabama band the Dexateens; the record sounds indebted to Drive-By Truckers' storytelling rock, pushed louder and more punk.
Builds directly on the horn arrangements introduced on 1372 Overton Park for the band's ATO Records debut.
A solo live document from the guitarist and co-songwriter who, with Patterson Hood, has anchored Drive-By Truckers since its 1996 formation in Athens, Georgia.

album: Heat Lightning Rumbles in the Distance
lineage: A more produced, band-based follow-up to Killers and Stars, keeping the plainspoken narrative voice Hood uses in Drive-By Truckers.
Continues the deadpan, funny-sad storytelling of East Nashville Skyline and The Devil You Know, now self-released on Snider's own label.
Sits close to the Core of the modern indie-twang scene, while its plainspoken Southern storytelling sounds indebted to the Drive-By Truckers lineage at a fraction of the volume.
A move to New West Records, the label most associated with Drive-By Truckers and Slobberbone, situating Lucas within the wider storytelling-rock label network.

A solo turn away from Moreland's earlier punk and bar-band projects; his plainspoken, unglamorous storytelling sounds indebted to Drive-By Truckers and John Prine while working in a quieter, mostly acoustic mode.

album: The Death of the Self Preservation Society
lineage: A Last Chance Records release continuing the band's songwriting direction from Sweet Saint Me.
A continuation of the quiet, close-harmony sound of Phantom Limb, released on the North Mississippi label Big Legal Mess, home to several hill-country and Southern roots acts.
A Last Chance Records release; its dark Southern songwriting sounds akin to the label's other storytelling-rock acts.
A more focused companion to Mutt on the same Bloodshot Records roster, with dense, funny-sad songwriting that sounds indebted to John Prine's storytelling tradition.
Marks the start of the long-running Hood/Cooley/Patton/Gonzalez lineup that carried the band through the 2010s.

artist: Lee Bains III & the Glory Fires
lineage: A label jump to Sub Pop that widened Bains's audience beyond the regional scene that produced There Is a Bomb in Gilead, while keeping the same politically direct, three-guitar Southern rock approach.
Its slow, quiet arrangements sound indebted to modern slowcore and hushed twang, while its Mississippi roots keep it tied to the wider Southern storytelling scene.
A direct sequel in subject matter to Burn. Flicker. Die., looking back at the same touring years from a more sober distance.
Builds directly on the plainspoken acoustic storytelling of In the Throes with fuller arrangements; younger Red Dirt and Oklahoma songwriters often sound indebted to it.
A continuation of the horn-driven Memphis-soul direction of Women & Work.

Extends The Dirty South's political streak into the present day, sitting alongside younger Southern bands like Lee Bains III & the Glory Fires and American Aquarium that write explicitly about the modern South's politics.
Extends the more personal songwriting of the band's earlier records into overtly political territory, released on Last Chance Records, the label that also issued John Moreland's early records.
Continues Moreland's plainspoken Oklahoma storytelling from High on Tulsa Heat with a fuller rock-band arrangement, on a notably different label (4AD) than his earlier Americana-specific releases.

artist: Lee Bains III & the Glory Fires
lineage: A further label move to Don Giovanni Records, continuing the politically direct Southern rock songwriting of Dereconstructed.

album: It Took the Shape of a Bird
lineage: The most recent entry in Faucett's Last Chance Records run, continuing the label's small roster of bleak, plainspoken Southern storytellers alongside John Moreland and Two Cow Garage.
American Aquarium's move to New West Records, a label that also released Drive-By Truckers albums, made with a rebuilt band lineup after Wolves.
A tonal shift away from the horn-driven party sound of Women & Work toward the more brooding, keyboard-centered atmosphere the band continued to explore on later records.
Its storytelling sounds indebted to Drive-By Truckers as it moves into explicitly political territory, and it follows DBT onto New West Records.
A same-year companion to The Unraveling, carrying its political urgency into the pandemic and protest summer of 2020.
A direct continuation of American Band's political turn, written in the same volatile stretch of American politics.
A deliberate departure from the straightforward full-band Americana of Big Bad Luv; its added studio texture sounds closer to the Core's more atmospheric indie-folk edges.
Extends the atmospheric, keyboard-centered direction of Among the Ghosts further from the band's horn-driven 2010s sound.

A full-circle return to the band's own origin story, naming the real Muscle Shoals-area club where Hood and Cooley cut their teeth in the 1980s, long before Southern Rock Opera made them known nationally.
A continuation of the textured direction Moreland took on LP5, keeping his Oklahoma storytelling roots while moving further from the full-band Americana of his mid-2010s records.

artist: Lee Bains III & the Glory Fires
lineage: A tonal shift toward warmth and reflection after the confrontational Dereconstructed and Youth Detention, while staying on Don Giovanni Records.
Long-running Memphis band whose punk-to-Southern-rock arc runs parallel to the Drive-By Truckers; its storytelling Southern rock sounds akin to later bands in the same vein.
The most recent entry in Hood's solo catalog, extending the storytelling approach of Heat Lightning Rumbles in the Distance into the mid-2020s.
Grew directly out of Burns and Convertino's time as Giant Sand's rhythm section, translating Howe Gelb's desert-rock sensibility into their own mariachi-tinged sound.
Sounds indebted to Neil Young, Crazy Horse and classic Southern rock, filtered through a cavernous reverb that would define My Morning Jacket's whole career.
Grew out of Uncle Tupelo's breakup and Tweedy's move away from country-rock; its studio pop sounds indebted to the Beatles and Beach Boys, setting up the more radical 'Yankee Hotel Foxtrot'.
An early, direct descendant of Gram Parsons and the Flying Burrito Brothers that predates and helped set up the 2000s-2010s cosmic-country revival scene.
An early, lo-fi document of the Omaha singer-songwriter scene that would later feed the fuller Americana of 'Lifted' and 'I'm Wide Awake, It's Morning'.
Sounds akin to the deadpan, funny-sad songwriting of Silver Jews and Palace, applied to a fuller alt-country band sound.
A record from the Giant Sand lineup that seeded Calexico, connecting the band's 1990s work to Gelb's more scattered 2000s output.
The culmination of Lambchop's 1990s Merge Records run, fusing Nashville countrypolitan arrangements with indie-rock songwriting ambitions.
Deepens Beachwood Sparks' Gram Parsons/Byrds-descended sound with fuller studio arrangements, a direct ancestor of the mid-2000s cosmic-country revival.
Refines the reverb-heavy Southern rock of 'The Tennessee Fire' into tighter, more melodic songwriting.

album: Lifted or The Story Is in the Soil, Keep Your Ear to the Ground
lineage: Expands the lo-fi songwriting of 'Fevers and Mirrors' with full string and horn arrangements, pointing toward the more polished 'I'm Wide Awake, It's Morning'.
A covers detour that shows the same desert-rock sensibility Gelb applied to his own songs, released on Thrill Jockey during the band's more experimental period.
A deliberate stripping-down from the orchestral 'Nixon', pushing Lambchop's sound toward minimalism rather than maximalism.

album: Don't Fall in Love with Everyone You See
lineage: An early document of the Austin-based literary folk-rock songwriting that would culminate in 'Black Sheep Boy'.

Follows directly from 'Summerteeth' but adds Jim O'Rourke and Glenn Kotche's avant-garde leanings, feeding forward into 'A Ghost Is Born'; later studio-experimental Americana bands sound indebted to it.
A document of the Denton, Texas DIY scene of the early 2000s; its ragged folk-rock sounds akin to fellow Denton bands such as Centro-matic.
The culmination of the Tucson desert-Americana sound built on 'The Black Light' and 'Hot Rail'.
The start of McCombs' long solo catalog, released via Monitor Records and 4AD before his later move to Domino.
From Chicago's early-2000s indie-folk scene, with Johnson later playing in the Shins; its soft-rock craft sounds indebted to '70s AM songwriting.
Recorded with Jim O'Rourke just before he mixed 'Yankee Hotel Foxtrot', effectively a dry run for that album's more experimental impulses.
Ward's move to Merge Records after two small-label albums, setting the template for the acoustic, tape-warm sound of 'Transistor Radio' and 'Post-War'.
The culmination of the reverb-drenched Southern rock built up across the first two records, and the album that connected the band to the wider jam and indie circuits alike.

album: Down the River of Golden Dreams
lineage: Bridges the spare debut and the fully arranged 'Black Sheep Boy', adding chamber-pop instrumentation to the band's folk-rock core.
The lo-fi seed of Houck's whole catalog, recorded alone and pointing toward the fuller-band records that followed.
Sounds akin to the gothic-Americana strain of 16 Horsepower and The Handsome Family, built around Fisher's baritone and a revolving cast of Boston-area musicians.
One half of a same-year twin release with 'No You Cmon', splitting the band's fuller-arrangement songs from its more countryish ones.
The countrier half of the 2004 twin release, closer to the band's alt-country roots than 'Aw Cmon'.
Emerged from the San Francisco freak-folk circle around Devendra Banhart, though Cabic's own sound stayed closer to soft 1970s folk-rock than his more outré collaborators.
Extends 'Yankee Hotel Foxtrot' toward extended guitar playing that sounds indebted to Neil Young and Crazy Horse, a thread the band kept pulling once Nels Cline joined full-time.
The culmination of the acoustic, country-facing side of Bright Eyes' sound, with Emmylou Harris and a full country band pulling the songs toward classic Americana.
Turns the storytelling craft of 'Tallahassee' toward Darnielle's own life, a shift that shaped the more confessional Mountain Goats records that followed.
A deliberate widening of the reverb-soaked Southern rock of 'It Still Moves' toward more varied, radio-friendly songcraft.
Named for and structured around Tim Hardin's 1960s folk song, extending the literate folk-rock of the first two Okkervil River albums into a full concept record.
Continues the spare, home-recorded approach of the debut just before Houck's sound opened up on 'Pride'.
Documents the six-piece lineup that would define Wilco's guitar-heavy sound through 'Sky Blue Sky' and beyond.
Sounds directly indebted to Neil Young and Crazy Horse's guitar tone and My Morning Jacket's reverb-heavy atmosphere, filtered into concise indie-rock songs.
A solo detour from Giant Sand that pairs Gelb's desert-rock songwriting with gospel choir arrangements, unlike anything else in his catalog.
Continues the hushed minimalism of 'Is a Woman' with more personal, grief-inflected songwriting.
A more conventional, song-oriented follow-up to the trio's experimental 2003 debut.
A fuller-band expansion of the sound established on 'Transfiguration of Vincent' and 'Transistor Radio'.
Formed out of Okkervil River as a side project for multi-instrumentalist Jonathan Meiburg before becoming its own band with 'Palo Santo'.
A move toward warmer, more explicitly Southern songwriting after the debut's Pacific Northwest-recorded reverb rock.
Continues and thickens the full-band Americana arrangements introduced on 'I'm Wide Awake, It's Morning'.
McCombs' first release for Domino Records, opening the more widely heard phase of his catalog that led to 'Catacombs'.
An early document of McCauley's songwriting before the band's touring lineup solidified.
Draws on The Band and The Beach Boys' vocal-harmony pop filtered through lo-fi home recording, closer to power-pop than straight Americana.
Sounds indebted to The Band's Catskills Americana and old-time string-band music, filtered through a scrappier, more chaotic live-band energy.
Builds on 'Black Sheep Boy' with a bigger, more rock-band sound and a recurring set of characters carried into its companion record 'The Stand Ins'.
The point where Houck's lo-fi home recordings gave way to fuller, more patient country-folk arrangements, carried forward on 'To Willie' and 'Muchacho'.
A deliberate turn toward warm guitar interplay that sounds indebted to the Band, the Grateful Dead and Crazy Horse after two more experimental records.
Blends Neil Young-style guitar rock with Bob Dylan's narrative folk-rock, a combination that defined the Portland band's mid-2000s run on Sub Pop.
A return to the widescreen desert-noir instrumentation of 'Feast of Wire' after the more straightforward songwriting of 'Garden Ruin'.
Continues the loose, old-time string-band Americana of the debut, now with backing from Conor Oberst's Team Love label.
Continues the Giant Sand desert-rock line; its rambling style sounds akin to the 2000s indie-folk scene it influenced.
A deliberate widening of subject matter after the autobiographical run of 'The Sunset Tree' and 'Get Lonely'.
Pushes the genre-hopping widened out on 'Z' even further, absorbing funk and prog alongside the band's Southern-rock and country roots.
A direct sequel to 'The Stage Names', drawn from the same recording sessions and cast of characters.
Continues the dynamically extreme chamber-folk approach of 'Palo Santo' on a larger label with a fuller studio budget.
Builds directly on the songwriting sharpened on 'Dropping the Writ', in a gentler, more country-tinged setting.
Grew out of Michael Nau's earlier band Page France; its hazy country-folk sounds indebted to '60s and '70s soft rock.
The record where the touring band replaced the one-man-band approach of 'War Elephant', pointing toward the tighter 'The Black Dirt Sessions'.
Expands the ramshackle Americana of the first two records into darker, more historical storytelling.
A fuller-band continuation of the warm, melodic indie-folk introduced on 'Mouthfuls' and 'Spelled in Bones'.
Shows the influence of Ward's work with Zooey Deschanel in She & Him carrying back into his own solo songwriting.
Grew out of the breakup of DeYarmond Edison, carrying that band's Wisconsin-to-North Carolina folk experimentation into a looser, more communal direction.
Joins members of Bright Eyes, My Morning Jacket and M. Ward's circle; sounds like a lighter, more commercial cousin of the Centro-matic and Molina records.
A direct, explicit tribute to Willie Nelson and outlaw country, making plain the country roots underlying Houck's original songwriting.
A move to Sub Pop and a fuller, more song-oriented sound after three albums of hazier, more improvisational folk-rock.
Continues the classic-rock-leaning sound of 'Sky Blue Sky' with a lighter, more pop-facing touch.
Smooths and polishes the reverb-heavy indie-Americana sound of the first two records for a wider audience.
Expands the classic-rock and folk-rock synthesis of 'Furr' into longer, more progressive song structures.
A turning point where the band, now including Ian O'Neil, settled into the sound that carried through 'Divine Providence'.
A cleaner, more produced continuation of the harmony-pop songwriting built on 'We All Belong' and 'Fate'.
The lo-fi seed of Taylor's long-running project, later reissued by Paradise of Bachelors.
A bridge between 'Gather, Form & Fly' and the band's self-titled 2011 album, keeping the same warm vocal-harmony approach.
Carries the full-band momentum built on the 'To Willie' tour into a looser, more rock-oriented set of originals.
An early, folk-leaning Strand of Oaks record before Showalter's turn toward the fuller, more electric sound of 'HEAL'.
The somber counterpart to 'Humor Risk', both released within months of each other in 2011 to show two sides of the same songwriting stretch.
Moves away from the indie-folk tag of the earlier records; its bar-band sound is indebted to the Replacements and the Kinks.
A deliberate break from the acoustic-leaning sound of the band's Team Love years, folding electronic textures into its Americana storytelling.
A direct continuation of 'Bad Debt', released the following year on the newly founded Paradise of Bachelors label.
Formed by musicians from North Carolina punk and metal bands (McEntire from Bellafea, Miller from Horseback), consciously turning toward country and gospel forms.
Recorded in Louisville like the band's earliest records, and its roomy sound feels like a conscious return to them after the genre experiments of 'Evil Urges'.
Pushes the orchestral tendencies of 'The Stage Names' era to their most maximalist extreme before the band's later records scaled back down.
Reconnects with the experimental impulses of 'Yankee Hotel Foxtrot' after two straighter classic-rock albums, now self-released through the band's own label.
A geographic and sonic shift, recording in New Orleans rather than Tucson, while keeping the mariachi-and-twang core intact.
An elegiac record for Vic Chesnutt, whose 1998 'The Salesman and Bernadette' Lambchop had backed, continuing the orchestral hush of 'Damaged'.
A polished counterpoint to 'Divine Providence', made with outside producer Steve Berlin.
Continues the path from 'Bad Debt' and 'Poor Moon' toward a fuller band sound, named for a North Carolina river.
A fuller-band, Merge Records-backed refinement of the sound introduced on the self-titled debut.
The full realization of the country-folk sound built across 'Pride', 'To Willie' and 'Here's to Taking It Easy', now with a wider, more polished production palette.
A dramatic widening of Strand of Oaks' sound from the folk records into 1980s-scaled rock, with J Mascis guesting on guitar on 'Goshen '97'.
The father-son duo format here became the template Tweedy carried into his later solo albums 'Warm' and 'Love Is the King'.
A late-period continuation of the widened, more melodic sound the band settled into after 'Z', now filtered through James's breakup songwriting.
Sounds like a return to the noisier, more abrasive guitar tone of 'A Ghost Is Born', compressed into much shorter songs.
Came out of the same sessions as 'Star Wars', and its hushed acoustic mode sounds like a preview of Jeff Tweedy's solo album 'Warm'.
A deliberate return to the acoustic folk mode of the band's earliest records, paired as a set with the rock-facing 'Vol. 2'.
The harder-rocking half of the 2017 pair, continuing the raw sound of 'Divine Providence'.
Continues the family-band arrangement first heard on Tweedy's 'Sukierae', and its hushed acoustic mode sounds close to Wilco's 'Schmilco'.
A later-career continuation of the pedal-steel-and-synth sound Houck perfected on 'Muchacho', now recorded in his own Nashville studio.
Directly connects Strand of Oaks to My Morning Jacket, whose members backed Showalter on this record.
Continues the hushed, interior songwriting of 'Schmilco' but foregrounds Kotche's drums as the main instrumental voice.
A direct sequel to 'Warm', again built around the same small family-band arrangement.
Circles back to the alt-country of Uncle Tupelo and Wilco's own 'A.M.', now filtered through twenty years of art-rock detours.
The band's most collaborative studio record, arriving after a long gap and produced by Dave Fridmann rather than a member of their usual circle.
A left turn from the pure-country statement of 'Cruel Country' toward Cate Le Bon's more angular art-pop sensibility.
Expands the family-band solo format of 'Warm' and 'Love Is the King' into a much larger, more dynamic statement recorded at the same Loft studio as Wilco's own records.
Draws openly on the Stanley Brothers and the Carter Family's mountain harmony; later hushed folk from Iron & Wine, Fleet Foxes and Big Thief sounds indebted to its duo template.

Continues directly from Revival's Stanley Brothers and Carter Family influence, and its stark duo arrangements sound like a forerunner of the Appalachian-gothic strain later heard in Iron & Wine and Anna & Elizabeth.

An early entry in Sub Pop's quieter, singer-songwriter-driven side, predating Iron & Wine's arrival on the label and part of the late-1990s turn toward hushed acoustic folk on labels known for louder music.

Extends the Carter Family-to-Townes Van Zandt folk lineage toward Bob Dylan and Neil Young territory, and its patient, long-form songwriting sounds like a forerunner of Big Thief's extended arrangements.
Sounds indebted to Nick Drake's hushed fingerpicking and to the Southern gothic folk of Gillian Welch, filtered through lo-fi four-track home recording rather than a Nashville studio.
An early-2000s example of the plainspoken folk-songwriter revival, running parallel to Gillian Welch and Iron & Wine and sounding built on classic American folk and country storytelling forms.

A deliberate loosening of the stark Revival/Hell Among the Yearlings sound toward something that sounds indebted to the Band and Bob Dylan's Basement Tapes, a mode later full-band indie-folk acts like Fleet Foxes echo.
Sounds rooted in old-time hymn and ballad singing, in the same plainspoken folk vein as Gillian Welch though recorded with far less studio polish.

The band Justin Vernon led before its breakup sent him back to Wisconsin to record For Emma, Forever Ago alone, making this a direct, documented root of the whole modern hushed-indie-folk singer-songwriter mode.
Builds on The Creek Drank the Cradle with cleaner studio production; its hushed intimacy sounds like a clear precursor to Bon Iver's For Emma, Forever Ago.

Grew out of Holland's time co-founding the Be Good Tanyas, carrying old-time and blues vocal phrasing into a looser, jazz-inflected songwriting style distinct from Gillian Welch's more formal old-time revivalism.
Plainspoken, nature-imagery folk songwriting that sits comfortably beside Pacific Northwest peers like Damien Jurado, carrying a geologist's precision into old-time-adjacent folk forms.
Pairs Iron & Wine's hushed Appalachian-inflected songwriting with Calexico's desert-noir, mariachi-tinged rock, foreshadowing the pair's full-length reunion on Years to Burn.
A continuation of Carbon Glacier's nature-focused folk songwriting with fuller indie-rock instrumentation, sounding of a piece with Northwest peers like the Decemberists.
A continuation of Escondida's blues-and-old-time hybrid songwriting; Holland had earlier been a member of Vancouver's Be Good Tanyas before settling in San Francisco.
Builds on the plainspoken storytelling of The Golden Age of Radio with fuller band arrangement, sounding of a piece with the 2000s singer-songwriter wave around Iron & Wine's early records.
Sounds like an extension of Iron & Wine's hushed home-recording model into falsetto-led songwriting, and its sound echoes through the 2010s bedroom-folk wave.
Widens Iron & Wine's Nick Drake/old-time base with Calexico-adjacent players and world-music percussion, moving the project further from bedroom folk toward full-band arrangement.

album: Songs III: Bird on the Water
lineage: Sounds rooted in old-time murder ballads and British folk balladry, in the vein of early Gillian Welch, slowed and reverbed into a gothic, slowcore-adjacent register distinct from the rest of the lane.

Grew out of Baird's time in Espers and the Philadelphia psych-folk scene, carrying Anglo-American folk-ballad singing into the indie-folk revival in a way that sounds close to Gillian Welch and early Iron & Wine.
Sits just before Jurado's long production partnership with Richard Swift, which would push his sound in increasingly experimental directions afterward.
Fuses Anglo-American folk-revival vocal harmony with Crosby, Stills & Nash-style folk rock, sitting alongside Bon Iver and Iron & Wine at the center of the late-2000s indie-folk wave.
Sounds indebted to '60s and '70s folk-rock harmony singing (Crosby, Stills & Nash, the Beach Boys) filtered through 2000s Sub Pop indie rock, and helped set up the late-2000s baroque-folk wave.

Part of the mid-2000s London nu-folk scene alongside Noah and the Whale and Mumford & Sons, closer in spirit to the American Gillian Welch/Iron & Wine axis than to the festival-folk mainstream that scene later fed.
Sounds of a piece with the late-2000s wave of hushed, antique-instrumented indie folk around Fleet Foxes and Bon Iver, though rougher and more rooted in old hymnal and gospel forms.

Builds directly on the hymn-and-ballad feel of The Pirate's Gospel with fuller band arrangement, and sounds of a piece with Laura Veirs and Laura Gibson in the 2000s Pacific Northwest indie-folk scene.
Bridges For Emma, Forever Ago's acoustic folk intimacy and the electronically processed vocal experiments that would come to define Bon Iver's later albums, with 'Woods' later sampled by Kanye West.
Grew directly out of David Rawlings' years as Gillian Welch's guitarist, harmony singer and co-writer, with Welch singing on the record.
A fuller-band continuation of Songs III's hazy, old-time-adjacent balladry, keeping Nadler in the same gothic-folk lane distinct from more upbeat 2000s indie folk.
Olsen went on to sing in Bonnie 'Prince' Billy's band, and the EP already sounds akin to that circle's lo-fi, unvarnished recording ethos.
The start of the Jurado-Swift partnership, before Jurado's sound drifted further into psychedelia on Maraqopa and beyond.

Continues Marling's move away from London nu-folk toward a more classic, Anglo-American folk-revival sound, produced by Ethan Johns in the same lineage as Ryan Adams and Kings of Leon's roots-rock records.
The most melodically accessible statement of Veirs' plainspoken, nature-focused folk songwriting, self-released independently after her Nonesuch years.
Sounds rooted in old-time Appalachian a cappella and shape-note singing; member Amelia Meath later carried that vocal sensibility into the electronic pop of Sylvan Esso.
Plainspoken, guitar-and-voice confessional songwriting that sounds indebted to early Cat Power and Bill Callahan.
A full-band evolution of To Be Still's folk-rock direction, credited jointly to the touring group that had become her creative partners.
Expands For Emma's bedroom folk into fuller, orchestrated arrangement while keeping its emotional rawness; later chamber-folk records by The National and others sound indebted to it.
Extends the debut's CSN-and-British-folk-style harmony singing into more structurally ambitious, suite-like songwriting that anticipates Crack-Up.

A return to the sparse duo arrangements of Revival and Hell Among the Yearlings after Soul Journey's full-band detour; later hushed songwriters like Julie Byrne and Joan Shelley sound indebted to this stripped-down sound.
Continues Iron & Wine's drift from bedroom folk begun on The Shepherd's Dog, arriving at arrangements that sound indebted to polished 1970s soft rock.
Follows her stint singing in Bonnie 'Prince' Billy's band, and its stripped-down, old-time-adjacent folk singing sounds indebted to his Palace-era records.
Expands Epic's confessional folk songwriting with the National's chamber-indie production sensibility, moving Van Etten from lo-fi folk singer toward a fuller indie-rock sound.
A return to The Pirate's Gospel's spare, solo-voice-and-guitar intimacy after two fuller-band records, driven by direct autobiographical songwriting rather than inherited folk-ballad form.
Continues the horn-and-string expansion begun on Kiss Each Other Clean, moving Iron & Wine closer to 1970s singer-songwriter pop than to its old-time folk roots.
Extends the traditional-song repertoire of the Anthology of American Folk Music into 2010s indie folk, sharing the song-collecting impulse behind Jake Xerxes Fussell's records.

album: Burn Your Fire for No Witness
lineage: Carries Half Way Home's old-time-folk vocal style into full-band arrangement for the first time, moving Olsen from cult lo-fi folk singer toward a wider indie-rock audience.
Sounds indebted to the hushed fingerstyle folk of Nick Drake and early Iron & Wine, recorded with the tape-based DIY informality of the 2010s Bandcamp folk underground.
The clearest, best-produced statement of the slow, reverb-drenched old-time balladry Nadler had developed since Songs III, bridging indie folk and the slowcore lane it borders.
Continues the Dave Rawlings Machine format established on A Friend of a Friend, with the same Nashville old-time circle of musicians built around Gillian Welch's orbit.

Descends from his apprenticeships with Piedmont blues musician Precious Bryant and folklorists George Mitchell and Art Rosenbaum, carrying field-recording-era Southern folk and blues directly into the Paradise of Bachelors indie-folk catalog.
Builds on Burn Your Fire's full-band folk-rock into glammier, more structurally ambitious pop songwriting, continuing to carry Olsen's old-time vocal phrasing into new arrangements.

album: Boots No. 1: The Official Revival Bootleg
lineage: A direct archival companion to Revival, documenting the Stanley Brothers-indebted sessions that launched Welch and Rawlings' career.
Rawlings' third album as a leader after two Dave Rawlings Machine records, still built around his partnership with Gillian Welch.
Pushes Helplessness Blues' suite-like songwriting further toward prog and art-rock structure, trading some of Fleet Foxes' earlier pastoral folk directness for knottier, more demanding composition.
A conscious return to Our Endless Numbered Days' small-band folk intimacy after a decade of expanding orchestration, back on Sub Pop where Iron & Wine began.
A fuller-band continuation of the debut's archival-folk method, still rooted in the same Southern field-recording tradition passed down from his folklorist father and mentors.
Extends Rooms with Walls and Windows' hushed fingerstyle folk with light electronic texture from producer Eric Littmann, a collaboration that continued on The Greater Wings.
Continues Diane's plainspoken, acoustic-led folk songwriting into a more domestic, matured phase, a decade and a half after The Pirate's Gospel.
The furthest point yet in Olsen's move from old-time folk singing toward orchestral art-pop, though its sibling release Whole New Mess pulls the same songs back to her folk roots.
The fullest expression of Fussell's method of turning archival Southern folk material into finished performances, an approach that recalls song collectors like Alan Lomax.
The raw solo counterpart to All Mirrors, recorded before that album's orchestration; its sparse, echoing performances sound closer to Half Way Home and Strange Cacti.
A deliberate return to melodic directness after Crack-Up's art-rock detour, closing the loop on the pastoral-harmony sound the band opened with in 2008 while pointing toward a more orchestral future.

album: Boots No. 2: The Lost Songs, Vol. 1
lineage: An archival release of unheard Welch/Rawlings songwriting outside the official album sequence; its bootleg-series framing recalls Dylan's own archival releases.

album: All the Good Times (Are Past & Gone)
lineage: A covers record that makes explicit the Dylan, Prine and old-time-ballad lineage that had always run underneath Welch's original songwriting.
A pronounced country turn away from her earlier folk and art-pop records, with pedal steel and arrangements that sound indebted to classic countrypolitan records.
Extends Fussell's traditional-song method, released on Paradise of Bachelors like his earlier records.
Completes the hushed, string-touched folk direction Byrne and Eric Littmann began on Not Even Happiness, turning their collaboration into an elegy after his death.
A direct continuation of the Welch/Rawlings catalog begun on Revival, now credited jointly to both.
A continuation of Beast Epic's return to small-band folk arrangement, back on Sub Pop where Iron & Wine began.
A label change but not a sonic one, continuing the archival-folk-adaptation method Fussell established on his Paradise of Bachelors run.
An early document of Case's move from punk drumming into honky-tonk singing, made before she developed the surreal, nature-haunted songwriting of her Bloodshot and Anti- albums.
A return to the band's Uncle Tupelo-adjacent roots-rock roots after a major-label run, keeping them within the wider 1990s-2000s insurgent country and roots-rock network.
Released on Bloodshot Records alongside labelmates like the Old 97's and Waco Brothers, placing Case squarely in the Chicago insurgent-country scene before she moved toward Anti-'s art-rock audience.
Grew directly out of Whiskeytown's alt-country lineage, released on the same Bloodshot Records roster that carried the Old 97's and Waco Brothers.
Sounds indebted to the Texas singer-songwriter lineage of Guy Clark and Townes Van Zandt, carried into the 2000s Americana boom.
Shows Adams pulling further from Whiskeytown's twang toward mainstream rock, on the then-new Lost Highway Records.

Brings Hancock's strict honky-tonk and Western-swing traditionalism, openly modeled on Hank Williams and Bob Wills, into the Bloodshot roster, giving the alt-country scene a direct link back to pre-rock country.
A direct continuation of the Whiskeytown lineage from the fiddle player who helped define that band's sound, now stepping into the frontwoman role on Yep Roc.
Draws on Alberta's ranching and rodeo culture the way American alt-country draws on the rural Midwest and South, giving the genre a distinctly Canadian regional voice.
Continues Willis's post-major-label reinvention as an Austin-based alt-country singer, following What I Deserve.
The last Case solo record fully on Bloodshot before she signed with Anti-, bridging the label's insurgent-country roster and the more expansive songwriting that followed.
A solo offshoot from the Old 97's frontman, sharing the band's pop-leaning direction of the early 2000s.
Its country-rock instrumentation sounds indebted to Gram Parsons and its songwriting to Raymond Carver's short stories, a template Vlautin kept refining with the band and later the Delines.
Continues the singer-songwriter thread from Heartbreaker while showing Adams's growing pull toward rock during his most productive stretch.
Places Merritt within the Raleigh, North Carolina scene that also produced Whiskeytown and Caitlin Cary, while giving the Lost Highway roster a country-soul counterpoint to its rockier acts.
Continues the Bottle Rockets' Neil Young and Replacements-indebted roots-rock lineage into a new decade, keeping them in the wider orbit of the alt-country scene they helped launch.
Keeps Cary within the Raleigh-based alt-country scene that grew out of Whiskeytown, alongside labelmates and collaborators on the Yep Roc roster.
Sounds indebted to Lucinda Williams's gritty, guitar-driven alt-country, carried into the Canadian scene.
Deepens the Portland-based band's country-rock sound just as Vlautin's parallel career as a novelist was taking shape, both feeding the same cast of down-and-out characters.
Sits at the punk-and-psychobilly edge of Bloodshot's insurgent-country roster, sounding closer to X-style cowpunk than to conventional twang.
Keeps Hancock's honky-tonk and Western-swing revivalism tied to the same Bloodshot label that carried punk-inflected insurgent country, showing the genre's range.
Grew out of the DIY punk touring network, with Whitmore's old-time banjo and gospel songwriting reaching hardcore audiences who then carried him into the wider alt-country and Americana world.
Documents Case's ongoing collaboration with the Sadies, the Toronto band who also backed Jon Langford and other figures in the wider Bloodshot-adjacent alt-country network.
A return toward the band's insurgent-country roots after their major-label detour, made on New West, a label that became a hub for 2000s alt-country and Americana veterans.
Extends the Sadies' instrumentally driven, cosmic-country sound; the band's work backing Neko Case and Jon Langford ties them to the wider Bloodshot-adjacent scene.
Extends Cleaves's Texas storytelling, keeping him in the same songwriter's-songwriter lineage as Guy Clark and the Kerrville folk circuit.
Continues the band's psychobilly-and-punk take on Southern gothic Americana, adjacent to but distinct from the more straightforwardly twangy Bloodshot roster.
Extends Merritt's country-soul hybrid further toward Memphis soul, keeping her within the Lost Highway roster's mix of alt-country and Americana songwriters.

album: Hair in My Eyes Like a Highland Steer
lineage: Sounds indebted to the American Bakersfield and honky-tonk tradition, filtered through Lund's Alberta ranch life.
Extends the Exile on Main St.-style country-rock lineage into the Bloodshot roster, giving the insurgent-country scene a British-rock-indebted counterpart to its punkier acts.
Continues the funny-sad, Prine-indebted songwriting line within Texas's singer-songwriter scene, distinct from but adjacent to the Bloodshot-style insurgent country further north.
Sounds indebted to Whiskeytown and Lucinda Williams, with Edwards's Canadian alt-country pushing toward bigger rock hooks.
Extends the Carver-and-Springsteen-indebted storytelling of Winnemucca and Post to Wire into a full concept album, tying the band's music explicitly to Vlautin's novels of the same milieu.
Sounds indebted to the Bakersfield and honky-tonk tradition, made by a songwriter who helped define the 1990s Bloodshot insurgent-country sound.
Caps Adams's remarkable 2005 run of three full-length albums on Lost Highway, all drawing on different corners of the alt-country and country-rock lineage.
Sounds indebted to the Cosmic American Music of Gram Parsons and the Grateful Dead's country-rock side, made during Adams's Lost Highway years.
Sounds indebted to classic honky-tonk and Bakersfield country, named after the North Carolina town where Adams grew up.

album: The Dirty Old One Man Band
lineage: Applies Bloodshot's insurgent-country ethos to a solo one-man-band format, closer to punk-blues than to any conventional country arrangement.
Places the Bottle Rockets on the Bloodshot Records roster that also carried Old 97's and the Waco Brothers.
Sounds indebted to the same pre-rock country and rockabilly revivalism as Wanda Jackson, filtered through a hushed, understated vocal delivery distinct from most alt-country peers.
Case's move to Anti- expanded her audience beyond the insurgent-country scene without abandoning pedal steel and drawl, becoming a touchstone for the 2000s wave of literary alt-country songwriters.
Extends Biram's fusion of Delta blues, honky-tonk, and punk energy, showing the rougher, punk-adjacent edge of the Bloodshot roster's insurgent-country umbrella.
Makes the Texas songwriter circuit Cleaves draws from explicit by covering songs from lesser-known peers rather than writing new originals.
Continues Whitmore's old-time, gospel-inflected solo banjo tradition, a direct link between the DIY punk circuit and the deeper roots of American folk and blues.
Extends Lund's Alberta-rooted country songwriting into broader historical storytelling, staying within the same traditionalist instrumentation as his earlier records.
Continues the Deadstring Brothers' British-rock-inflected country-rock within the Bloodshot Records catalog, a rockier counterpart to the label's twangier acts.
Continues Jewell's blend of 1950s and '60s country phrasing with a spare, indie-folk sensibility, part of the broader 2000s retro-country revival.
Sits alongside Justin Townes Earle and Caitlin Rose as a Nashville outsider working in classic country forms, a kinship of approach rather than a direct link.
Pushes Willis's Austin alt-country toward rockier textures; it sounds akin to the Texas songwriter scene of Robert Earl Keen and Slaid Cleaves.
Brings the Southwestern desert-rock textures of Calexico into Richmond Fontaine's Portland-based alt-country, widening the sound without abandoning its short-story songwriting.
Shows the pop-leaning endpoint of Adams's mid-2000s evolution away from strict alt-country, still on Lost Highway.
Ties the Sadies directly to the original No Depression-era alt-country generation through producer Gary Louris of the Jayhawks.
An early entry point into Rose's Nashville-outsider country sound, part of the same 2000s scene of indie-adjacent country singers working outside Music Row.
Joins Carll to the Lost Highway roster that carried Ryan Adams and Lucinda Williams, tying his Texas troubadour style into the broader 2000s alt-country and Americana network.
Grew out of Mayfield's bluegrass-family background in Ohio, filtered through a slower, more hushed indie-country sensibility distinct from her family band's traditional sound.
Draws directly on his father Steve Earle's Nashville lineage while developing his own fingerpicked, pre-rock-and-roll country sound on Bloodshot Records.
Extends Edwards's alt-country songwriting into more political territory, sounding of a piece with the guitar-driven work of Neko Case and Lucinda Williams.
Continues the band's steady New West run, keeping them tied to the alt-country network even as their sound leans further toward power pop.
A quieter turn in Merritt's catalog after the more rock-oriented Tambourine, still rooted in the same Raleigh-bred country-soul sensibility.
Keeps the Bottle Rockets on Bloodshot; their roots rock sounds indebted to Woody Guthrie and the Replacements.
Draws on gospel and soul as much as country, part of the wider 2000s Americana boom's spiritual-folk wing alongside artists like the Civil Wars.

album: Novel Sounds of the Nouveau South
lineage: Brings Ozark-region folk harmony singing into the Bloodshot roster's insurgent-country umbrella, alongside rock-leaning labelmates like the Bottle Rockets.
Continues Earle's pre-rock acoustic style on Bloodshot Records; it sounds indebted to Delta blues and early Nashville country.
Extends the widescreen songwriting of Fox Confessor Brings the Flood into more maximalist territory on Anti-.
A continuation of Hancock's strict honky-tonk revivalism on Bloodshot, a lineage that ties the insurgent-country scene directly back to prewar country and Western swing.
Extends Whitmore's old-time punk-and-gospel hybrid into a fuller, more political sound, joining him to the same Anti- label roster as Neko Case.
Places Rose within the Nashville-outsider wing of 2000s-2010s alt-country, working in classic country forms without the trappings of the city's mainstream industry.
Continues Cook's classicist Nashville-outsider country into a more expansive, rock-adjacent sound while keeping her family's honky-tonk roots audible throughout.
Grew out of Segarra's time in New Orleans's busking and old-time string-band scene, a starting point for the more polished alt-country songwriting that followed.
Sounds indebted to the Woody Guthrie-to-Dylan folk songwriting lineage, closer to folk revivalism than to twangy alt-country proper.
Broadens Earle's acoustic Nashville sound with gospel and soul textures that sound indebted to his new New York surroundings, still on Bloodshot Records.
A return to a rootsier, faster version of the band's sound after the more polished Blame It on Gravity, still on New West alongside labelmates working the same alt-country circuit.
Grew out of Shires's years as a fiddle player for Texas swing and country acts before she stepped forward as a singer-songwriter within the wider Americana scene.
Sounds indebted to classic country and rockabilly, given a cool, cinematic treatment in the manner of other retro-minded 2000s Americana singers.
Extends Ha Ha Tonka's Ozark-folk-harmony take on Southern rock, staying within the Bloodshot lineage while pushing toward more anthemic, radio-ready songwriting.
Shows Carll pushing his Texas troubadour songwriting into more explicitly political and expansive territory, while staying rooted in the same storytelling tradition.
Continues Mayfield's slow-motion, hushed take on Midwestern country-folk, keeping her tied to the same indie-adjacent Americana scene as her Black Keys collaborator.
Sounds indebted to the deadpan, funny-sad songwriting of John Prine and Tom T. Hall, sharing a Nashville outsider scene with Andrew Combs and Caitlin Rose.
Places Loveless directly in the Bloodshot Records lineage that runs from the Old 97's and Waco Brothers through to 2010s cowpunk revivalists.
The furthest extension of Vlautin's parallel careers as novelist and songwriter, turning Richmond Fontaine's alt-country into a vehicle for a single sustained narrative.
Closes the loop back to Heartbreaker's spare singer-songwriter sound after a decade of genre experiments, released on Adams's own Pax-Am imprint after his Lost Highway years.
Sounds indebted to the 1970s Nashville songwriter tradition, of a piece with contemporaries like Caitlin Rose working outside the mainstream industry.
Released through New West Records, tying Lund's Alberta ranch-country to an American alt-country label network.
Continues Chisel's gospel-and-soul-inflected Americana into fuller orchestration, keeping him tied to a wider network of Nashville and Wisconsin collaborators.
A transitional record between Hurray for the Riff Raff's busking roots and the more pointed songwriting of Small Town Heroes, released in the UK by Loose Music.
Extends Pug's folk-revivalist songwriting into fuller arrangements, keeping him adjacent to the alt-country scene without fully adopting its twang.
Marks Edwards's furthest drift from the Lucinda Williams-style alt-country of her debut toward indie-folk, before she paused her music career to run a coffee shop.
Continues Shires's evolution from sideman fiddler to singer-songwriter, sounding of a piece with the literate Americana she would later pursue with the Highwomen.
Continues Rose's classicist country songwriting in a more polished register; it sounds akin to other Nashville-outsider traditionalists such as Justin Townes Earle.
A deliberate, scholarly homage to the Nashville Sound and honky-tonk era, made by a Canadian songwriter who came to country music through punk rather than family tradition.
Sounds indebted to John Prine's deadpan, funny-sad songwriting, now with cleaner production.

album: The Worse Things Get, the Harder I Fight, the Harder I Fight, the More I Love You
lineage: Continues Case's Anti- run of increasingly personal, orchestrated songwriting, distinct from but indebted to the twangier records that launched her out of the Bloodshot scene.
Returns Fulks to the Bloodshot roster he helped define in the 1990s, this time working in a stripped-down old-time and bluegrass mode.
Formed by Richmond Fontaine's Willy Vlautin, moving his short-story songwriting toward a soul-country hybrid built around a different vocalist.
Rewrites the murder-ballad and old-time folk tradition, sounding indebted to the Carter Family line, with New Orleans's traditional-music scene as its launching point.
Continues Earle's finger-style, Nashville-rooted songwriting into a new chapter after leaving Bloodshot, still tracing back to the same Southern storytelling lineage.
Grows out of Nashville's East Side DIY country scene, the same milieu that produced Margo Price, applying it to a traditional honky-tonk sound rooted in rural Kentucky.
Continues Loveless's run on Bloodshot; its harder-rocking alt-country sounds indebted to the label's cowpunk tradition.
A late-career return to the loose, twangy rock of the band's earliest Bloodshot records, now filtered through two decades of road experience.
Keeps Biram's punk-blues-gospel hybrid within the Bloodshot roster, a rougher counterpart to the label's more straightforwardly twangy acts.
Extends Combs's countrypolitan songwriting into fuller, more orchestrated arrangements, keeping him within the same Nashville-outsider lineage as Elizabeth Cook and Caitlin Rose.
A late entry in the Bottle Rockets' Bloodshot Records run, still rooted in the same Missouri-Illinois roots-rock scene that produced Uncle Tupelo.

album: If I've Only One Time Askin'
lineage: Extends Romano's studious honky-tonk revivalism into the classic country duet tradition, joining the same New West roster as several other 2000s-2010s alt-country acts.
Grew out of the same New Orleans scene that produced Hurray for the Riff Raff and Esther Rose, several of whose members have crossed paths with the Deslondes.
Grew out of the Chapel Hill, NC scene, and its Bloodshot reissue tied it into the Bloodshot Records alt-country network; its storytelling also resembles the Drive-By Truckers-descended lane.
Sounds of a piece with the classic honky-tonk revivalism of Daniel Romano and other Canadian traditionalists working a vintage Nashville sound.
A personal, fiddle-centered entry in the same Nashville Americana scene that also produced Isbell's solo work, though tracing its own distinct songwriting path.
Pulls Romano's honky-tonk revivalism toward the Cosmic American Music lineage of Gram Parsons and the Byrds, broadening his sound considerably.
Shows Cook stretching her Nashville-outsider country sound toward rock and psychedelia, while staying tied to the same classic-country vocal foundation.
Marks a mature turn in Carll's Texas singer-songwriter catalog toward the hushed, confessional end of the alt-country spectrum.
Continues Waldon's traditional honky-tonk songwriting just before she joined the Oh Boy Records roster built around John Prine's own catalog.
Pulls Loveless's Bloodshot-rooted alt-country toward textures that sound indebted to 1980s heartland pop.
Extends Fulks's late-career turn toward spare, old-time-inflected songwriting, keeping him tied to Bloodshot Records across three decades of the label's history.
Shows Combs stretching his Nashville countrypolitan sound toward moodier, more contemporary production while staying within the same songwriter-focused Americana lineage.
Continues Romano's move from honky-tonk purism toward psychedelic country-rock that sounds indebted to Gram Parsons-era Cosmic American Music.
Continues the Deslondes' revival of pre-Beatles country and rockabilly forms, part of the same New Orleans-adjacent scene as several other 2010s alt-country acts.
Pushes Hurray for the Riff Raff's Americana roots toward Segarra's own Puerto Rican heritage, widening the band's palette well past the string-band sound of their earlier records.
A later-career return to reflective, autobiographical songwriting within the same acoustic Nashville tradition Earle had worked in since his Bloodshot debut.
Continues the Sadies' long-running cosmic-country instrumental style, still tied to the wider Canadian and Bloodshot-adjacent alt-country network they've anchored for two decades.
Extends Rose's vintage honky-tonk revivalism, sounding akin to the classic-country reverence of Daniel Romano's records.
The furthest extension yet of the art-rock direction Case took after leaving Bloodshot, still carrying the alt-country DNA of her early records in its storytelling and vocal delivery.
The follow-up to Sidelong on Bloodshot Records, the Chicago insurgent-country label; its punk-edged honky-tonk sounds indebted to that label's outlaw-leaning tradition.
Continues the Delines' refinement of Richmond Fontaine's storytelling lineage into a hushed, horn-inflected style closer to countrypolitan soul.
Grew out of the same New Orleans old-time and Cajun-adjacent scene that also shaped the Deslondes and Hurray for the Riff Raff, applying it to spare, direct breakup songwriting.
The last chapter of Earle's finger-picked songwriting, its socially conscious folk sounding indebted to Woody Guthrie and his father's protest songs.
Ties Waldon directly to the deadpan, storytelling lineage of John Prine, whose label released the record, while keeping her sound in a straight honky-tonk mode.
Extends Cook's late-career move from honky-tonk revivalism toward rawer, more autobiographical rock-inflected songwriting.
Marks Loveless's departure from the Bloodshot roster into full independence, still carrying the label's cowpunk DNA into a more rock-oriented sound.
A late continuation of the Old 97's catalog on ATO Records, still tracing directly back to the Bloodshot-era Dallas scene that first defined the band.
Extends Rose's New Orleans-rooted old-time country songwriting, keeping her closely tied to the city's small but influential traditional-country revival scene.
A later chapter in Rose's Nashville-outsider country catalog, returning to the same classicist sound after a decade-long gap between albums.
Extends the Delines' soul-country sound with a new regional focus, keeping the band tied to Vlautin's wider body of fiction and song about working-class American life.
A continuation of the Deslondes' old-time and honky-tonk revivalism, tying the New Orleans scene into the wider 2010s-2020s new alt-country and honky-tonk movement.
Shows Segarra's evolution from New Orleans folk and old-time string-band music into a larger, electronically inflected songwriting practice, still tied to the same storytelling instincts.
Closes out the Sadies' three-decade run within the Bloodshot-adjacent Canadian alt-country scene they helped anchor alongside Neko Case and Jon Langford.
Continues the honky-tonk-and-punk sound of Sidelong and Years under a new label home, with Pete Anderson producing.
Keeps Rose within the same New West roster as Corb Lund and the Deslondes, broadening her New Orleans old-time sound toward more mainstream alt-country production.

album: Nothing's Gonna Stand in My Way Again
lineage: Returns Loveless to Bloodshot Records; her twangy rock sounds akin to the label's Old 97's-style insurgent country.
A late-career return to Hurray for the Riff Raff's Americana and old-time roots after a detour into electronic pop, closing a circle back to the New Orleans folk scene that produced the band.
Continues the honky-tonk-punk sound established on Sidelong within the same North Carolina-rooted band.
The latest entry in the Delines' ongoing extension of the Richmond Fontaine storytelling tradition into hushed, soul-inflected country.
The latest chapter in Rose's New Orleans-to-New-West arc, extending the city's old-time country revival into a more polished, wider-audience sound.
The latest chapter of Case's post-Bloodshot Anti- catalog, still tracing back to the twangy songwriting that first got her grouped with the 2000s alt-country scene.
Channels 1960s girl-group toughness and classic honky-tonk sass (Wanda Jackson, early Loretta Lynn) into the emerging 2010s outlaw revival.
Grows out of the hard country of Merle Haggard and George Jones, filtered through Simpson's bluegrass background; it set the stage for the genre-hopping he started on Metamodern Sounds.
Builds on Walk of Shame's honky-tonk sass with more polished outlaw-revival production, of a piece with the wave that includes Margo Price and Colter Wall.

Sounds indebted to Gram Parsons's Cosmic American Music filtered through outlaw twang; its crossover success helped open doors for the 2010s neo-traditional wave, including Tyler Childers, whose breakout Simpson co-produced.
Grows out of his years as a street musician steeped in old blues and country 78s, the raw seed of the vintage-soul-and-country sound he'd refine on later albums.
Grows out of the DIY Texas country touring circuit, following a self-reliant independent path similar to Whitey Morgan's.
Sounds indebted to the old-time Appalachian ballad tradition, filtered through a Canadian prairie perspective.
Sounds indebted to the Southern California country tradition of Buck Owens and the Bakersfield sound, filtered through LA's contemporary Americana scene.
Sounds like a direct continuation of 1970s outlaw country (Waylon Jennings, David Allan Coe) relocated to a Rust Belt touring circuit.
Draws on Southern country-soul and the laid-back groove of J.J. Cale and Tony Joe White, a softer, funkier strand within the neo-traditional revival.
Jinks came to country after playing in a metal band; the record sounds indebted to Waylon Jennings-style outlaw country, an unusually heavy entry in the revival.
Directly channels Loretta Lynn and Tammy Wynette-style honky-tonk confessional songwriting into the 2010s outlaw revival.
Fuses classic outlaw country with East Texas gospel and soul traditions, an unusually theatrical entry within the neo-outlaw revival.
Follows Metamodern Sounds' genre-blurring instinct further from Nashville orthodoxy, sounding indebted to Muscle Shoals soul and Waylon Jennings-era concept records.
Refines the vintage honky-tonk sound of his early records, closer to 1950s Nashville than to contemporary country, with phrasing that sounds indebted to George Jones.
Extends the Imaginary Appalachia sound with Dave Cobb's spare production, tying Wall to the same outlaw-revival lineage as Sturgill Simpson and Jason Isbell (also Cobb productions).
Echoes the classic outlaw-country confessional tradition, including Merle Haggard's prison songs, from a contemporary perspective.
Extends her honky-tonk foundation toward socially conscious songwriting that sounds indebted to Merle Haggard and Loretta Lynn's message songs.
Pulls the honky-tonk outlaw persona toward imagery that recalls Gram Parsons's Cosmic American Music and desert-rock atmosphere.
Continues the same Bakersfield-by-way-of-LA countrypolitan lineage established on Angeleno.

Sounds indebted to the hard-luck storytelling of John Prine and Steve Earle, recast in a specifically eastern-Kentucky voice; Sturgill Simpson's co-production ties it directly to the 2010s outlaw revival.
A direct homage to the countrypolitan and Bakersfield sounds of Ray Price, Merle Haggard, and George Jones, carried out from an unexpected New York honky-tonk scene.
Continues the same Southern country-soul lineage of his debut, tying the neo-outlaw scene to a gentler, groove-driven Georgia strand.
Bridges his honky-tonk base with New Orleans and Gulf Coast soul, broadening the sound beyond straight Bakersfield revivalism.
Continues the heavy-outlaw formula of I'm Not the Devil with slightly more mainstream polish, reflecting his growing crossover audience.
Sounds indebted to classic cowboy songs and Marty Robbins's Western records, with Wall covering traditional material alongside his originals.
Sounds like a studious recreation of the 1960s Nashville Sound (Owen Bradley, Ray Price), the most classicist corner of the lane alongside Zephaniah OHora.
Continues the same 1970s-outlaw-revival lineage as Sonic Ranch, keeping Morgan's Midwestern honky-tonk persona intact.
Sounds indebted to old-time folk and cowboy-poetry traditions, connecting the Guthrie-to-Townes folk songwriting line to the current DIY neo-traditional scene.
Sounds indebted to the Southern storytelling rock line from Skynyrd through Drive-By Truckers, with a specifically West Virginia focus.
Continues his vintage honky-tonk sound while turning it toward direct autobiography, reinforcing his connection to Texas borderland country traditions.
Follows the Prine/Tom T. Hall deadpan storytelling line and sits alongside Tyler Childers as part of the Appalachian-storyteller strand of the neo-outlaw scene.
Sounds indebted to classic honky-tonk storytelling (George Jones, Roger Miller), with an unusual, almost yodeling vocal style.
Draws directly on Jimmie Rodgers-style yodeling and old-time string-band music, an unusually deep-roots strand within the neo-outlaw revival.
Continues the gospel-outlaw fusion of My Gospel with darker, more personal songwriting.
Owes more to Southern arena rock and Neil Young & Crazy Horse's guitar noise than to country, showing how far the neo-traditional wave's most restless figure would range.
Extends Purgatory's plainspoken storytelling with a rockier band sound, continuing the Hickman Holler lineage that runs through his whole catalog.
Sounds indebted to the Texas songwriter tradition of Guy Clark and Townes Van Zandt feeding into the 2010s revival.
Signed to John Prine's Oh Boy label, McKinley writes in a plainspoken, hard-luck style that sounds indebted to Prine, set in the Rust Belt Midwest.
Draws on bluegrass and old-time picking traditions applied to a specifically northern-prairie songwriting focus, distinct from the lane's Southern and Texan centers of gravity.
Pushes his classic country sound toward a more cinematic, countrypolitan-adjacent arrangement style while keeping the same vintage vocal delivery.

album: Western Swing & Waltzes and Other Punchy Songs
lineage: Sounds indebted to Bob Wills-style Western swing, connecting the neo-outlaw revival back to Texas swing traditions.
Adds Shooter Jennings' cosmic-country and glam influences to Wyatt's outlaw-confessional foundation, linking her to the broader Cosmic American Music strand.
Continues the honky-tonk character-study approach of Wish You Were Here, part of the Dallas-based wing of the neo-traditional revival.
Shows the same Simpson-produced pivot toward rock textures that also marked Sound & Fury, pulling the neo-traditional scene toward 1970s Southern rock.

album: Cuttin' Grass, Vol. 1 (The Butcher Shoppe Sessions)
lineage: A direct bluegrass reworking of his own outlaw-country catalog, connecting back to the old-time/bluegrass tradition that also runs through Colter Wall and the Local Honeys.

album: Cuttin' Grass, Vol. 2 (The Cowboy Arms Sessions)
lineage: Continues the Vol. 1 concept of recasting his outlaw-country songbook as bluegrass, tying his catalog to the old-time string-band tradition.
Rooted directly in old-time Appalachian fiddle music, with the title track extending the Southern storytelling tradition into explicit contemporary politics.
Continues the countrypolitan lineage of This Highway, further cementing the New York honky-tonk scene's ties to 1960s Nashville production values.
Continues the Southern storytelling rock lineage of Seneca, moving slightly closer to arena-Americana production.
Closes out the honky-tonk character-study trilogy begun with Wish You Were Here, keeping Walker's distinctive vocal style and Dallas-scene ties intact.
Continues his old-time/yodeling lineage while sharpening the political edge, connecting the deadpan-funny-sad songwriting strand to explicit rural politics.
Sounds of a piece with the plainspoken, rural-life storytelling of Colter Wall, from an explicitly Montana ranching perspective.
Draws directly on old Appalachian ballad and ballad-opera tradition (Carter Family-style narrative song), a return to the roots strand of the 'new outlaw' movement after Sound & Fury's detour.
Bridges folk-punk and Piedmont-style country-blues fingerpicking with plainspoken country-folk songwriting, an unusual entry point into the neo-traditional scene.
Rodney Crowell's production ties Emerson directly to the outlaw-era Texas songwriter generation; the writing itself sounds indebted to Guy Clark and Townes Van Zandt.
Continues the Prine-indebted Midwestern storytelling of his debut, again on Prine's Oh Boy label.
A direct extension of Bob Wills-style Western swing via Asleep at the Wheel, connecting the neo-outlaw revival back to pre-war Texas dance-hall music.
Sounds indebted to Marty Robbins' gunfighter ballads and Texas outlaw mythology, continuing the classic-country storytelling strand within the neo-outlaw scene.
Continues the classic honky-tonk lineage of Loretta Lynn and Dolly Parton filtered through Nashville's contemporary lower-Broadway honky-tonk scene.
Extends the Prine-indebted storytelling of Between the Country with fuller band arrangements, continuing the Kentucky-storyteller strand of the scene.
Continues Hedley's classic-Nashville-Sound lineage while shifting toward a rowdier honky-tonk sound.
Sits between the neo-traditional revival and the more mainstream Red Dirt and Texas-country scene of acts like the Turnpike Troubadours.
Continues her established classic-country lineage with a more reflective, settled songwriting focus.
Sounds indebted to Western swing and pre-war country, connecting the neo-traditional revival to honky-tonk-era bass-driven dance music.
Returns to the rockier honky-tonk grit of Walk of Shame after two more polished, cosmic-leaning records, with Homme's desert-rock fingerprints audible throughout.

album: Can I Take My Hounds to Heaven?
lineage: Builds on Long Violent History's gospel streak while pushing toward psychedelia that recalls the cosmic-country turns of Sturgill Simpson, a mentor figure throughout Childers' career.
Sounds indebted to the folk-songwriting line running from Guthrie through Gillian Welch, with sharper storytelling.
Deepens the Southern country-soul lineage of his earlier albums with gospel shading that sounds indebted to Bobby Charles-style swamp soul.
Continues the Southern storytelling rock of his earlier albums, drifting further toward arena-Americana production.
Continues Wall's cowboy-song lineage while adding fuller band arrangements, moving him slightly closer to mainstream neo-traditional country.
Moves Wyatt's outlaw-confessional songwriting toward soul and rock textures, an arc that resembles Margo Price's later albums.
Continues the classic-rock drift of That's How Rumors Get Started, pushing further from honky-tonk toward Southern psychedelic rock.
Continues the same old-time/yodeling and rural-politics lineage of his earlier records, part of the scene's deepest-roots wing.
Sounds indebted to classic Texas honky-tonk, sitting alongside revivalists like Joshua Ray Walker.
A deliberate return to the country-folk directness of Purgatory and Country Squire after the experimental Hounds to Heaven.
Adds Shooter Jennings' outlaw-country pedigree to Emerson's Texas-songwriter foundation, linking him more directly to the broader neo-outlaw scene.
Keeps faith with the vintage country sound of his whole catalog while reflecting his growing commercial profile within the neo-outlaw scene.
Extends her honky-tonk foundation with more polished songwriting, still tied to the contemporary Nashville honky-tonk circuit.
A continuation of Simpson's genre-roaming outlaw country under a new name, still rooted in the same Kentucky-honky-tonk-to-cosmic-country arc.
Combines musical-theater storytelling with contemporary Texas and Red Dirt country production, a hybrid of the lane's narrative focus and arena-Americana sound.
Continues the folk-songwriting and cowboy-poet lineage of his earlier records with fuller arrangements and wider ambition.
Sounds indebted to the late-1980s neotraditionalist country of Randy Travis and Keith Whitley, carrying that revival into the 2020s.
Continues the same vintage honky-tonk and classic-country lineage running through his entire post-2015 catalog.
Circles back toward the honky-tonk core of her debut after the rock detours of Strays and That's How Rumors Get Started.
Continues Childers' Kentucky storytelling lineage while loosening the arrangements, working again with high-profile outside production after RCA's backing.
Sounds indebted to the folk-songwriting line running from Guthrie through Gillian Welch.

Fahey drew on Charley Patton, Blind Willie Johnson and Southern hymnody, and this record founded the Takoma label lineage that runs through Robbie Basho, Leo Kottke and every fingerstyle guitarist who followed.

album: Death Chants, Breakdowns, and Military Waltzes
lineage: A direct sequel to Blind Joe Death that deepened Fahey's fusion of Delta blues fingerpicking with modal drone, feeding directly into Robbie Basho's and Peter Lang's own Takoma records later in the decade.

An early, largely independent forerunner of American Primitive guitar's raga and drone side, closer in spirit to Robbie Basho than to Fahey, and a clear ancestor of the long-form instrumental pieces later made by Marisa Anderson and Chuck Johnson.

album: The Dance of Death & Other Plantation Favorites
lineage: Continues the early Takoma run of Blind Joe Death and Death Chants, Breakdowns and Military Waltzes, cementing the catalog of American and blues source material that later primitivists like Jack Rose and Daniel Bachman would keep returning to.
A contemporary of Fahey and Basho's earliest records, rediscovered decades later when Tompkins Square reissued it as part of its excavation of forgotten American Primitive-era guitarists.

album: The Transfiguration of Blind Joe Death
lineage: Extends the Blind Joe Death persona and style into one of Fahey's fullest early statements; later Takoma players like Robbie Basho and Leo Kottke sound directly indebted to it.

album: The Seal of the Blue Lotus
lineage: A direct outgrowth of John Fahey's Takoma label, with Basho pushing its fingerstyle vocabulary toward Indian raga; Jack Rose's 2000s raga pieces sound indebted to it.

Its tape collage points toward the noisier, more abstract end of the American Primitive lineage; later experimenters such as Jim O'Rourke, who went on to produce Fahey, and Bill Orcutt sound indebted to it.
Follows Requia in pushing Fahey's guitar pieces toward longer, more textured forms, an approach echoed later when Marisa Anderson and William Tyler added electric texture to solo-guitar composition.

Released on John Fahey's Takoma label, it brought a faster, more technically flashy strain of American Primitive guitar to a wider audience; the 1970s–80s new-acoustic and Windham Hill players sound indebted to it.
Extends the raga-guitar approach Basho began on his Takoma records; the cosmic intensity of William Tyler's and Marisa Anderson's electric pieces sounds akin to it.
Represents the fullest expression of Fahey's raga-and-drone side; the extended instrumental workouts later favored by Jack Rose and Daniel Bachman sound indebted to records like this.
Continues the meditative, raga-indebted style of America; later drone-leaning guitarists like Daniel Bachman and Chuck Johnson sound indebted to this side of Fahey.
Sits in the long run of Takoma albums between Fahey's raga-drone period and his stranger 1980s work.
Basho's move to Windham Hill placed American Primitive guitar next to the emerging New Age instrumental scene.
An openly Fahey-indebted record from a musician who went on to produce Fahey himself, filtered through O'Rourke's background in the Chicago experimental and Drag City scenes.

Marks Fahey's late-career turn toward noise and abstraction, a move that gave permission to younger primitivists like Jim O'Rourke and Bill Orcutt to push the tradition toward dissonance rather than pastoral fingerpicking.

Grew directly out of Rose's work in the drone group Pelt and out of his study of John Fahey and Robbie Basho, launching the 2000s Philadelphia-centered revival of American Primitive guitar alongside Glenn Jones.

album: This Is the Wind That Blows It Out
lineage: Jones was a longtime friend of John Fahey and recorded with him as part of Cul de Sac, and alongside Jack Rose he became one of the central figures of the 2000s fingerstyle revival.
Follows his earlier records in developing Rose's raga-guitar side, sounding like a direct continuation of the line Robbie Basho and Sandy Bull opened in the 1960s.

Synthesizes John Fahey's blues-ragtime foundation, made explicit by its Fahey cover, with the raga drone of Rose's earlier albums; later players such as Daniel Bachman and Hayden Pedigo sound indebted to it.
Sounds like a UK extension of the Fahey-Basho raga lineage filtered through minimalism, released on Tompkins Square, the label then reviving American primitivists.
Shares the old-time strand of American Primitive guitar that Jack Rose and the Black Twig Pickers were exploring at the same time; Daniel Bachman's later records sound akin to it.
Sounds rooted in the same 2000s free-folk and raga-guitar underground as Jack Rose, representing the instrumental side of Gunn's catalog before vocal albums like Time Off moved him toward C6.
Widens Rose's solo-guitar language with old-time accompaniment; later band-inflected instrumental records by Daniel Bachman and Nathan Salsburg sound akin to it.

Grew out of Tyler's session work with Lambchop and Silver Jews and out of the Fahey-Basho tradition Tompkins Square was reviving, launching a solo career that would push American Primitive guitar toward the Cosmic American sound of C6.

Approaches the same blues and old-time American song sources as John Fahey from a noise-rock and free-improvisation background, making Orcutt the harshest, most abstracted branch of the tradition alongside late-period Daniel Bachman.
Released on VHF, the label behind Jack Rose's Kensington Blues, it adapts the American Primitive vocabulary through an Irish and British folk-guitar lens that sounds akin to James Blackshaw's.
Jones's first album for Thrill Jockey, a label that later also released Marisa Anderson's solo-guitar records.
Grew out of Salsburg's work with Alan Lomax's archive, channeling old-time and British Isles folk melody through a solo-guitar format that sounds indebted to Fahey.
Bachman came up in the wake of fellow Virginian Jack Rose, and his playing sounds deeply indebted to Rose and the Black Twig Pickers' string-band-and-solo-guitar world.

album: Hard for to Win and Can't Be Won
lineage: Continues Salsburg's folklorist approach to solo guitar, sitting alongside Glenn Jones's old-time-inflected records as part of the 2010s revival's gentler, melody-first wing.
Builds on Behold the Spirit's Fahey-derived fingerstyle base with fuller studio production, carrying the tradition onto Merge Records, an indie-rock label.
Sits in the Fahey and Basho line as carried on by the 2010s Scissor Tail and VDSQ circle; its drones point toward the ambient-country crossover of Chuck Johnson's own later pedal-steel work.

Anderson's blues and old-time vocabulary sounds indebted to John Fahey and Sandy Bull's drone-and-raga side, and this record's electric widescreen sound runs parallel to William Tyler's and Chuck Johnson's moves toward ambient texture.

Extends Tyler's move from solo Fahey-style fingerpicking toward full-band Cosmic American Music, aligning him with the Grateful Dead-indebted C6 lane even as the core guitar language stays rooted in American Primitive technique.
Sounds indebted to the Fahey-descended solo-guitar tradition, filtered through a very specific Texas Panhandle sense of place.

A British contemporary of the original American Primitive generation whose intricate steel-string playing has long been championed by that scene's labels and younger players like Steve Gunn, even though most of his records, this one included, are built around his own singing.
Pushes the drone side of American Primitive guitar that runs back to John Fahey's Requia into more abstract territory, sounding akin to Jim O'Rourke's and Bill Orcutt's experiments.

album: You Never Were Much of a Dancer
lineage: Brings a punk-scene background to a fingerstyle and banjo style that sounds deeply indebted to Fahey and pre-war blues, released on Tompkins Square, a label central to the American Primitive revival.
A return toward an acoustic blues-and-hymn foundation that sounds indebted to Fahey's early Takoma work, after the electric detour of Into the Light.
Completes Salsburg's first run of three folk-song-rooted solo guitar records; he has also recorded a duo guitar album with James Elkington.
Sounds like the Fahey-descended fingerstyle tradition entered from an unusual technical angle, her own lap-tapping method setting her apart from the picking styles of Basho, Kottke and Rose.

Continues Tyler's arc from solo American Primitive guitar toward arranged instrumental Americana, sounding of a piece with Marisa Anderson's and Chuck Johnson's textured fingerstyle records of the same decade.
Continues the small-town, road-movie instrumentalism of Pedigo's earlier records, bringing Fahey-descended solo guitar into Mexican Summer's indie orbit.

Expands Williams's percussive-tapping guitar style with kalimba and banjo, sounding of a piece with peers like Marisa Anderson and Gwenifer Raymond who are also reshaping the Fahey-descended solo-guitar tradition.
Sounds like a continuation of the raga-inflected, collaborative wing of American Primitive guitar associated with Jack Rose and Six Organs of Admittance, colored by Chicago's improvised-music scene.

Continues Anderson's arc toward spare, meditative solo guitar begun on Cloud Corner, part of a broader early-2020s turn toward slow, minimal instrumental guitar shared with Hayden Pedigo and Eli Winter.

album: The Happiest Times I Ever Ignored
