Chris Hillman's second and final Asylum solo album, closing out the direct post-Byrds/Burritos country-rock line before his later work moved toward the more mainstream Nashville country of the Desert Rose Band.
Continues Harris's project of canonizing Gram Parsons' songbook while widening her sources to Townes Van Zandt and rock and roll covers.
Closes out Gene Clark's 1970s run with a return to a more commercial country-rock sound after No Other's ambitious detour.

album: Quarter Moon in a Ten Cent Town
lineage: A late entry in Harris's 1970s run that grew out of the Gram Parsons partnership, sounding a shade more polished than her earlier records.

A recording of the pre-Byrds, pre-Burritos band that trained several of this lane's key players (Clarence White, Gene Parsons, Gib Guilbeau) in hot country picking before they scattered into the Byrds, Flying Burrito Brothers and Swampwater.

Grows directly out of the Greenwich Village folk revival (Guthrie, Van Ronk) and electric Chicago/Chess blues; its fusion of rock band and literary lyric is the founding document the whole V22 lane, and later Neil Young and The Band, build on.
Follows directly from Bringing It All Back Home's electric side; later roots-rock songwriters from The Band to Drive-By Truckers sound indebted to its extended narrative-song form.

Extends the electric trilogy begun on Bringing It All Back Home and Highway 61 Revisited; the Nashville sessions directly set up Dylan's later country records and the whole Nashville-adjacent wing of the V zone.
Follows the Basement Tapes sessions with The Band, and sounds like it anticipates Dylan's own country records and the country-rock turn of the Byrds and Gram Parsons.

Grew directly out of The Band's years backing Dylan and the informal Basement Tapes sessions; Eric Clapton has said the record's plainness helped break up Cream, and it is a founding document for Southern rock, country rock and Americana alike.
The high-water mark of The Band's own catalog; the Southern storytelling rock of the Allman Brothers and, decades later, Drive-By Truckers' novelistic songwriting sound indebted to it.

Pushes the country move hinted at on John Wesley Harding all the way into Nashville proper, lending weight to the country-rock movement of V21 that the Byrds' Sweetheart of the Rodeo had kicked off the year before.
Follows the character-study songwriting of The Band with more autobiographical unease, reflecting the pressure of following two acclaimed records.
Sounds like a continuation of the plainspoken, domestic mode of John Wesley Harding and the Basement Tapes, and its warmth resembles the singer-songwriter records of V13 and V25.
An extension of the covers-and-traditionals instinct from the Basement Tapes sessions, and an early model for later artists' 'anti-image' covers records.
Shows the same Woodstock-honed roots-rock voice as the first three Band albums beginning to strain, foreshadowing the covers-driven Moondog Matinee.
Captures The Band's core studio catalog (Big Pink through Cahoots) in performance, and its horn-driven arrangements anticipate the larger ensemble sound of The Last Waltz.
Shows the R&B and rockabilly roots underneath the group's own original songwriting, the same well the band drew on for its own sound on Music from Big Pink.
Reunites Dylan with the Basement Tapes-era Band and directly sets up the tour that produced Before the Flood; its loose, road-worn feel points toward Blood on the Tracks the following year.
Grew out of the same 1974 reunion that produced the studio album Planet Waves, and stands as the definitive document of Dylan and The Band performing together on a large stage.
A late creative peak that shows the group's original songwriting voice intact after the covers-heavy Moondog Matinee, though it would be their last full album of new material before Islands.
A return to acoustic, lyric-first songwriting after the full-band Planet Waves, and a record later confessional and narrative songwriters across the V zone often sound indebted to.

Grew out of Dylan and The Band's convalescence-era sessions before John Wesley Harding; its ramshackle, communal recording ethic feeds The Band's own catalog and resembles later lo-fi/DIY roots recording.

Follows Blood on the Tracks' narrative songwriting into wider, almost theatrical storytelling, and its Rolling Thunder-era sound feeds directly into the live document Hard Rain and the tour film/album that followed.
Documents the second, harder-edged leg of the Rolling Thunder Revue that followed Desire, and its rough rearrangements set a precedent for Dylan's later habit of remaking his catalog live.
The last studio album released under The Band's original lineup, issued after their 1976 farewell concert and closing out the catalog covered by this lane.
An offshoot of The Band's mid-'70s dispersal into solo projects, sounding close to the Woodstock-scene singer-songwriter records made around it.
Closes The Band's story as a working group and, by assembling so many of their collaborators and influences on one stage, functions as a family tree for the whole roots-rock lineage this lane covers.
Bridges the Rolling Thunder era to the born-again gospel trilogy that begins with Slow Train Coming the following year.
A hard turn from the loose road-rock of Street-Legal into gospel testimony, directly setting up Saved and Shot of Love as a trilogy.
Closes out Dylan's religious period and re-establishes the dense, image-driven songwriting of his '60s and '70s work in a modern production context.
The first of two Lanois-produced comeback records (with Time Out of Mind) that reestablished Dylan as a vital songwriter for a new generation of roots-rock artists.
Continues the Lanois atmosphere of Oh Mercy but with a heavier, more haunted band sound, opening the door to the more traditional, self-produced records ('Love and Theft' onward) that follow.
Moves out of the Lanois-produced fog into the leaner, self-produced sound Dylan keeps for the rest of his career, and its blues/swing pastiche is a direct model for Modern Times.

album: The Bootleg Series Vol. 5: Bob Dylan Live 1975, The Rolling Thunder Revue
lineage: Part of Dylan's ongoing Bootleg Series of archival releases; it fills in the Rolling Thunder era alongside Desire and Hard Rain and is treated as canonical by Dylan scholars and podcasts like Jokermen.
The middle record of Dylan's 2000s self-produced trilogy alongside 'Love and Theft' and Together Through Life, deepening his late-career habit of channeling pre-rock American song forms.
Draws on the same Southern folk and old-time repertoire The Band mined, filtered through Helm's own Arkansas roots, and it directly set up his Electric Dirt and Ramble at the Ryman period.
Widens the acoustic Dirt Farmer sound into the full electric, horn-driven Band-style roots rock Helm helped invent, his last studio album before his 2012 death.
Continues the antique-blues persona of 'Love and Theft' and Modern Times toward longer, more explicitly mortality-obsessed narrative songs, setting up Rough and Rowdy Ways.
The culmination of the self-produced late style begun on 'Love and Theft', and a record much of the 2020s Americana and indie-folk scene sounds like it treats as a living reference point.

Its 'Seven Bridges Road' later became an Eagles hit, and Young's songwriting fed the outlaw scene directly when Waylon Jennings built an album around his 'Lonesome, On'ry and Mean'; its sound resembles the outlaw records that followed.
Establishes the ex-convict persona and blues-rooted grit that Coe carried into The Mysterious Rhinestone Cowboy and his later Columbia albums.
Predates Waylon Jennings's and Willie Nelson's outlaw breakthroughs by several years; Jennings recorded its songs, and the literary-songwriter model both men followed sounds indebted to it.

album: Help Me Make It Through the Night
lineage: Built around a Kris Kristofferson song recorded before his own version reached wide audiences, tying Smith's career directly to the outlaw movement's key songwriter.

album: The Silver Tongued Devil and I
lineage: Cements the confessional-songwriter model Kristofferson introduced on his debut, one that Waylon Jennings's and Billy Joe Shaver's songwriting sounds indebted to.
The first sign of the stripped-down, self-directed concept-album approach Nelson perfected on Red Headed Stranger, made while he was still pushing RCA for creative control.
Extends the socially conscious songwriting strand Kristofferson opened on his first two Monument albums, a thread that fellow Nashville outsiders like Bobby Bare and Tompall Glaser sound close to.
Its songs 'Seven Bridges Road' and 'Lonesome, On'ry and Mean' became touchstones for the outlaw movement, the latter as the title track of a Waylon Jennings album.
Grows out of Jennings's early-1970s push against RCA's countrypolitan production, and points directly at the fuller outlaw sound he found the next year on Honky Tonk Heroes.

album: Old Five and Dimers Like Me
lineage: The songwriter's-own-voice companion to Honky Tonk Heroes; the plainspoken storytelling of Steve Earle and Todd Snider sounds indebted to it.

album: Bobby Bare Sings Lullabys, Legends and Lies
lineage: The fullest statement of Bare's partnership with Shel Silverstein, the same writer Tompall Glaser devoted a whole album to the following year.
Its best-known song gave Waylon Jennings the title of his 1972 album Ladies Love Outlaws and helped name the movement.

Draws directly on Billy Joe Shaver's songwriting; the hinge point between Nashville countrypolitan and outlaw country, with later Jennings, David Allan Coe and Johnny Paycheck records sounding indebted to it.
Follows directly from Jennings's contract renegotiation with RCA and feeds straight into Honky Tonk Heroes; its title track comes from fellow outlaw precursor Steve Young.
Marks Nelson's break from Nashville production and the start of the Austin-based, genre-blending style that runs through Phases and Stages and Red Headed Stranger.
Coe's first Columbia record after Penitentiary Blues, and the start of a run of albums (Once Upon a Rhyme, Longhaired Redneck) that made him one of outlaw country's most theatrical figures.
A bleaker sequel to Jesus Was a Capricorn, the same Nashville-outsider songwriting turned inward.

album: Tompall (Sings the Songs of Shel Silverstein)
lineage: Tompall Glaser's Hillbilly Central studio was the hub where Waylon Jennings and other outlaw artists worked outside the Nashville label system, and this record ties that circle to Shel Silverstein's songwriting.
Extends the artist-controlled model Jennings won after Lonesome, On'ry and Mean and Honky Tonk Heroes, cementing his independence within RCA's Nashville system.
Builds on Shotgun Willie's Atlantic-era freedom and rehearses the story-album format Nelson used on Red Headed Stranger the following year.
Follows Lullabys, Legends and Lies in Bare's mid-1970s run of song-interpreter albums, this time drawing on the Texas progressive-country scene around Ray Wylie Hubbard and Jerry Jeff Walker.
Another mid-1970s Bare concept record following Lullabys, Legends and Lies, built around outside songwriters and sounding close to the funny-sad John Prine school.
A direct sequel to The Mysterious Rhinestone Cowboy, and its closing track ties Coe to the Prine and Goodman school of funny-sad songwriting that runs through the wider atlas.
Bridges outlaw country and Southern rock directly, pulling Allman Brothers and Marshall Tucker Band musicians into a Nashville country session.
Recorded at the height of the Nashville outlaw scene her husband Waylon Jennings and Tompall Glaser were building, but in a quieter, more introspective register than either man's records.
Follows Honky Tonk Heroes and This Time and precedes the outlaw movement's commercial peak on Wanted! The Outlaws and Ol' Waylon, showing the quieter side of the same songwriter-first approach.
The culmination of the narrative concept-album approach Nelson tried on Yesterday's Wine and Phases and Stages, proving outlaw country's stripped-down aesthetic could top the charts.
Follows Old Five and Dimers Like Me and, through the Capricorn Records connection, links Shaver's outlaw songwriting to the Southern-rock scene around the Allman Brothers.
Coe's declaration of independence within the outlaw scene, building directly on the persona introduced on The Mysterious Rhinestone Cowboy.
A quick Capitol follow-up to I'm Jessi Colter, released the same year as Wanted! The Outlaws, on which Colter also appeared.
Part of the Billy Sherrill-produced Epic run, with a hard-country delivery that sounds indebted to George Jones, and a direct lead-in to Take This Job and Shove It the following year.

album: The Great Tompall and His Outlaw Band
lineage: Made in the same Hillbilly Central studio and the same year as Wanted! The Outlaws, by one of that compilation's four featured artists.

album: Are You Ready for the Country
lineage: Its title-track cover of Neil Young links the outlaw scene directly to the Crazy Horse lineage the wider atlas traces, arriving right at the commercial peak Wanted! The Outlaws would soon confirm.

artist: Waylon Jennings, Willie Nelson, Jessi Colter and Tompall Glaser
lineage: The compilation that named and commercially confirmed the outlaw country movement, gathering the four artists whose Hillbilly Central-adjacent records define this lane.
Sits between Red Headed Stranger's austerity and Stardust's full embrace of pop standards, both records grown out of the creative control Nelson won at Columbia.
A sibling record to Shotgun Willie and Phases and Stages from the same Atlantic sessions period, delayed until Nelson's Columbia-era commercial power got it released.
Closes out Shaver's Capricorn run alongside When I Get My Wings, continuing the plainspoken songwriting that shaped Waylon Jennings's outlaw sound.
Continues the outlaw self-mythology Coe built across his Columbia albums, explicitly naming Jennings and Nelson as his peers in 'Willie, Waylon and Me'.
Released the same year as Rides Again, continuing Coe's prolific mid-decade run on Columbia.
Continues Colter's Capitol run after I'm Jessi Colter and Diamond in the Rough, turning the outlaw circle's plainspoken style toward devotional songwriting.

album: Take This Job and Shove It
lineage: Its title song, written by David Allan Coe, is direct evidence of the outlaw scene's songwriter-sharing culture, and the album's success made Paycheck a mainstream outlaw figure alongside Jennings and Nelson.
Represents outlaw country's full absorption into the mainstream that Wanted! The Outlaws had opened up the year before.
Connects the outlaw movement directly back to honky-tonk forebear Lefty Frizzell, the hard-country tradition this lane's style vocabulary is drawn from.
Its song 'Silver Stallion' was later covered by the Highwaymen, tying Clayton directly back to the movement's biggest names.
Draws directly on Townes Van Zandt's songwriting, linking the outlaw scene's Nashville wing to the Texas singer-songwriter tradition centered on Van Zandt and Guy Clark.
A self-aware sequel to Ol' Waylon and Wanted! The Outlaws, turning the movement's own marketing into songwriting material.
Follows Wanted! The Outlaws in pairing Jennings and Nelson as a duo act, and its hit single made the outlaw brand a household name beyond country radio.
Extends the pop-standards move hinted at on The Sound in Your Mind's medley into a full album, using the creative freedom Nelson's outlaw-era Columbia deal secured him.
The clearest outlaw-country-to-Southern-rock crossover record of the decade, and a direct precursor to the harder-edged mainstream country Williams built through the 1980s.
Clayton's commercial peak, extending the outlaw persona he introduced on his 1973 debut into more explicit, harder-edged territory.
A direct homage to Bakersfield hard-country figure Merle Haggard, tying Paycheck's outlaw-era catalog back to the honky-tonk tradition the whole movement drew from.

Predates Walker's move to Austin; 'Mr. Bojangles' itself became one of the most widely covered songs to come out of the Texas songwriter world, recorded by everyone from Nina Simone to the Nitty Gritty Dirt Band.

album: For the Sake of the Song
lineage: Grew out of the Houston folk clubs around Guy Clark and Mickey Newbury; Guy Clark and Steve Earle drew on Townes directly, and later writers like Jason Molina and Big Thief sound indebted to the same well.

Doug Sahm became a connective figure for the whole Texas scene, later recording with Bob Dylan and with Flaco Jiménez in the Texas Tornados, and the genre-blending, Tex-Mex-inflected side of Texas progressive country sounds indebted to him.

A direct continuation of the Houston/Nashville songwriter circuit around Guy Clark and Mickey Newbury; its bleak, riverine imagery echoes forward into Steve Earle and Jason Molina's own flood-and-mountain songs.

A foundational record of the Texas songwriter tradition; Guy Clark and Steve Earle drew on Townes directly, and Jason Molina's and Big Thief's hushed, plainspoken folk sound indebted to it generations later.
Bridges the early Poppy Records run with the harder-touring, harder-drinking persona that Blaze Foley and the outlaw wing of the Texas scene would later pick up wholesale.
'To Live Is to Fly' became a widely covered standard, carrying the Poppy Records-era songwriting into the alt-country and indie-folk generations, whose hushed songwriting often sounds indebted to it.

Marks Walker's turn from Greenwich Village folk toward the Austin cosmic-cowboy scene that would produce ¡Viva Terlingua! a year later, and helped introduce Guy Clark's songwriting to a wider audience.
Feeds the same Austin circle that produced Jerry Jeff Walker's Viva Terlingua, which covered its 'Backslider's Wine'; Murphey would name the 'cosmic cowboy' scene on his next album.

album: The Late Great Townes Van Zandt
lineage: Contains the two songs ('Pancho and Lefty,' 'If I Needed You') most responsible for carrying Townes's name past the Texas songwriter circle into outlaw and mainstream country.

A key Austin-scene contemporary of Jerry Jeff Walker and Guy Clark; 'Ballad of Spider John' and 'Muskrat Candlelight' were widely covered and helped establish the Austin songwriter circle's reputation in Nashville and beyond.
Part of the Austin cosmic-cowboy circle around Murphey and Steve Fromholz; its crossover success showed Nashville and the pop charts that Austin's songwriters could compete commercially, briefly.

A hub record for the whole scene, pulling in Bob Dylan as a collaborator and folding conjunto, Western swing and honky-tonk into a single album the way the Austin and San Antonio scenes were doing on stage.
Companion record to Doug Sahm and Band, further cementing the Tex-Mex/country/soul fusion that made Sahm a bridge figure between the Austin scene and San Antonio's conjunto tradition.

The clearest document of the cosmic-cowboy/progressive-country scene that Michael Martin Murphey and Willie Nelson's move to Austin also fed; the outlaw movement's live, unpolished aesthetic sounds close to it.

A satirical, provocation-first extension of the outlaw-country scene around Willie Nelson and Waylon Jennings; its funny-sad, taboo-baiting songwriting anticipates the deadpan school that runs from John Prine through Drag City decades later.
Gave the 'cosmic cowboy' scene its name, directly describing the same Austin crowd (Jerry Jeff Walker, Willie Nelson, Rusty Wier) that the rest of this lane's Austin artists belonged to.
A continuation of the Sold American persona within the outlaw-country mainstream.

Grew out of the same Houston folk scene as Townes Van Zandt and Mickey Newbury; Clark mentored Rodney Crowell and Steve Earle, and the Nashville songwriter tradition that follows sounds indebted to its detail-driven craft.

album: Ray Wylie Hubbard and the Cowboy Twinkies
lineage: Hubbard's songwriting was already central to the outlaw-country scene via Jerry Jeff Walker's recording of 'Redneck Mother', tying this record directly to the ¡Viva Terlingua! circle.

album: Don't It Make You Wanna Dance?
lineage: Represents the dancehall, bar-band end of the Austin cosmic-cowboy scene alongside Jerry Jeff Walker's Lost Gonzo Band and Michael Martin Murphey's early records.

Allen came out of Lubbock alongside the Flatlanders' circle; Juarez's conceptual, gothic storytelling sounds like a forerunner of the Southern-gothic strain later heard in Drive-By Truckers and Jason Molina.
A direct continuation of the Old No. 1 songwriting style, later covered and cited by Rodney Crowell and the wider Nashville songwriter circle Clark helped seed.

album: A Rumor in My Own Time
lineage: A central Austin-scene songwriter alongside Guy Clark and Jerry Jeff Walker; 'Texas Trilogy' was later covered by Lyle Lovett and remains one of the enduring pieces of writing from the progressive-country movement.
Grew directly out of the Flatlanders and Butch Hancock's songwriting; the alt-country bands of a decade later sound indebted to its full-band, rock-forward take on West Texas songwriting.

album: Live at the Old Quarter, Houston, Texas
lineage: The touchstone live solo singer-songwriter record for the Texas lane; later stripped-down live documents by Guy Clark and Robert Earl Keen sound like they follow its model.

album: West Texas Waltzes & Dust-Blown Tractor Tunes
lineage: Established Hancock as the songwriter engine of the Lubbock triangle, supplying material that Joe Ely turned into full-band rock and Jimmie Dale Gilmore turned into honky-tonk covers throughout the 1980s.
Closes the 1970s run of Guy Clark records that established the songwriting standard Texas and Nashville songwriters kept measuring themselves against for decades after.
Showcases Butch Hancock's songwriting through Ely's rocking band arrangements, a combination the Uncle Tupelo/alt-country generation's hard-driving country songwriting sounds indebted to.

album: There's a Light Beyond These Woods
lineage: The starting point of Griffith's career in the Texas folk scene that also produced Lyle Lovett and Robert Earl Keen; her plainspoken, small-town storytelling sounds indebted to Guy Clark's example.
Reclaims 'Redneck Mother' for its own writer after Jerry Jeff Walker's Viva Terlingua made it an outlaw-country standard, closing the loop on one of the scene's most-covered songs.
Closes out the classic-era Townes catalog before the long gap to At My Window, and 'No Place to Fall' became another widely covered standard for the Texas songwriter tradition.
Its harder edge sounds like it anticipates the punk-adjacent audience Ely found when the Clash took his band on tour the following year.
Shares players such as Lloyd Maines with Joe Ely's late-'70s records, and Drive-By Truckers' and Todd Snider's funny-bleak Southern narratives sound indebted to its satirical small-town storytelling.
Continues the self-released, DIY model Hancock kept using throughout his career, a direct precedent for the independent-label ethos later Texas and alt-country songwriters relied on.
A direct product of the Clash/Joe Ely Band connection, one of the clearest real-world links between Texas progressive country and the UK punk scene of the same moment.

Documents the mid-1980s Texas A&M/Austin songwriter circle that produced both Keen and Lyle Lovett, a direct continuation of the Guy Clark/Townes Van Zandt storytelling tradition into the next generation.
An essential later record that carried Townes's songwriting into the emerging Americana world, where songwriters like Nanci Griffith, Lyle Lovett and Robert Earl Keen sound close to his example.
An essential later record from the Lubbock triangle, turning Butch Hancock's songwriting into classic honky-tonk vocal performance.

Documents the Austin outlaw-folk fringe around Townes Van Zandt that Foley belonged to; 'If I Could Only Fly' was recorded by Merle Haggard and 'Clay Pigeons' by John Prine, carrying his songwriting far past the small club it was taped in.
Deepens the honky-tonk-by-way-of-Lubbock sound Gilmore established on Fair & Square, bridging the Flatlanders' 1972 sessions and his eventual mainstream Nashville-adjacent career.

Keen's storytelling sounds grown directly out of Guy Clark and Townes Van Zandt's example, and 'The Road Goes On Forever' became a widely covered anthem for the Texas/Red Dirt country scene of the 1990s and 2000s.

album: More a Legend Than a Band
lineage: The founding document of the Lubbock songwriter triangle, sending Gilmore, Ely and Hancock off on separate solo careers that fed back into the same scene; later alt-country writers' fascination with lost, authentic records sounds shaped by its legend.
Shows the Old No. 1 songwriting style fully matured, and sits comfortably beside the 1990s Americana records of Rodney Crowell and Steve Earle, which share its plainspoken approach.
Its cover of Steve Earle's Townes Van Zandt tribute ties Clark's 1970s Texas songwriting circle directly to the Americana format that formed around it.

An archival release of pre-fame recordings by the same Austin outlaw-folk songwriter documented on Live at the Austin Outhouse, filling out the picture of Foley's writing before Townes Van Zandt and the Outhouse crowd took notice of him.

Within Hazlewood's own catalog it sets up the narrated, character-driven persona of his later albums, and its narrated-town format sounds like an early model for the storytelling song cycles this lane is built around.

A cornerstone Greenwich Village folk record; Karen Dalton, who worked the same Village circuit as Neil, and later country-folk storytellers sound indebted to its plain, image-based songwriting and warm baritone delivery.

Part of the same Greenwich Village folk circuit as Fred Neil and Karen Dalton; his songs were widely covered by other singers, and later confessional singer-songwriters sound indebted to its plain, direct writing.
Set a template for Southern gothic narrative songwriting that later Delta-set storytellers, including Prine's Kentucky material and the modern Southern storytelling rock lane, draw on.

Consolidates the confessional folk style of Hardin's debut, and through 'If I Were a Carpenter' became one of the most widely covered songs to come out of the Greenwich Village scene, feeding directly into mainstream pop and country repertoires.

Deepens the Southern gothic storytelling Gentry began on Ode to Billie Joe, and its song-cycle structure sounds like a forerunner of later Delta-set narrative records in the Southern storytelling rock lane.

Extends the plainspoken, unhurried songwriting of Neil's self-titled album into looser studio-jam territory, closing out his brief major-label recording career before he withdrew from the music industry.

Ford's country-soul songwriting fed directly into other artists' hits, including Aretha Franklin's 'Niki Hoeky' and Bobby Womack's catalog, even as his own recording career stalled, and Harlan County has since been reclaimed by reissue labels as a missing link between Southern storytelling and Muscle Shoals-style country soul.

album: It's So Hard to Tell Who's Going to Love You the Best
lineage: Emerged from the same early-1960s Greenwich Village folk scene as Dylan, Fred Neil, and Tim Hardin, several of whose songs she interprets here, and her phrasing has been cited as a direct influence on singers from Nick Cave to later indie-folk vocalists.
Newbury's Nashville circle overlapped directly with Kris Kristofferson and Waylon Jennings, and the outlaw songwriters who followed sound indebted to his hushed, mood-driven song construction.

album: Boy Named Sue (And His Other Country Songs)
lineage: Silverstein's Nashville songwriting connections to Johnny Cash and Bobby Bare tie him directly into the outlaw and mainstream country worlds this lane borders, and his comic, plainspoken storytelling is a direct precursor to the funny-sad tradition Prine and Goodman built up at the same time.

album: Ballad of Forty Dollars and His Other Great Songs
lineage: Set the template of narrative country singles that Hall expanded into full concept albums over the next several years, running parallel to (and sounding close to) Prine's own early songwriting.

Establishes the small-town, first-person narrative style Hall carried through In Search of a Song and The Storyteller, and resembles the plainspoken songwriting Prine was developing in Chicago around the same time.

Extends the hard-luck Southern narrative songwriting of Gentry's earlier records, and Reba McEntire's 1990 cover of the title song carried it into mainstream country; later Southern storytelling songwriters sound indebted to its unsentimental voice.

Produced by Robbie Robertson and steeped in the same rootsy, plainspoken songwriting the Band was developing at the same time, directly linking Winchester's exile narratives to the Dylan and the Band lineage (V22) this whole zone traces back to.

Extends the narrated concept-album approach of Trouble Is a Lonesome Town into lush orchestration; its later Light in the Attic reissue brought it to a new indie audience, and cosmic-country revivalists sound indebted to its blend of cowboy persona and orchestral pop.

Came out of the late-1960s New York and Boston folk-club circuit; its funny-sad, talk-sung confessionals run parallel to John Prine's early records and sound like a template for later deadpan, self-mocking songwriters.
Caps Gentry's run of Capitol records; its self-produced, orchestrated storytelling sounds like an early model for later singer-songwriters who shape their own records.

Emerged from the early-1970s Chicago folk-club scene alongside Steve Goodman, who helped bring Prine to Kris Kristofferson's attention; the deadpan funny-sad line through Bill Callahan and David Berman to MJ Lenderman sounds indebted to it.
Recorded in the Woodstock orbit; its reissue-era rediscovery made Dalton a reference point, and later indie folk singers sound indebted to her unguarded, behind-the-beat phrasing.

Continues the song-cycle storytelling of Hazlewood's earlier concept records, tightened into a single breakup arc; later breakup-concept records in country and indie songwriting sound indebted to its spoken, confessional framing.

Continues directly from Wainwright's debut; its diaristic, self-mocking storytelling sits alongside Prine's outward-looking character studies as a parallel strand of early-1970s funny-sad songwriting that later deadpan writers sound indebted to.

Written within the early-1970s Nashville songwriter circle around Kris Kristofferson and Townes Van Zandt, both of whom Newbury knew and encouraged; its slow, orchestrated mood pieces sound like an ancestor of later hushed, atmospheric country songwriting.

Goodman championed John Prine on the Chicago folk-club circuit and helped bring him to Kris Kristofferson's attention, making the two songwriters' debuts the twin foundation of this lane's Chicago wing.
Draws directly on Kentucky small-town material and shares a plainspoken narrative style with Prine, Goodman and later Southern storytelling songwriters.

Moves Andersen's songwriting away from the topical Greenwich Village folk of his Vanguard years toward plainer, more personal storytelling that sounds close to Mickey Newbury and Jesse Winchester in the same period.
Follows directly from Winchester's debut, keeping the exile-songwriter perspective that ties him to the same Band-adjacent roots-rock lineage running through this lane.
Follows directly from John Prine (1971) and pulls its stripped-down string-band sound from the Carter Family and pre-bluegrass roots music that the Roots lane (R1) supplies to the whole atlas.
Stretches the storytelling persona of Cowboy in Sweden and his earlier concept albums into funk- and soul-derived production, keeping the voice while dropping most country instrumentation.
Its full-band arrangements pulled Wainwright's plainspoken storytelling toward a more commercial folk-rock sound, setting it apart from the sparer Chicago-scene records of Prine and Goodman.

Silverstein's work as a Nashville songwriter, including 'A Boy Named Sue' for Johnny Cash and many songs for Dr. Hook & the Medicine Show, made him a direct bridge between comic verse and country songcraft; later deadpan songwriters in the Prine line sound indebted to that mix.
Grew from the same Chicago folk scene as Goodman's debut, where he and John Prine shared stages and traded songs through the early 1970s.
Named for the nickname Hall already carried, it sums up the plain, first-person narrative approach that makes him a direct peer of Prine within this lane.

Extends the narrative-song format of Ballad of Forty Dollars and In Search of a Song into topical and political territory, a move later storytelling songwriters in the Southern storytelling rock lane (V3) resemble.
Continues the storytelling style of the first two Atlantic albums while pulling Prine's sound closer to the honky-tonk and outlaw country of the neighboring V23 and V26 lanes.
Johnny Cash's 1994 cover of 'The Man Who Couldn't Cry' carried one of its songs into mainstream country storytelling, much as Prine's songs travelled through other singers.

Completes Newbury's early-1970s run of mood-piece albums that made him a songwriters' songwriter in Nashville; its slow, bleak arrangements sound like a forerunner of later hushed country and slowcore-leaning songwriting.

album: Songs of Fox Hollow (For Children of All Ages)
lineage: An outgrowth of the same plain, story-first songwriting Hall used on his adult albums, showing the storyteller approach carrying over into any subject matter.
Marks Prine's furthest reach toward rock production before he moved to Asylum and pulled back toward the sparer sound of Bruised Orange.
Continues the collaborative songwriting of Goodman's earlier records, here extended to a co-write with Jimmy Buffett.
Marks Winchester's return to U.S. stages after his years in Montreal, closing the arc that began with his Robbie Robertson-produced debut.

Produced by fellow Chicago songwriter Steve Goodman, tying the two together as this lane's central Chicago-scene pairing; the deadpan funny-sad line that runs to David Berman and MJ Lenderman sounds indebted to its balance of humor and grief.
Closes the run of 1970s Atlantic and Asylum albums that established Prine's plainspoken template before his 1980s hiatus and 1984 return on his own Oh Boy label.
Begins the Oh Boy era of Prine's career, a self-released model that later songwriters in the Drag City deadpan school (V2) and the modern barroom-storyteller lane (C2) resemble.
Reconnects 1990s roots-rock production with Prine's founding storytelling style, and sounds like the album that brought him back into view for younger roots songwriters.
Pulls the lane's storytelling style back toward its honky-tonk roots in V26, and 2010s husband-and-wife Americana duet acts sound indebted to its DeMent duets.
Represents the mature, unhurried version of the plainspoken storytelling Prine established in 1971, which later deadpan writers like MJ Lenderman sound indebted to.
Closes Prine's catalog on the same plainspoken storytelling that opened it, and its Dave Cobb production connects it to the 2010s Americana revival that includes many artists in the C2 and C5 lanes.
An early example of the storytelling concept-album instinct Cash returned to on Bitter Tears; later folk-leaning country songwriters sound indebted to its narrated history.

An early-career record that shows Owens still working through Nashville songwriters' material just before he and Don Rich developed the treble-forward Bakersfield guitar sound that Merle Haggard and others then built on.
A commercial baseline of early-1960s Nashville honky-tonk, notable for launching Willie Nelson's songwriting career years before Nelson's own outlaw-country records redefined the genre.

Wells's answer song 'It Wasn't God Who Made Honky Tonk Angels' opened the door for women answering back in honky-tonk; Loretta Lynn started out modeling herself on Wells, and Jean Shepard and Tammy Wynette sound indebted to her plain delivery.
Tubb's Texas Troubadours sound predates Bakersfield, and the guitar-forward honky-tonk of Buck Owens and the plainspoken vocals of Merle Haggard and George Jones sound indebted to it.
An early example of the George Jones duet format that later defined his Epic-era partnership with Tammy Wynette, made while Jones was still on United Artists before his Musicor and Epic periods.

A transitional record between 1950s honky-tonk shuffle and the countrypolitan sound Price would help popularize later in the decade, and a documented early showcase for Willie Nelson's songwriting before his outlaw years.

The high point of Owens and Don Rich's mid-1960s Buckaroos sound; Dwight Yoakam later brought Owens back for a 1988 duet, and Gram Parsons-era country rock, cowpunk and alt-country bands sound indebted to its twangy, uptempo drive.

album: Bitter Tears: Ballads of the American Indian
lineage: Extends the storytelling-concept-album approach of Ride This Train into explicit protest songwriting, a strand later picked up by outlaw-era and Americana songwriters addressing similar material.

album: I've Got a Tiger by the Tail
lineage: Extends the Together Again-era Buckaroos sound at faster tempos; cowpunk bands like X and the Blasters sound indebted to its guitar-forward energy two decades later.
Established Smith as one of the defining honky-tonk voices of the mid-1960s; Dolly Parton has named her among the very few true singers, and later traditionalist women sound indebted to her phrasing.
Documents Cash's mid-1960s absorption of Bob Dylan's songwriting just before their own creative relationship deepened, tying this lane directly to V22 (Dylan and The Band).

Haggard played bass in Wynn Stewart's band before going solo, and this record extends the Bakersfield honky-tonk sound Stewart and Buck Owens had popularized, opening the run of Haggard albums that became the hard-country reference point.
A victory-lap document of the Buckaroos' mid-1960s prime; later roots-rock and alt-country live records sound indebted to its bright, fast stage sound.

One of several mid-1960s Buckaroos albums that kept the Bakersfield sound in heavy rotation on country radio while Merle Haggard's parallel Capitol catalog pushed it in a harder, more narrative direction.

artist: Hank Thompson and His Brazos Valley Boys
lineage: Thompson's Texas Western-swing-inflected honky-tonk runs alongside the Bakersfield and Nashville strands of this lane, connecting hard country back to the pre-1965 Western swing tradition covered in Roots.
An early model for women singing hard, unsoftened honky-tonk; Loretta Lynn's blunt drinking-and-heartbreak songwriting sounds indebted to it.

album: Swinging Doors and the Bottle Let Me Down
lineage: Follows directly from Strangers and cements the Haggard/Strangers honky-tonk sound; later alt-country bands' lean barroom arrangements sound indebted to it.
A Bakersfield-scene songwriter who carved out the trucker-song niche within hard country; the 1970s trucking novelties and outlaw road songs sound indebted to it.
Parton's Monument-era debut, made before Porter Wagoner brought her to RCA and before the self-written, more fully country records like Coat of Many Colors.

album: Don't Come Home A-Drinkin' (With Lovin' on Your Mind)
lineage: Establishes Lynn's blunt, first-person honky-tonk songwriting voice that runs through Fist City and Coal Miner's Daughter; the alt-country women of the 1990s and after sound indebted to it.
Continues the ex-convict narrative voice from I'm a Lonesome Fugitive; later outlaw-country writers like Waylon Jennings and David Allan Coe sound indebted to the template it hardens.
Deepens the ex-con storytelling voice introduced on Strangers and points toward the more explicitly autobiographical Sing Me Back Home and Mama Tried the following year.

album: The Cold Hard Facts of Life
lineage: Part of Wagoner's long-running story-song tradition; later Southern-gothic narrative songwriting across country and Americana sounds indebted to it.

album: Your Good Girl's Gonna Go Bad
lineage: The start of the Wynette/Sherrill partnership that produced D-I-V-O-R-C-E and Stand by Your Man, and a founding document of the string-laden countrypolitan sound alongside George Jones's contemporaneous Epic records.

album: It's Such a Pretty World Today
lineage: Haggard played bass in Stewart's band early in his career; Buck Owens's bright Bakersfield shuffles sound close kin to Stewart's late-1950s and 1960s sides.

album: George Jones Sings the Songs of Dallas Frazier
lineage: Represents Jones's late-1960s Musicor period, the rawer honky-tonk sound that preceded his more polished Epic-era records with producer Billy Sherrill.

Lewis's Sun-era rock and roll roots (shared with Johnny Cash and Carl Perkins) get redirected into honky-tonk country here, connecting this lane back to the pre-1965 Sun rockabilly scene covered in Roots.

The record that reestablished Cash as a major artist and set the template for the prison and outsider empathy that ran through the rest of his catalog, directly followed by At San Quentin the next year.
Continues the frank, combative persona introduced on Don't Come Home A-Drinkin' and points toward the more explicitly autobiographical Coal Miner's Daughter a few years later.
The culmination of Haggard's 1967-68 run of ex-convict songs; the Grateful Dead covered the title track, and 1990s alt-country bands sound indebted to its lean shuffle.
Sits between Branded Man and Mama Tried in Haggard's run of ex-convict narratives; later story-songwriters from the outlaw scene through Steve Earle sound indebted to its restraint.
A commercial and artistic peak of the Wynette/Sherrill countrypolitan sound, released the same year as George Jones's Musicor work and a direct precursor to Stand by Your Man the following year.
The direct sequel to At Folsom Prison, cementing Cash's outsider-empathy persona and giving him his biggest crossover pop hit via Shel Silverstein's songwriting.
Grows out of Pride in What I Am's working-class themes and turns Haggard into the era's most visible country voice on the other side of the culture wars from Woodstock-adjacent rock.
Bridges the ex-convict narratives of Branded Man and Sing Me Back Home with the working-class populism of Okie from Muskogee and the records that followed it.
Explicitly connects Haggard's Bakersfield sound back to Jimmie Rodgers and the pre-1965 country roots this lane's parent lane (Roots) covers.
The commercial peak of the Wynette/Sherrill partnership and one of the most-covered and most-discussed songs to come out of the countrypolitan wing of this lane.
Marks Twitty's move from Elvis-indebted rock and roll into mainstream Nashville country, sounding close to the Jones and Wynette countrypolitan records of the same years.
Made at the height of Cash's late-1960s comeback, when his ABC television show was also giving a platform to younger Nashville songwriters like Kris Kristofferson.
Continues the bleak, narrative-driven story-song tradition of The Cold Hard Facts of Life, part of Wagoner's pre-Dolly-Parton solo catalog of hard-luck character studies.
One of several Wynette/Sherrill Epic albums released in rapid succession around 1969-70 that kept the countrypolitan ballad formula in constant rotation on country radio.
The record where Parton's own songwriting, rather than assigned Nashville material, became the center of her albums, directly setting up My Tennessee Mountain Home and Jolene.

The definitive Loretta Lynn autobiographical statement; Jack White, a longtime admirer, later produced her 2004 comeback Van Lear Rose, and Southern storytelling songwriters sound indebted to its plain autobiography.
Part of Haggard's early-1970s turn toward more varied, album-oriented work between the topical hits of Okie from Muskogee and the song-based records that followed.
Represents the more reflective, adult-leaning side of Haggard's early-1970s catalog; the songwriterly wing of outlaw country sounds indebted to this strand.

album: Let Me Tell You About a Song
lineage: An unusually explicit statement of the storytelling ethic that runs through the whole Bakersfield and hard-country lane; later spoken-intro and songwriter-focused records in country and Americana sound indebted to it.
A piano- and soul-inflected variant of the Sherrill countrypolitan sound that dominates the Epic side of this lane, made by a Sun Records alumnus.
Extends the autobiographical, self-written songwriting Parton established on Coat of Many Colors, part of her early-1970s run of albums about her Tennessee upbringing.
Part of the long-running Jones/Wynette duet catalog produced by Billy Sherrill, a commercial and emotional high point of 1970s countrypolitan dueting.

album: Whiskey River / There Stands the Glass
lineage: Bush's Texas dancehall honky-tonk, developed alongside his former bandleader Willie Nelson, directly supplied the outlaw-country movement's signature entrance music via the title song.
Parton's songwriting peak of the mid-1970s, directly following Coat of Many Colors and My Tennessee Mountain Home, and among the most covered country songwriting of the era.
Brings the Texas Tejano and swamp-pop scenes directly into the Nashville country mainstream, a border-crossing strand of hard country distinct from both Bakersfield and Nashville proper.

A high point of the Jones/Sherrill Epic partnership that also produced Tammy Wynette's biggest records, and a clear influence on the vocal-forward ballad tradition later country singers kept returning to.

album: If We Make It Through December
lineage: Continues the working-class storytelling of Pride in What I Am and Okie from Muskogee; later Southern storytellers like the Drive-By Truckers sound indebted to its unsentimental view of hard times.

album: I Just Started Hatin' Cheatin' Songs Today
lineage: Part of a mid-1970s traditionalist honky-tonk strain alongside Gene Watson and Vern Gosdin; the neo-traditionalist and new-outlaw scenes covered in V7 and V19 sound indebted to it.
Part of Parton's mid-1970s run of self-written RCA albums between Jolene and her later pop crossover, still working in the classic-country mode this lane covers.

Draws on the Bakersfield and honky-tonk tradition of Haggard and Owens but pushes the vocal delivery toward something rawer and more rock-inflected; later alt-country and loud-twang bands sound indebted to it.

album: You're Not the Woman You Used to Be
lineage: Stewart's pre-RCA debut, showing his signature vocal style already intact before Out of Hand made it famous.

A Texas honky-tonk-club breakthrough that reached national distribution on Capitol; it sounds of a piece with the mid-1970s traditionalist current of Moe Bandy and Vern Gosdin pushing back against countrypolitan production.
Continues Bandy's traditionalist honky-tonk stance from his debut, drawing directly on his pre-music career as a professional rodeo rider for its central metaphor.
A direct continuation of the Out of Hand sound, part of Stewart's mid-1970s RCA run that made him a cult favorite among honky-tonk purists even as his chart fortunes cooled.
Continues the Jones/Sherrill countrypolitan ballad style established on The Grand Tour, recorded during the same personal turmoil that shaped his and Wynette's duet records.
The bleakest and most narratively pointed entry in the Jones/Wynette duet catalog, made after their real marriage ended, and a touchstone for later divorce-themed country records.
Part of Stewart's mid-1970s RCA streak, maintaining the honky-tonk-rock intensity of Out of Hand as his commercial momentum began to slow.

Gosdin's path runs from 1960s California country-rock circles, singing with Chris Hillman in the Hillmen and recording with Gene Clark, into 1970s traditionalist honky-tonk, connecting this lane to the Byrds and Burrito Brothers scene in V21.
The tail end of Stewart's classic RCA period; 2010s and 2020s alt-country and loud-twang bands sound indebted to this catalog's raw, yelping honky-tonk.
A late, harder-bitten entry in Haggard's honky-tonk run; the more confessional, worn-in country songwriting of the 1980s sounds indebted to it.
The peak of the Jones/Sherrill Epic partnership; the neo-traditionalist wave that followed sounds indebted to its proof that classic vocal country could still reach the top in 1980.
A late-career return to the plain, Telecaster-driven Bakersfield sound of Haggard's Capitol years, made just as neo-traditionalists like George Strait were bringing that plainness back into fashion.

A bridge from classic Haggard and Jones-style hard country into the 1980s neo-traditionalist and new-outlaw movements this lane feeds (V19, V7); those later records sound indebted to its plain, drawled approach.

A 2004 return to Lynn's plainspoken honky-tonk songwriting, filtered through Jack White's garage-rock production; included here as the culmination of her hard-country storytelling even though its era and sound sit outside this lane's classic 1965-1977 core.

Sits at the hinge between the Dead's early acid-rock period and the Hunter-Garcia songwriting partnership that defined Workingman's Dead and American Beauty; several of its songs stayed in rotation alongside the country-folk catalog for the rest of the band's career.

Documents the raga- and blues-based jamming the Dead developed out of the Bay Area psychedelic ballroom scene before Robert Hunter's songwriting and pedal steel pulled the band toward country; the extended-jam template here fed every later version of the band's live sound.

A direct sequel to Workingman's Dead in sound and method, drawing on the same country-rock vocabulary the Byrds and Gram Parsons had opened up; its songs became lifelong staples for Jerry Garcia's own solo bands and for jam-band and Americana acts that followed.

Grew out of the Byrds' and Gram Parsons' country-rock turn and the vocal-group discipline of Crosby, Stills & Nash; it set the template for Bob Weir's Ace and for New Riders of the Purple Sage, born from the same Marin scene with Garcia on pedal steel.

Bridges the songwriting of Workingman's Dead and American Beauty with the road-tested jam band the Dead became on Europe '72, and its Merle Haggard cover ties the record directly to the Bakersfield honky-tonk tradition underneath the whole lane.

artist: New Riders of the Purple Sage
album: New Riders of the Purple Sage
lineage: Born directly out of the Grateful Dead's Bay Area circle, with Garcia on pedal steel; the New Riders extended the Dead's own country turn into a dedicated band that opened for the Dead on the road.

A direct extension of the same Hunter/Garcia-adjacent Marin scene, co-written largely with lyricist John Perry Barlow; its songs entered the Grateful Dead's own live repertoire almost immediately, blurring the line between solo album and band album.

Extends the country-song repertoire of Workingman's Dead and American Beauty into a full electric live show; later jam-band and cosmic-country road bands sound indebted to its loose, song-first touring sound.

Grew out of the same Hunter-Garcia songwriting partnership behind Workingman's Dead and American Beauty, performed almost as a one-man home-recording experiment; several songs became permanent fixtures of both the Dead's and the Jerry Garcia Band's live shows.

artist: New Riders of the Purple Sage
lineage: Follows directly from the band's self-titled debut, with new pedal steel player Buddy Cage taking the group further into straight honky-tonk territory than Garcia's playing had allowed.
Moves the Dead's country-folk songwriting toward jazz-leaning textures that sound close to Garcia's parallel work with Merl Saunders, setting up From the Mars Hotel and Blues for Allah.

artist: New Riders of the Purple Sage
lineage: Represents the New Riders at their commercial height, drawing on Peter Rowan, whose songs also anchored Old & In the Way, from the same Bay Area circle.

Continues the Grateful Dead Records-era blend of concise songwriting and country-rock instrumentation; later jam-band and Americana sets sound indebted to it, with 'Scarlet Begonias' becoming a widely covered staple.

album: Tales of the Great Rum Runners
lineage: Written by the same lyricist behind Workingman's Dead and American Beauty, it is the clearest standalone statement of the plainspoken, rustic-American songwriting Hunter supplied to Garcia, Weir and the New Riders throughout the era.

Represents the outer edge of the country-psych lane, where the Dead's playing drifts furthest from the folk songwriting of Workingman's Dead toward the jazz and modal improvisation Garcia pursued in parallel with Merl Saunders.

Draws directly on the pre-rock bluegrass tradition of Bill Monroe and the Stanley Brothers, filtered through Garcia's own 1960s jug-band and bluegrass background; it is the direct ancestor of Garcia's later acoustic work with Grisman and the Jerry Garcia Acoustic Band.

Continues the Hunter-Garcia solo songwriting line begun on Garcia, feeding directly into the permanent Grateful Dead and Jerry Garcia Band setlists, since Comes a Time became a live standard for both groups.

Formed out of the same Marin County scene as the New Riders, with Torbert moving over on bass and Bob Weir joining as an active member, making it one more branch of the Grateful Dead family tree operating alongside the main band.

Represents the country-psych lane stretching toward mainstream studio pop, produced by the same Keith Olsen who worked with Fleetwood Mac; it marks the point where the Dead's studio sound gets furthest from the acoustic folk of American Beauty.

The fullest studio statement of the Jerry Garcia Band that grew out of Garcia's 1970s side projects with Merl Saunders and his own earlier solo albums, extending the Hunter-Garcia partnership a step further from the Dead's country-folk core.

A direct, self-conscious return to the acoustic country-folk mode of Workingman's Dead and American Beauty, and clear evidence that those two 1970 records remained the band's core songwriting language even after a decade of electric jamming.

Picks up the acoustic bluegrass thread Garcia opened with Old & In the Way in the mid-1970s, carrying it into the late 1980s with a new lineup and confirming how central that pre-electric repertoire stayed to his identity.

Revives the Garcia-Grisman partnership first heard in Old & In the Way, this time as a studio duo rather than a bluegrass band, and anchored the Dead-adjacent acoustic releases on Grisman's Acoustic Disc label through the 1990s.

Formed in Jacksonville, Florida and relocated to Macon, Georgia under Capricorn Records founder Phil Walden; Lynyrd Skynyrd, the Marshall Tucker Band and the rest of the Capricorn-era Southern rock bands sound indebted to its blues-and-jazz guitar interplay.

The album's Muscle Shoals-style songwriting and gospel-soul harmonies drew Eric Clapton, George Harrison, and Duane Allman into Delaney & Bonnie's orbit, making the duo a connective node between British rock and Southern country soul.
Cut at Stax in Memphis, Home ties Delaney & Bonnie's duet-and-horns sound directly to the Memphis soul studio scene.

A quick follow-up to Black and White that consolidates rather than expands White's swamp-rock sound; his original 'Rainy Night in Georgia' became a country-soul standard covered by Brook Benton and many others.

White's swamp-rock sound, mixing blues, country and Cajun rhythm, sounds like a reference point for the Southern rock and country-soul records cut in Muscle Shoals and Macon later in the decade; Elvis Presley's cover of 'Polk Salad Annie' carried it into the mainstream.

Bridges the loose blues-jam approach of the 1969 debut and the extended live improvisation of At Fillmore East, with 'In Memory of Elizabeth Reed' becoming a signature instrumental the band revisited for the rest of its career.
Scott Boyer and Tommy Talton later played in Gregg Allman's solo band, tying this gentler country-rock corner of the Capricorn roster directly to the Allman circle.
Lynyrd Skynyrd, the Marshall Tucker Band and the Capricorn Records acts that followed sound indebted to its extended-jam, dual-lead-guitar approach.

Lowell George left Frank Zappa's band to form Little Feat, and 'Willin'' was soon covered by Linda Ronstadt and others, carrying its truck-stop country songwriting into the Los Angeles singer-songwriter scene.
Completed the band's shift from Duane Allman's blues-slide leadership to Dickey Betts' more country-flavored songwriting, a change that deepened on the following year's Brothers and Sisters.
His 1961 'You Better Move On' was the first hit cut at Rick Hall's FAME studio, making him a foundational figure for the Muscle Shoals country-soul scene that produced Dan Penn and Eddie Hinton.
Bridges the straightforward roots-rock of the debut and the funkier, more expansive sound the band reached on Dixie Chicken with a new rhythm section.

Betts' country-leaning songwriting on this album pulled the Allmans closer to the honky-tonk and hard-country lineage of the Bakersfield/outlaw world (V26) while keeping the twin-guitar Southern rock core intact.

Penn co-wrote Muscle Shoals and American Sound Studio soul standards including 'Dark End of the Street' and 'Do Right Woman, Do Right Man' before making this rare album under his own name, tying the Southern rock lane directly to Muscle Shoals country-soul songwriting.
Made alongside the Allman Brothers Band's Brothers and Sisters sessions; its turn toward the gospel and R&B side of Southern music sounds close to Wet Willie and Eddie Hinton's records.

The expanded lineup and New Orleans-funk turn on this record became the sound most identified with Little Feat, directly shaping the horn-and-groove arrangements of the later live album Waiting for Columbus.

Establishes the Jacksonville three-guitar Southern rock sound that Blackfoot and Molly Hatchet extended, and that Drive-By Truckers took as explicit subject matter on Southern Rock Opera; newer bands like Wednesday sound indebted to that storytelling trunk line.
Formed in Spartanburg, South Carolina and signed to Capricorn Records alongside the Allman Brothers Band, the Marshall Tucker Band added jazz and country color to the label's guitar-rock sound.

A Texas variant on the same blues-rock foundation the Allman Brothers and Skynyrd drew on, ZZ Top's tighter, riff-based songwriting is a regional counterpart to the more improvisational Georgia and Florida Southern rock scenes.

Daniels's Nashville session career fed directly into a Southern rock band that name-checked the Allman Brothers and Marshall Tucker Band on 'The South's Gonna Do It,' an explicit statement of the genre's shared identity.
Formed by an Allman Brothers Band roadie and signed to Capricorn Records, Grinderswitch shows the twin-guitar Southern rock format being adopted by second-tier bands across the label's roster.
Continues the New Orleans-funk direction of Dixie Chicken with a fuller, more democratic songwriting approach across the band's three principal singers.

Follows directly from the debut and directly answers the Neil Young & Crazy Horse lineage (V20) that runs through the rest of this atlas, folding the Southern-versus-Young dialogue into the trunk line's own history.
Pairs new studio songs with the band's first official live recordings, documenting how far the Marshall Tucker Band's arrangements had opened up onstage by 1974.
Signed to Capricorn Records alongside the Allman Brothers Band and the Marshall Tucker Band, Wet Willie represented the label's horn-and-soul wing of Southern rock rather than its guitar-jam wing.
Appeared alongside Guy Clark and Townes Van Zandt in Heartworn Highways; his plainspoken storytelling sounds close to the country-folk songwriting of John Prine and Mickey Newbury.
Extends the Jacksonville three-guitar formula the debut established, trading some of Second Helping's polish for rawer, touring-band energy.
The high point of the band's mid-1970s Capricorn run, made with the same lineup that recorded the first three albums and setting up the more polished Carolina Dreams two years later.

Formed in Tampa and signed to Arista, the Outlaws brought a country-rock vocal-harmony sensibility, closer to Buffalo Springfield and the Byrds, into the same Southern rock circuit as the Capricorn bands.

Follows Fire on the Mountain and Nightrider as Daniels' band consolidated its audience, moving from the Southern rock underground toward the country-chart crossover it achieved fully with 1979's Million Mile Reflections.
Marks the brief two-guitar period between Ed King's exit and Steve Gaines's arrival later in 1976.

Documents the fully realized three-guitar Skynyrd lineup with Steve Gaines just before Street Survivors, and stands alongside live records by the Allman Brothers and Marshall Tucker Band as the genre's touring-document format.
Formed by Dickey Betts during the Allman Brothers Band's mid-1970s breakup, Great Southern kept the twin-guitar Southern rock sound alive under Betts' own name until the Allmans reunited in 1978.
Closes out the original Lynyrd Skynyrd lineup's catalog; the plane crash that followed its release is the climax of Drive-By Truckers' Southern Rock Opera.
Follows Searchin' for a Rainbow and tightens the band's jazz-and-country Southern rock into its most radio-ready form.

Formed by Allman Brothers Band members Chuck Leavell, Lamar Williams, and Jai Johanny Johanson during the Allmans' 1976 breakup, Sea Level is a direct Capricorn Records offshoot of the flagship band's sound.
Hinton's work as a Muscle Shoals session guitarist fed directly into this rare turn as a featured artist, connecting the Muscle Shoals soul catalog to the rest of this lane.
Captures the fullest live version of the New Orleans-funk-meets-Southern-rock sound the band built from Dixie Chicken onward, and stands as the closing statement of Lowell George's Little Feat.

Formed in Jacksonville in the wake of Skynyrd's success, Molly Hatchet represents the harder, more metal-adjacent direction Southern rock guitar bands took as the genre moved into the arena-rock era of the late 1970s and early 1980s.

Formed by Jacksonville musicians connected to the same scene that produced Lynyrd Skynyrd, Blackfoot pushed the Southern rock template toward a harder, more radio-friendly hard-rock sound by the end of the 1970s.

Written largely by her Velvet Underground and Greenwich Village circle, the album is the folk-pop bridge between the Velvets' orbit and Nico's own turn toward stark, avant-garde songwriting on The Marble Index.

Grew out of Lou Reed's pop-song craft and John Cale's minimalist drone background, packaged by Andy Warhol; it is the direct root of glam, punk, No Wave, and the deadpan indie songwriting later carried by Jonathan Richman, Pavement, and Yo La Tengo.
John Cale's arrangements carry the Velvet Underground's drone directly into stark solo songwriting; the record sounds like a root of gothic rock and of the slow, glacial end of slowcore.
Pushed the drone experiments of the first album to their extreme, setting a template that Sonic Youth, Swans, and other noise-rock and No Wave bands later followed.

John Cale's production is a direct, documented line from the Velvet Underground's drone experiments to Detroit proto-punk, and the album's raw, three-chord amateurism became a foundational text for punk rock itself.

Reacted directly against the noise of White Light/White Heat; Jonathan Richman was an avowed Velvets devotee, and slowcore acts like Low and Galaxie 500 and deadpan songwriters like Bill Callahan sound indebted to its quiet, guitar-based intimacy.

Shows the Velvet Underground's classically trained member turning immediately toward pop songcraft, a strand of his work that later jangle and chamber-pop indie bands, drawing equally on drone and melody, sound indebted to.
Continues the Cale-Nico partnership that turned Velvet Underground drone into stark solo song-form; hushed, harmonium- or organ-based indie and slowcore artists sound indebted to that approach.
Strips the band's earlier drone and noise down to concise, guitar-driven pop songs; Yo La Tengo and the Feelies, both open Velvets admirers, and power pop from Big Star onward sound indebted to it.
Marks Reed's first attempt to carry Velvet Underground songwriting into a solo career, a template of plainspoken narrative over conventional rock backing he refined across the rest of the decade.

Takes the Velvet Underground's deadpan character sketches and dresses them in glam-pop production by Bowie and Ronson; later art-pop and indie songwriters who mine outsider characters for empathy sound indebted to it.
A bootleg-quality document of live-in-the-room recording; later cassette-culture and lo-fi indie acts like Guided by Voices and Daniel Johnston sound indebted to its unpolished aesthetic.
Applies a Velvet Underground alumnus's classically trained arrangement skill to accessible pop songwriting, a combination that later chamber-pop and orchestral indie acts sound indebted to.

Extends the Velvet Underground's interest in unglamorous, novelistic character studies into full-album form, a model later followed by concept-minded songwriters from the Mountain Goats to Sun Kil Moon.
Extends the Cale/Nico drone sound into early electronic textures, a mix of synth and harmonium drone that later post-punk and dream-pop acts sound indebted to.
Its long, exploratory live arrangements sound like a forerunner of the extended guitar jamming that Yo La Tengo and Sonic Youth would later build whole albums around.
Shows the deadpan Velvet Underground storyteller turning inward toward quiet sincerity, a mode that hushed, plainspoken songwriters like Smog and Bill Callahan sound indebted to.
Carries the Velvet Underground's feedback drone to its logical, songless extreme, and noise and drone musicians have long claimed it as an early precedent for pure guitar noise as music.

artist: Jonathan Richman and the Modern Lovers
album: Jonathan Richman and the Modern Lovers
lineage: Shows Richman consciously stripping the Velvet Underground's noise out of his own sound, a move toward radical simplicity and lo-fi songwriting later mirrored by acts like Daniel Johnston and the Moldy Peaches.

Richman was an avowed Velvet Underground devotee and John Cale produced some of these sessions; the Sex Pistols later played 'Roadrunner', making the record a documented bridge from the Velvets to punk.

artist: Jonathan Richman and the Modern Lovers
album: Rock 'n' Roll with the Modern Lovers
lineage: Continues Richman's post-Velvets turn toward radical simplicity, an approach that fed directly into the amateurish, unpolished aesthetic later prized by lo-fi and slacker indie bands.

Grew out of the same downtown New York scene the Velvet Underground had helped seed, and its interlocking guitar lines sound like a template for R.E.M., Sonic Youth, and the broader American college-rock guitar vocabulary.

Reed's most punk-adjacent solo record, made as the CBGB scene the Velvets had helped inspire was breaking; its blunt, live-sounding production and long-form storytelling sound like a forerunner of art-punk and slowcore alike.

artist: Jonathan Richman and the Modern Lovers
lineage: Pushes Richman's post-Velvets embrace of simplicity and amateurism to its furthest point, prefiguring the deliberately childlike, lo-fi sensibility of artists like Daniel Johnston.
Robert Quine, formerly of Richard Hell and the Voidoids, brought the downtown New York punk guitar vocabulary the Velvet Underground had helped seed back into Reed's solo sound.
A vault release that filled in the melodic, song-oriented side of the Velvets' catalog; several of its songs were later reworked on Lou Reed's solo records.
Documents the noisier, unfinished corners of the Velvets' late catalog and shows how directly Lou Reed mined the band's shelved material for his own solo records.

Returns to the plain-spoken, street-level songwriting of the first Velvet Underground album, and its bare productions sound like a template for later songwriters who let lyrics, not arrangement, carry a record.

The song 'Velvet Underground' is an explicit tribute to the band Richman idolized, and the record's loose, unpretentious sound sits close to the 1990s lo-fi and slacker acts that treated him as a touchstone.

A direct root of the British folk-rock and fingerstyle-guitar lineage: Davy Graham's playing here shaped Bert Jansch, John Renbourn and John Martyn, and Collins's song choices fed the repertoire Fairport Convention later electrified.
Grew out of the Soho folk-club scene alongside Davy Graham and led directly to Pentangle; players from Jimmy Page to Neil Young have credited his influence.
Follows Bert Jansch's 1965 debut deeper into traditional ballad material and his partnership with John Renbourn, which led to their duo album and then Pentangle.

album: What We Did on Our Holidays
lineage: Grew out of the London club and Witchseason-production circuit around Joe Boyd, and set up Unhalfbricking and Liege & Lief, the records that made British trad song a rock instrument.
Part of the same late-1960s London singer-songwriter scene as Nick Drake and John Martyn, distinguished by John Peel's direct patronage through his own Dandelion label.

Directly followed What We Did on Our Holidays and Unhalfbricking, set the template for Steeleye Span and the whole British folk-rock movement, and is cited by later folk-indebted songwriters up through the Big Thief circle.

Bridges Fairport's early American folk-rock covers and the fully traditional Liege & Lief, and 'Who Knows Where the Time Goes?' became one of Sandy Denny's most covered songs across folk and indie circles.

Sounds of a piece with the late-'60s UK folk-guitar wave of Bert Jansch and Nick Drake; later in life Chapman worked with American guitarist Steve Gunn, who produced his 2017 album 50, linking him to the modern American Primitive circle.
Emerged from the same Witchseason/Joe Boyd stable as Fairport Convention and John Martyn; the modern indie-folk lineage running through Iron & Wine to Big Thief sounds deeply indebted to it.
Built from the individual folk-club careers of Bert Jansch and John Renbourn, fusing British folk song with jazz musicianship in a way few contemporaries attempted.
Continues the electric-trad sound Liege & Lief established and shows the jam side of British folk-rock, which later jammier folk-adjacent indie acts sound indebted to.
A direct continuation of Denny's Fairport Convention sound with her own band, sitting between Unhalfbricking-era Fairport and her solo albums.

Shares bassist Rick Kemp with Steeleye Span and sits in the Harvest-era British folk scene; the modern American fingerstyle circle, which Chapman later recorded with via Steve Gunn, sounds indebted to his open-tuned playing.

Produced by the same Joe Boyd/Witchseason circle as Nick Drake and Fairport Convention, and its rediscovery shaped 2000s freak-folk: Devendra Banhart championed and worked with Bunyan, and later pastoral indie folk sounds indebted to it.

Briggs's traditional singing directly shaped Bert Jansch, who learned songs like 'Blackwaterside' from her; this, her most song-based album, sits at the acoustic, least electric edge of the British folk-rock lane.
Follows Martyn's earlier folk-club albums and points toward Solid Air, carrying the same Danny Thompson/Pentangle-adjacent musicians who linked the London folk and jazz scenes.

The most arranged and outward-looking of Drake's three albums, sitting between the string-laden Five Leaves Left and the stripped-down Pink Moon, and drawing on the same Island/Witchseason session players as Fairport Convention and John Martyn.

album: The North Star Grassman and the Ravens
lineage: Follows directly from Fotheringay's breakup and keeps Denny's songwriting in the same Fairport-adjacent folk-rock lineage that later solo albums Sandy and Like an Old Fashioned Waltz continued.
Formed by ex-Fairport Convention bassist Ashley Hutchings as a harder-line continuation of the Liege & Lief experiment, pushing British trad song even further from rock band conventions.
The final, most minimal Nick Drake album; hushed acoustic indie folk from Elliott Smith through Adrianne Lenker and Big Thief sounds deeply indebted to it.
Thompson's first post-Fairport statement, setting up the guitar style and dry, story-driven songwriting he carried into the Richard and Linda Thompson albums.
Continues the Fairport-and-Fotheringay folk-rock sound in a more orchestrated, singer-songwriter direction that influenced later British female singer-songwriters.
Martyn's peak Island-era record, tied directly to Nick Drake through its title track and continuing the jazz-folk direction begun on Bless the Weather.
Follows Bert Jansch's solo run and Pentangle years, crossing British fingerstyle folk with the Los Angeles country-rock world via producer Michael Nesmith.

album: I Want to See the Bright Lights Tonight
lineage: Follows Richard Thompson's exit from Fairport Convention and his solo debut, and starts the Richard and Linda Thompson partnership that runs through Shoot Out the Lights.
The least folk-rock of Denny's solo run, pulled toward orchestral pop, though it still follows directly from Sandy and The North Star Grassman and the Ravens.
Continues the Richard and Linda Thompson partnership begun on I Want to See the Bright Lights Tonight, folding music-hall humor into the same folk-rock band.
The most explicitly devotional record in the Richard and Linda Thompson catalog, following Hokey Pokey and preceding a break before their late-1970s and early-1980s albums.

The later landmark of the Richard and Linda Thompson catalog, closing the folk-rock partnership that began with I Want to See the Bright Lights Tonight and pointing toward Richard Thompson's long solo career.

The template for the topical, talking-blues singer-songwriter tradition that runs through Pete Seeger and Bob Dylan, who modeled his early persona on Guthrie. The folk-songwriting trunk line reaching Townes Van Zandt and, eventually, Big Thief sounds indebted to it.

album: Singing the Traditional Songs of Her Kentucky Mountain Family
lineage: Her repertoire and dulcimer playing fed directly into the 1960s folk revival - Bob Dylan and Fairport Convention both drew on 'Nottamun Town' - and helped establish the dulcimer as a folk-revival instrument that indie folk artists still reach for.

The single most important source text for the folk revival: it directly shaped Bob Dylan and the New Lost City Ramblers, and its rediscovered artists fed the American Primitive guitar line. Gillian Welch and the 2010s indie-folk revival sound indebted to its songbook further downstream.

Cleared the commercial path for Patsy Cline, Loretta Lynn, Tammy Wynette and Dolly Parton to sing frankly about women's experience in country music; alt-country and Americana women songwriters sound indebted to that plainspoken woman's-eye view.

The close-harmony duo singing here was a model for the Everly Brothers, and Gram Parsons and Emmylou Harris covered Louvin songs. Its stock of tragic-ballad narratives sounds like an ancestor of the Southern gothic storytelling that runs down through Southern rock into Drive-By Truckers.

A direct and often-cited influence on Bob Dylan, Joan Baez and Janis Joplin, and a key figure in bringing spirituals and blues into the folk-revival concert repertoire that the whole folk-songwriting trunk line draws on.
Scruggs' banjo style became the default vocabulary for bluegrass banjo playing and fed into newgrass; indie and alt-country bands that add banjo to their sound still echo his clean, fast picking.

album: Johnny Cash with His Hot and Blue Guitar!
lineage: Set the minimal, rhythm-forward Sun sound and the plainspoken outlaw-adjacent persona that Cash carried into the Outlaw country movement; Southern storytelling songwriters from Steve Earle to Jason Isbell sound indebted to it.
'Freight Train' became a folk standard that generations of fingerstyle guitarists learned, and the American Primitive guitar line (John Fahey, Jack Rose) sounds indebted to her fingerpicking.
A direct bridge between old-time Appalachian duet singing and the brother-harmony sound that Simon & Garfunkel, the Byrds and Gram Parsons and Emmylou Harris's duets all drew on.

album: Johnny Cash Sings the Songs That Made Him Famous
lineage: Closes out the Sun era that established Cash's train-rhythm sound before his Columbia years broadened him into the Outlaw and Americana movements' patron saint.
Bridges Cash's Sun-era minimalism and his Columbia-era ballad writing, carrying his plainspoken storytelling forward into the Outlaw country and Americana songwriters who followed.

Drew directly on prewar string-band 78s and Harry Smith's Anthology of American Folk Music; the group's scholarly revivalism helped shape the 1960s folk revival and later roots-conscious players who dug into pre-war sources.

The Stanleys' raw mountain harmony style carried into Ralph Stanley's later solo career (including O Brother, Where Art Thou?), and the old-time-leaning wing of the 2010s bluegrass and indie-folk revival sounds indebted to it.

As one of honky-tonk's founding artists, Tubb helped make the electric guitar a country lead instrument; hard country and later alt-country bands built on that electric-guitar-led template sound indebted to him.
Their harmony-singing template runs forward into the Beatles, the Byrds' vocal blend, and the duet tradition Gram Parsons and Emmylou Harris carried into country rock.

Its gospel fervor and Southern-gothic imagery directly influenced the Byrds (who covered 'The Christian Life' on Sweetheart of the Rodeo) and Emmylou Harris, and it stands as a touchstone for later alt-country and indie artists drawn to sacred-and-profane country songwriting.

Its story-song format and Western imagery sound like a source for the outlaw-country movement's cowboy mythology and for narrative country songwriting generally, including the storytelling-heavy Southern rock and alt-country writers who followed.

The Bakersfield sound this record establishes was a direct model for Dwight Yoakam's 1980s revival of the style, and the Telecaster-driven honky-tonk that runs through the whole hard-country wing of the V sounds indebted to it.

Owen Bradley's Nashville Sound production model here shaped the country mainstream for the next decade; k.d. lang built an early persona around Cline, and later alt-country singers like Neko Case sound indebted to her vocal-forward torch style.

The starting point of Dylan's catalog, which this lane logs here by release year before his songwriting and 1965 electric turn move him into the Dylan and The Band lane (V22); 'Song to Woody' is an explicit tribute naming Woody Guthrie as his direct source.

album: Modern Sounds in Country and Western Music
lineage: Its genre-blurring template sounds like an ancestor of later crossovers between soul, pop and country songwriting, and its success kept country standards like Hank Williams's catalog in wide circulation outside Nashville.

Established Dylan as a songwriter rather than an interpreter; the plainspoken folk-songwriting line of Townes Van Zandt and John Prine, running on through Gillian Welch to Big Thief, sounds deeply indebted to it. Logged here by year before his 1965 electric turn carries him into V22.
