Watson's flatpicking vocabulary is foundational to the acoustic-guitar wing of American folk and bluegrass playing, and the 2010s indie-folk pickers sound indebted to it.

The core honky-tonk songbook that country music keeps rewriting; a model for George Jones, the outlaw country of Waylon Jennings and Willie Nelson, and the plainspoken heartbreak songwriters downstream through John Prine to today's alt-country.

album: The Essential Bill Monroe And His Blue Grass Boys (1945-1949)
lineage: The direct source of the entire bluegrass genre; its high-lonesome vocal style and hard-driven picking fed Flatt & Scruggs and the Stanley Brothers, and the 2010s bluegrass-inflected wing of indie folk sounds indebted to it.

Western swing's blend of jazz-informed horns and string-band instruments fed directly into Merle Haggard (who recorded a full Wills tribute album) and the Bakersfield sound, and its steel-guitar lead lines are an ancestor of the steel vocabulary the whole V draws on.

album: Where Did You Sleep Last Night: Lead Belly Legacy, Vol. 1
lineage: Directly covered by the folk revival (the Weavers took 'Goodnight, Irene' to number one) and by Lonnie Donegan's skiffle version of 'Rock Island Line,' which helped spark the UK skiffle boom that fed into the Beatles and, further downstream, the whole folk-into-rock trunk line.

album: Avalon Blues: The Complete 1928 Okeh Recordings
lineage: His gentle fingerstyle approach was a model for 1960s folk-revival guitarists like Dave Van Ronk, and the American Primitive guitarists sound indebted to his syncopated picking.

Established the singing-brakeman persona and blue-yodel sound that shaped Bob Wills, Hank Snow, Merle Haggard and Lefty Frizzell, and fed the train-and-drifter songwriting strain that runs through Woody Guthrie into the outlaw and Americana lines.
His vocal phrasing is a direct, oft-cited influence on Merle Haggard and Randy Travis, keeping the honky-tonk singing style alive as a technique that later alt-country and Americana singers study.

album: This Land Is Your Land: The Asch Recordings, Vol. 1
lineage: Preserves the bulk of Guthrie's Asch-era songwriting, the direct source for Pete Seeger, the Almanac Singers' topical-song lineage, and the folk-revival singer-songwriters who followed him into the 1960s.

The founding act of recorded country and folk music; Woody Guthrie borrowed Carter Family melodies, Johnny Cash married into the family via June Carter, and Bob Dylan and the folk revival covered their songs. Gillian Welch and the modern indie-folk line sound deeply indebted to that plain harmony-and-guitar style.

A pop-crossover cousin to the Nashville Sound records of V26 (Patsy Cline, Jim Reeves), taking countrypolitan toward Hollywood session sheen; its polish seems to point forward to Kenny Rogers and 1990s pop-country.

album: Does Fort Worth Ever Cross Your Mind
lineage: Pulls the mainstream back toward honky-tonk instrumentation after the countrypolitan pop-country of the 1970s; later traditionalists like Randy Travis, Alan Jackson and Luke Combs sound like they follow his template.
Part of the same mid-1980s neotraditionalist wave as George Strait; its commercial template seems to run forward through Alan Jackson and Garth Brooks into 1990s mainstream country.

Grows out of the neotraditionalist instrumentation Strait and Travis reestablished, but redirects it toward arena-scale showmanship and crossover production; it seems to open the path toward 1990s superstar country and bro-country's stadium ambitions.

A continuation of the Strait/Travis neotraditionalist lane, its title track openly defending traditional country against pop-country encroachment even as the format moved toward the Garth Brooks arena model.

Takes the pop-crossover ambitions of countrypolitan (Glen Campbell, and later Garth Brooks's arena scale) to a commercial extreme, largely abandoning traditional instrumentation; its pop-first approach seems to anticipate the hook-driven side of 2010s mainstream country.

A hinge point between 2000s arena country and full bro-country, grafting rap cadence onto Southern-rock guitar muscle; it seems to set up Florida Georgia Line's 2012 breakthrough and the wave that followed.

Sounds descended from the arena-scale, pop-crossover ambitions of Garth Brooks and Shania Twain, replacing steel and fiddle with programmed beats and rap cadence; alongside Jason Aldean's 'Dirt Road Anthem,' it is a defining bro-country record whose style Luke Bryan and Morgan Wallen carried on.

Sounds like a traditionalist correction inside the bro-country era, pulling the mainstream back toward guitar-driven arrangements while keeping its party-and-heartbreak subject matter; runs parallel to Morgan Wallen.

Sounds like the commercial endpoint of the bro-country line running from Jason Aldean and Florida Georgia Line, scaled to streaming-era volume and blended with hip-hop and pop; Luke Combs runs parallel as the more traditionalist pole of the same moment.
A 2020s continuation of the mainstream-country lineage running through Combs and Wallen, with rock-leaning production that sounds closer to the Southern-rock edge of the format.

A newer, more atmospheric strand of the mainstream-Nashville lineage, closer in mood to Kacey Musgraves's pop-leaning country turn than to bro-country's party anthems, suggesting a possible future branch away from the Wallen/Combs commercial center.

Descends directly from the outlaw-country tradition (Waylon Jennings/Willie Nelson) filtered through the same Stillwater, Oklahoma scene that produced Cross Canadian Ragweed, establishing Red Dirt as a self-sustaining regional alternative to Nashville.

Grows out of outlaw-country and Southern-rock lineages (V24 Texas songwriter tradition, V23/V7 rock) but stays a self-contained regional scene; its live-circuit model seems to lead into Turnpike Troubadours and the wider Red Dirt scene of the 2000s-2010s.
Bridges the independent Texas-country college-circuit tradition (V13/V24) with the Nashville mainstream, sounding like a forerunner of later regional acts crossing into arena Americana.
Carries the Cross Canadian Ragweed/Jason Boland generation's Red Dirt scene into the 2010s, with storytelling that sounds indebted to Guy Clark and Robert Earl Keen.
Draws on Southern-rock and outlaw-country lineages (V7, V23) through Dave Cobb's rootsy production; it seems to open the commercial lane that Zach Bryan and later arena Americana scaled further.
Follows a Texas-country-to-mainstream trajectory like Pat Green's two decades earlier, but sounds closer to the neotraditionalist wing of mainstream country than to bro-country's programmed beats.

Sounds akin to the Oklahoma singer-songwriter and Red Dirt tradition of Turnpike Troubadours, scaled to streaming-era volume with a rougher delivery; younger Oklahoma songwriters like Wyatt Flores sound like they follow in its wake.
A direct continuation of American Heartbreak's plainspoken, streaming-first songwriting, further cementing Bryan as the commercial center of the arena-Americana wave alongside Stapleton.

A geographically distinct (Appalachian rather than Texas/Oklahoma) branch of the same arena-Americana wave that Stapleton and Zach Bryan lead commercially, sharing festival bills and touring circuits with them.
Sounds like a stylistic descendant of Zach Bryan, working a Red Dirt-adjacent singer-songwriter lane at a smaller scale.
Bridges old-time and bluegrass tradition (X4) with a punk-energy, festival-scaled string-band sound that seems to foreshadow the stomp-clap-folk wave of the Avett Brothers and Mumford & Sons.

Grows out of the Avetts' earlier punk-folk scrappiness and string-band roots, redirected toward a festival-scale Americana sound akin to what Mumford & Sons and the Lumineers would soon ride commercially.
Sounds like the festival-Americana energy of Old Crow Medicine Show and the Avett Brothers turned into a UK indie-folk formula, a template for the stomp-clap-folk wave of the early 2010s.
A Pacific Northwest, Sub Pop variant of the festival-folk wave the Lumineers and Mumford & Sons rode, sounding closer to indie-pop harmony singing than to old-time string-band roots.
Sounds like a stripped-down American counterpart to Mumford & Sons' folk-revival formula; alongside the Avett Brothers, it helped define the festival-Americana mainstream of the 2010s.

Shares the festival-crowd, singalong-anthem instinct of Mumford & Sons and the Lumineers but channels it through horn-driven soul that sounds indebted to Stax, an adjacent branch of big-tent Americana.

album: By the Way, I Forgive You
lineage: A singer-songwriter-driven, less banjo-dependent branch of the festival-Americana mainstream, sounding closer in vocal scale to 1970s folk-rock than to stomp-clap folk proper.
Sits at the overlap of the big-tent Americana festival scene and the Southern/Texas songwriter tradition, closer to swampy roots-rock songcraft than to stomp-clap folk's banjo-strum anthems.
A gospel-and-soul-rooted branch of the festival-Americana mainstream that sounds akin to Brandi Carlile's emotional bigness; the duo later collaborated with Zach Bryan.

Descends from first-generation bluegrass (Bill Monroe, the Stanley Brothers; R1) but breaks from its strict traditionalism; its improvisational, genre-blending path seems to lead to Nickel Creek, Punch Brothers and Billy Strings.
Sounds like a newgrass descendant of New Grass Revival's genre-blending example, filtered through pop songcraft; Chris Thile went on to form Punch Brothers.
A polished, vocal-forward continuation of first-generation bluegrass (R1), sitting opposite the jam-leaning newgrass of New Grass Revival and Billy Strings.

Extends Nickel Creek's newgrass genre-blending toward classical composition and long-form suites, the most art-music-oriented branch of the bluegrass lineage that eventually feeds Billy Strings' and Molly Tuttle's more jam- and roots-rock-facing 2010s-2020s bluegrass.
Sounds like the clearest recent inheritor of New Grass Revival's improvisational newgrass, scaled to jam-band festival culture, alongside peers Molly Tuttle and Sierra Ferrell.
A former member of the Carolina Chocolate Drops, McCalla uses old-time banjo technique (R1) for Haitian-American and Creole storytelling, a culturally distinct branch of the tradition.
A 2020s culmination of the newgrass lineage running from New Grass Revival through Nickel Creek, sounding like a peer of Billy Strings in the current bluegrass revival.
A genre-blurring newgrass and old-time descendant that shares Molly Tuttle's and Billy Strings's bluegrass-revival moment while pulling in vintage pop and gypsy-jazz textures.

Sounds rooted in the same lo-fi DIY folk instincts as V11 and the American Primitive line near V8; Banhart's documented ties to the 2000s freak-folk scene (Vetiver, CocoRosie) lead it outward rather than back into Core twang.
A Drag City labelmate record that shares DNA with V11's home-recording aesthetic before Newsom's own arc pushes toward the chamber-folk maximalism of Ys.

Shares the wordy, storytelling instinct of V25/V13 songwriting but channels it into ornate chamber-folk theater, leading the band toward the prog-folk suites of The Hazards of Love rather than toward Core twang.
Extends the freak-folk branch further from V8/V11's DIY roots into a fuller, more collaborative psych-folk sound that fed the wider 2000s indie-folk scene rather than the Core.

Shares the rootsy indie-folk instincts of V5 (Iron & Wine) but pushes past songwriter-plus-guitar into full chamber arrangement, sitting alongside Beirut, the Decemberists and later 2010s art-folk rather than feeding the Core twang sound.

Shares the ornate-folk impulse of V5's rootsy indie folk and V30's UK folk-rock chamber pop, but its Balkan-brass focus sits with orchestral indie pop (Arcade Fire, Beirut's own later catalog) rather than Core twang.
Pushes the chamber-folk storytelling of Picaresque toward full prog suites, a path that leads outward into folk-rock and prog rather than back toward Core twang.
Sounds rooted in the DIY and American Primitive folk instincts near V8 and V11, but detours into art-song orchestration that points toward chamber folk rather than back toward Core twang.
A continuation of the Balkan/chamber-pop branch that Gulag Orkestar opened, feeding forward into Beirut's later, more electronic-tinged records rather than into the Core.
Sounds like a retreat from X5's ornateness back toward the rootsy, hushed indie folk of V5, showing how the chamber-folk branch can circle back near the Core's acoustic sound without joining it.

album: The Pilgrim, Their God and the King of My Decrepit Mountain
lineage: Descends from the same UK folk-rock chamber-pop lineage as V30 and the concept-album ambitions Sufjan Stevens and the Decemberists set for X5, carrying it into the current UK indie scene.
Sounds indebted to the Beirut/Decemberists chamber-folk template, a sign the X5 branch still produces new records rather than folding back into the Core.

Emerges from the Sub Pop/Seattle underground-rock world of V16's college-rock lineage and launches the emo line (X6) that seems, by way of American Football and the emo revival, to feed the twangy crossover of Core's C9.

Sounds like an offshoot of the American underground/college-rock noise of V16 and the punk foundation of X14; through shared members it directly opens the line to American Football and Joan of Arc and, later, the 2010s emo revival rather than Core twang.
Sounds of a piece with Sunny Day Real Estate in the second-wave emo line growing out of V16's underground rock scene, pointing toward the 2000s emo mainstream rather than the Core.
Sounds grown from the Midwest hardcore scene near X14 into the jangly, pop-facing wing of X6, pointing toward 2000s pop-emo and Modern Baseball-style revival bands rather than the Core.

A direct offshoot of Cap'n Jazz within X6 through Mike Kinsella, trading noise for math-rock jangle; the sound it codified seems to feed both later Midwest emo bands and the twangy emo crossover of Core lane C9.
Carries the American Football math-rock jangle forward into the 2010s emo revival within X6, part of the same scene that overlaps with Core's C9.
Another 2010s branch of the emo-revival wave within X6 that sounds indebted to Sunny Day Real Estate's dynamics, part of the same scene that overlaps with Core's twangy-emo crossover lane C9.
Sounds like a 2010s emo-revival descendant of the American Football/Promise Ring lineage within X6, part of the same wave that seems to feed the twangy emo crossover of Core lane C9.
Grows from the Dylan/Band roots-rock songwriting of V22 into full arena scale, defining the heartland rock lane (X7) that mostly stays outside the Core except for its stripped-down cousin Nebraska.
Represents the Midwest bar-band wing of X7's arena-rock lineage, staying within classic-rock radio rather than crossing into the Core's DIY scene.

album: Darkness on the Edge of Town
lineage: Continues the arena-scale storytelling of X7, tightening the sound in a way that anticipates Nebraska's stark turn back toward the Core's folk-songwriting roots.
A parallel Southern branch of X7's arena-rock lineage feeding out of the Byrds/Dylan-adjacent jangle of V22, staying in FM-radio rock rather than crossing into Core twang.
Continues the Midwest bar-rock strand of X7, staying firmly on classic-rock radio rather than feeding back into the Core.

The one heartland-rock record that reaches back into the V: its home-recorded, Woody Guthrie-indebted starkness directly influenced alt-country and indie-folk songwriters in V22's Dylan/Band lineage, making it the exception that feeds the Core rather than leading away from it.
Represents heartland rock's full pop-mainstream turn within X7, moving further from the Core's DIY roots than any other Springsteen record here.
Sounds like a Midwest counterpart to Springsteen's Nebraska within X7; its small-town storytelling brushes against the Core's songwriting without fully crossing into it.
Extends the Southern branch of X7 further from its jangle-rock roots into 1980s studio polish, staying outside the Core's rawer sound.
The true ground-zero record of the Seattle line (X8), growing directly from the noise-rock/underground scene of V16 without ever crossing into the Core's twang.

Grows out of the noise-rock and underground scene near V16 and the SST/college-radio DIY network, opening the Seattle grunge line (X8) that would explode into mainstream alt-radio rather than feed the Core.
The commercial explosion point of the Seattle line (X8), turning underground-rock roots shared with V16 into '90s mainstream alt-radio, a path that runs parallel to rather than through the Core.
A Seattle-scene record within X8 that leans on the same classic-rock instincts as V20's Crazy Horse universe, feeding '90s alt radio rather than the Core.
A metal-leaning branch of the Seattle scene within X8, drawing on the same noise-rock underground as V16 but pushing toward hard rock rather than the Core.
A Crazy Horse-tinged outlier within X8's Seattle scene, closer in guitar tone to V20 than to punk-rooted grunge, though its commercial path still runs through '90s alt radio rather than the Core.
Loops the Seattle line back toward the noise-rock aesthetic of V16 via Albini's production, without leaving the X8 lane's mainstream alt-radio orbit.
Continues Pearl Jam's classic-rock-leaning wing of X8's Seattle scene, staying in '90s alt radio rather than crossing toward the Core.
The mainstream apex of X8's metal-leaning Seattle branch, fully embedded in '90s alt radio rather than the Core.

An earlier, vocal-forward ancestor of the shoegaze branch off V29's drone lineage; its atmosphere prefigures My Bloody Valentine and Slowdive, and Slowdive in particular have acknowledged the band as an influence.

Grows out of Velvet Underground/Jesus and Mary Chain noise-drone (the V29 line) crossed with C86 jangle; leads directly to Loveless and the entire shoegaze/dream-pop vocabulary that countrygaze borrows textures from, not toward V29's deadpan songwriting side.

Sits alongside Slowdive and Lush in the dream-pop wing of the shoegaze branch off V29; its melodic clarity influenced later dream-pop and indie-pop rather than feeding the noisier Core-adjacent lanes.

A 4AD-scene branch off V29's shoegaze lineage that keeps more jangle-pop clarity than My Bloody Valentine; its melodic guitar interplay anticipates later British indie guitar bands rather than the Core's country side.

Part of the same Creation-label shoegaze scene as My Bloody Valentine; its more melodic, jangle-inflected guitar wall seems to point toward Britpop's guitar bands rather than back toward the Core's twang.

A Thames Valley contemporary of Ride within the shoegaze branch off V29; its electronic leanings seem to point toward 90s indie-dance crossover rather than back into the Core's acoustic-and-twang lineage.

The aesthetic peak of the shoegaze branch off V29's drone lineage; its guitar-wall production sounds like a source for the noise/slowcore Context lane and, at a distance, the pedal-steel-and-fuzz textures of Core countrygaze bands like Wednesday.
Another 4AD-rooted branch off V29's shoegaze/dream-pop lineage, produced by a Cocteau Twins member; its close-harmony vocal approach echoes forward into later dream-pop and twee-adjacent indie pop.

Continues Pale Saints' branch off V29's dream-pop/shoegaze lineage with a lineup change that ties it to Lush; the record's melodic focus feeds forward into 90s British indie pop rather than back toward the Core.
Continues Ride's place in the Creation-label shoegaze scene; its arena-ready hooks show the guitar-wall aesthetic drifting toward mainstream British guitar rock rather than the DIY/Core lineage.

The tail end of Chapterhouse's branch off V29's shoegaze lineage, released as the UK press turned toward Britpop; its dance-pop instincts fed forward into 90s electronic-indie crossover rather than back toward twang.

Descends from the same C86/shoegaze branch of V29 as My Bloody Valentine but pushes toward ambient dream pop; that softer, glacial guitar tone echoes forward into slowcore and the hushed textures some countrygaze bands borrow.

Transplants the UK shoegaze branch of V29 into the Boston DIY/college-radio network; its noisy, tape-collaged version of the guitar wall sounds closer to American noise-pop and lo-fi than to the UK dream-pop line.

The most minimal extension of Slowdive's branch off V29's drone lineage, trading guitar-wall density for ambient space; anticipates the glacial, slow-build side of slowcore more than it feeds directly back toward twang.

Splits off V29's art-punk deadpan and the punk foundation of X14 into a more clipped, structurally radical post-punk; its influence runs forward through Minor Threat and Fugazi's DIY rigor rather than toward twang or country.
Continues Wire's branch off X14/V29 into more textured, synth-inflected post-punk; its atmosphere influenced the goth and art-rock wings of the genre rather than the twangier Core lineage.

The final entry in Wire's initial branch off X14/V29's post-punk lineage before a long hiatus; its polish anticipated 80s art-rock production more than the DIY roughness that fed the American noise-rock wing.

An American, Boston-scene branch off X14's punk foundation and V29's art-noise lineage; its tape-loop noise and structural aggression sound like groundwork for the noise-rock wing of X10 rather than any twang-adjacent lane.

Splits from X14's hardcore roots into a colder, drum-machine-driven noise rock distinct from Wire or Mission of Burma's more melodic post-punk; Albini's engineering work afterward directly shaped the Pixies, Nirvana and much of 90s indie production.

The endpoint of Big Black's branch off X14's punk lineage before Albini's influence shifted from performing to producing; its scorched-earth sound directly informed Shellac and the broader 90s noise-rock underground.

Grows out of X14's hardcore-punk roots (MacKaye's earlier Minor Threat) with an art-rock structural sense that recalls V29; Fugazi's DIY model became a touchstone for the independent touring network that runs into lo-fi indie and the Core.

Continues Fugazi's post-hardcore branch, with abandoned Albini sessions brushing it against the noise-rock wing of the same lane; its aggression seems to have shaped 90s post-hardcore more than any twang-adjacent lineage.
A later, more experimental branch off Fugazi's X14/V29 post-hardcore lineage; its loosened structure anticipated post-rock's use of dynamics more than it fed back toward the lane's noisier origins.
A late-career continuation of Mission of Burma's original branch off X14/V29's noise-punk lineage, with a Shellac/Big Black connection tying it to the Chicago noise-rock wing of the same lane.

A modern American continuation of the post-punk branch off X14/V29, closer to the Fall's deadpan delivery than to noise rock's abrasiveness; feeds today's post-punk revival (Idles, Shame) rather than the Core's twang.
Continues Protomartyr's modern post-punk branch off X14/V29; its political storytelling parallels Southern-gothic songwriting elsewhere in the atlas without ever crossing into twang.

Not a sonic descendant of the post-punk canon above; included in X10 because her music runs angular and punk-adjacent rather than twangy, and because she shares the Asheville scene (not the sound) with Core artists like Wednesday and MJ Lenderman.

Not a direct sonic descendant of classic post-punk; included in X10 because their noisy, angular guitar rock fits the lane's sound while their real connection to the wider atlas is scene (Burlington, VT DIY) rather than genre lineage into twang.
Extends V28's Skynyrd/Allman Southern-rock guitar lineage through a Texas outlaw-country filter, heading toward mainstream Red Dirt/Southern-rock touring circuits rather than the indie-twang Core.

Carries V28's Skynyrd/Allman/Marshall Tucker Southern-rock guitar lineage into 2010s mainstream rock and country-adjacent radio, heading toward jam-band and classic-rock revivalism rather than the punk-inflected storytelling that produced Drive-By Truckers and the Core.
Continues Whiskey Myers' branch off V28's Southern-rock lineage into a wider national touring audience, still oriented toward mainstream rock radio rather than the Core.
Continues Blackberry Smoke's branch off V28's Southern-rock lineage into commercial country-rock crossover, far from the Core's indie/DIY route.
A polished entry in Whiskey Myers' branch off V28's Southern-rock lineage, aimed at mainstream rock-radio and streaming audiences rather than the DIY/indie route.

Extends V28's Southern-rock lineage through a heavier outlaw-country filter that sounds indebted to Waylon Jennings and Skynyrd, backed by its David Allan Coe cover; closer to the Core's storytelling instincts than most of this lane but still landing in mainstream rock/Americana touring rather than indie twang.

Sounds like a blues-rock-leaning branch of V28's Southern guitar-rock lineage, indebted in particular to Allman Brothers-style slide guitar, heading toward the contemporary blues-rock circuit rather than the punk-adjacent Core.

A direct, literal continuation of V28's Allman Brothers lineage carried by the founders' own children; heads toward legacy-act jam-band touring rather than the twangier, punk-inflected Southern storytelling of the Core.
Sounds indebted to V28's Southern-rock lineage, with deepening Americana songwriting; oriented toward mainstream rock/Americana audiences rather than the Core.
A more expansive, horn-and-gospel-inflected entry in Whiskey Myers' branch off V28's Southern-rock/soul lineage, still aimed at mainstream rock audiences rather than the Core.
Continues the Allman Betts Band's direct-inheritance branch off V28, leaning further into the jam-band side of Southern rock rather than toward the Core's more compact songwriting.

A recent entry in Blackberry Smoke's ongoing branch off V28's Southern-rock lineage, produced by Dave Cobb, whose work elsewhere ties the mainstream and Americana wings of Southern music together without pulling this record into the Core.

Continues Larkin Poe's slide-guitar blues-rock, which sounds indebted to V28's Southern guitar lineage; distinct from both the boogie-rock (Blackberry Smoke) and jam-band (Allman Betts) wings of the same lane.

Made within mainstream Nashville (X1), with a plainspoken, Cosmic American-leaning songwriting voice that sounds indebted to V21; leads forward into Musgraves' own pop-crossover arc rather than toward the Core scene.

Sounds like a split from the mainstream-Nashville/Cosmic American line (X1/V21) toward adult-pop production; the branch resembles later 2020s pop-country crossovers like Cowboy Carter and F-1 Trillion rather than the indie-twang Core.

Sounds indebted to country's outlaw-and-crooner imagery (X1) filtered through the indie label system rather than the twang scene proper; his branch continues through Bronco and Stampede rather than into Core indie twang.

album: If My Wife New I'd Be Dead
lineage: Sounds indebted to mainstream country's confessional songwriting mode (X1), seen through an Irish indie-pop lens; leads onward through CMAT's own catalog rather than into the twang Core.
Continues Peck's outlaw-persona sound, which draws on mainstream country imagery (X1), into major-label pop-country territory; does not feed back into the indie-twang Core.
Continues CMAT's country-pop, which sounds indebted to mainstream country songwriting (X1), toward arena-pop scale; stays in the pop-country lane rather than joining indie twang.

album: The Land Is Inhospitable and So Are We
lineage: Sounds indebted to Americana and country folk's spare, string-backed songwriting (adjacent to X1/V21 territory), filtered through Mitski's indie-rock background; the branch stays within her own art-pop catalog rather than feeding the Core scene.

Positions itself against mainstream Nashville country (X1) and its sidelining of Black artists, drawing in elder figures like Linda Martell; the branch runs forward into pop and country radio rather than into indie twang.

Plugs directly into mainstream Nashville duet culture (X1) through its guest list, with outlaw-country signifiers that are more resemblance than lineage; leads forward into country radio rather than into the indie twang Core.
Continues CMAT's pop-country branch, which sounds indebted to mainstream country songwriting (X1); the newest data point in the trend, feeding forward rather than back toward the Core.

Formed by David Crosby (the Byrds), Stephen Stills (Buffalo Springfield) and Graham Nash (the Hollies), directly linking it to the folk-rock lineage behind V21, with Young's later arrival tying it to V20; this harmony branch leads into the LA soft-rock mainstream rather than the twangier Core sound.

Runs parallel to the Laurel Canyon songwriter scene (V21/V22-adjacent) rather than descending from country rock; his documented ties are to Randy Newman, whose songs he recorded on Nilsson Sings Newman, and to the Beatles, and the branch leads into orchestral pop rather than toward the Core.

Sounds rooted in the folk-revival songwriting that also fed Cosmic American Music (V21) and Dylan/The Band's roots turn (V22); its confessional line runs forward into mainstream singer-songwriter pop rather than into the twang-scene Core.

Splits directly from the Cosmic American Music/country-rock lineage (V21) through shared members from the Flying Burrito Brothers and Poco, trading V21's rawer twang for tighter pop songcraft; leads forward into the soft-rock mainstream rather than the Core.

Browne co-wrote the Eagles' 'Take It Easy', tying him to the same LA country-rock circle (V21) as the Eagles and Linda Ronstadt; his own records stay within the soft-rock singer-songwriter mainstream rather than crossing into twangier Core territory.
Continues Mitchell's folk-rock songwriting, rooted in V21/V22-adjacent traditions, toward jazz-pop sophistication; sounds closer to the smoothed-out LA session sound than to country rock's twang.

Tied to V21's country-rock network: Glenn Frey and Don Henley played in Ronstadt's backing band before forming the Eagles; her interpretive, hit-single approach leads into mainstream pop-country rather than the twang Core.
Completes the Eagles' drift away from V21's Cosmic American Music twang toward mainstream arena rock; the branch ends here rather than feeding back into the Core scene.
Continues Browne's Laurel Canyon songwriting, close to the Cosmic American circle (V21), into fuller studio-pop arrangements; sounds firmly of the soft-rock mainstream rather than the Core.

Extends Mitchell's folk-rock songwriting (V21/V22-adjacent) into jazz-fusion territory; a dead end for country-rock purposes, though its drifting art-folk sound is echoed by later songwriters outside the Core.
Extends Browne's Laurel Canyon songwriting (V21-adjacent) into a road-diary live format; stays outside the Core twang scene.
Continues Ronstadt's covers-based country rock, rooted in the V21 scene; sounds squarely of the mainstream pop-country lane rather than feeding the Core.

Its deadpan drone and deliberate amateurism sound indebted to the Velvet Underground and proto-indie scene (V29); this branch runs forward into hardcore, cowpunk and the college-rock underground rather than continuing V29's own art-rock line.
Continues the Ramones' minimalism, which sounds indebted to Velvet Underground deadpan (V29), toward the hardcore and DIY scenes that followed; not part of V29's own art-rock trajectory.
Extends the Ramones' minimalist sound, indebted to V29's deadpan simplicity, with stronger pop hooks, feeding forward into power pop and the DIY underground rather than back into V29's own catalog.
Represents the UK punk scene running alongside this lane's American hardcore lineage; its rockabilly-and-reggae blending resembles what cowpunk and LA roots punk (V14) would do next.

Grows directly out of the same Hermosa Beach/LA hardcore scene as Black Flag (a former member founded the band); feeds the American hardcore underground (V16) and DIY network rather than back into earlier NY punk.

Runs parallel to Black Flag's Southern California hardcore; Biafra's own Alternative Tentacles label ties the band to the American hardcore underground (V16) and the broader DIY network rather than back toward V29.

Takes the punk template of peers like the Ramones into a harder, more nihilistic hardcore sound; as the flagship band of Ginn's SST label it feeds directly into the SST/college-rock underground (V16) rather than back toward V29.

The band's DC shows helped ignite the local hardcore scene that produced Minor Threat; it feeds into the American hardcore underground (V16) and later crossover thrash rather than back toward V29's art-rock roots.

Splits from Black Flag's own faster hardcore template (this lane) into slow, sludgy tempos that anticipate noise rock and slowcore textures; feeds forward into SST's own stranger later catalog and indirectly into post-punk/noise rock (X10) rather than back to the Core.

Came out of the DC hardcore scene that Bad Brains had ignited; through MacKaye's own Dischord label it feeds directly into the DIY-label model and the American underground/college rock scene (V16) rather than back toward earlier UK or NY punk.
